ymir.fullDescription: In the yawning void called Ginnungagap, where the heat of Muspellheim met the killing ice of Niflheim, the first life stirred. From melting rime rose Ymir (also named Aurgelmir; the name's two members remain open between clay, gravel, barley or sheaf and roarer or similar, not a settled "clay-roarer") neither fully god nor fully giant, but the wet, roaring beginning of both.
ymir.mysteryNote: Some say the surviving giants still taste his blood in every sea. When the tide runs red at sunset, listen: that is not only the sun.
ymir.fate: Killed by Odin, Vili and Vé; the world was built from his corpse.

sections.story:
The Norse cosmos does not begin with a maker. It begins with a gap.

Ginnungagap lay between Muspellheim's fire and the killing ice of Niflheim, and where the two met the rime began to drip. From that meltwater rose Ymir, called Aurgelmir in the older poems, neither god nor giant but the wet, roaring precondition of both. The primeval cow Auðumbla licked the salt-rime for nourishment and fed him; from his sweat, under his arm, a man and a woman took shape, and from his legs a six-headed son. The jötunn line was established before the gods had names.

He was killed by his own descendants. Odin, Vili and Vé (sons of Borr and the giantess Bestla, and so Ymir's own kin) struck him down. His blood came out as a flood, and it drowned very nearly all the frost-giants. Only Bergelmir escaped with his household, aboard something the sources will not agree on: a hollowed log, a chest, a mill-frame. Every later giant in the North descends from that one survivor.

Then the brothers built the world from the corpse. Flesh became earth; bone became mountain; teeth and jaw-shards became scree and stone. The blood was poured out as sea and lake. The skull was raised as the sky's vault and set on four dwarfs at the corners, named for the compass. The brains were thrown up as cloud. The maggots that had bred in the dead flesh were given wit and shape, and became the dwarfs.

This is not decoration. It is a cosmology in which the ground is a body, and every ridge you walk is a piece of someone the gods murdered.
sections.origins:
The account survives in two thirteenth-century Icelandic compilations of much older material.

Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda gives the fullest narrative version in Gylfaginning, where the world's construction from the body is laid out piece by piece. Snorri was a Christian writing around 1220, some two centuries after Iceland's conversion, and he is systematising traditions that reached him already fragmented: a point worth holding onto, because his tidiness is partly his own.

The Poetic Edda preserves the older, stranger layer. Vafþrúðnismál has Odin and the giant Vafþrúðnir trade cosmological riddles, and it is there that Ymir's other name, Aurgelmir, and the detail of Bergelmir's escape appear. Grímnismál gives the body-to-world correspondences in compressed verse form. These poems are undated and probably circulated orally for a long time before anyone wrote them down.

The two sources do not fully agree, and Snorri appears at points to be reading the poems much as we do: as an inheritor working out what they meant.
sections.disputed:
What Bergelmir escaped in is genuinely unresolved. The Old Norse phrase á lúðr has been read as a chest, a hollowed trunk, a boat, a cradle and a mill-box; each reading pulls the episode in a different direction, and the flood-and-ark resemblance that some scholars have drawn to Near Eastern material depends heavily on which one you pick.

Whether that resemblance means anything at all is contested. It may be inherited, it may be borrowed, it may be Snorri's Christian formation showing through, or the pattern may simply be one that many flood traditions arrive at independently.

The relationship between Ymir and Aurgelmir is also not settled: one being under two names, or two beings that merged before the poems were fixed.

chain.claim: Ymir's name means "Scream": the primordial scream in the void, so that the giant out of whose body the Norse world was built is named for the sound of the beginning.
chain.verdict: The Old Norse texts that name Ymir give the name and one alternative name for him and do not say what either means; the reading "Scream" is a modern argument about what a medieval audience would have heard in the word, published in 2003 and picked up from there.

rungs.witness: The article Ymir on norse-mythology.org (Norse Mythology for Smart People)
rungs.date: Undated web page, consulted 8 August 2026; it cannot predate the 2003 paper it cites
rungs.reads: This is where the claim reaches general readers in the form the catalogue has it. The article opens: Ymir (pronounced "EE-meer;" Old Norse Ymir, "Scream"[1]) is a hermaphroditic giant and the first creature to come into being in the Norse creation narrative. Footnote 1 is Kure 2003, pages 311 to 319. The gloss is presented flat, as the meaning of the name, with none of Kure's hedging about audience association versus derivation, and with no mention of the twin etymology that Kure himself concedes is the accepted one.
rungs.evidence: https://norse-mythology.org/gods-and-creatures/giants/ymir/. The opening line is quoted as it stands on the page, and the reference list at the foot of the article gives Kure, Henning. 2003. In the Beginning Was the Scream ... Edited by Rudolf Simek and Judith Meurer. p. 311-319 as the source for the gloss. The article's author is not named on the page; he identifies himself there as the author of The Love of Destiny.
rungs.note: This page is the top general-web result for Ymir's etymology, which is the likely route by which a one-word gloss became a catalogue fact.

rungs.witness: Guus Kroonen, Etymological Dictionary of Proto-Germanic (Leiden Indo-European Etymological Dictionary Series 11; Leiden: Brill, 2013), page 274, lemma *jumja-
rungs.reads: It sets up the twin derivation as the standard reconstruction: Old Norse Ymir from Proto-Germanic *jumjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ym-yo- beside *yemH-, with an original sense of twin, comparanda being Sanskrit yama and Latin Remus. It offers no noise etymology.
rungs.evidence: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Ymir, whose Old Norse etymology cites Kroonen 2013 at page 274 under *jumja- for this reconstruction, and whose reference list gives the full series and publisher. The same entry adds that the name has been folk-etymologically connected to Old Norse ymja and points to the homonym ymir meaning hawk, literally groaner or screamer, citing Elena Gurevich's edition of the Anonymous Thulur, Jotna heiti I, in Poetry from Treatises on Poetics (Skaldic Poetry of the Scandinavian Middle Ages 3, Brepols, 2017), page 707.
rungs.note: Second-hand: the printed Brill page was not consulted, and Brill's site is not reachable from this session. The Gurevich note is third-hand and is not being used as a rung of its own.

rungs.witness: Henning Kure, In the beginning was the Scream: Conceptual thought in the Old Norse myth of creation, in Rudolf Simek and Judith Meurer (eds.), Scandinavia and Christian Europe in the Middle Ages: Papers of the 12th International Saga Conference, Bonn 2003, pages 311 to 319
rungs.reads: This is the scholarly source that the scream reading is actually resting on, and its argument is narrower than the claim. Kure writes: The immediate association to the name Ymir would be the noun ymr 'scream, noisy sound'. His case is about what an Old Norse audience would have heard, not about historical derivation: he grants that the twin etymology has been generally accepted by scholars since it was first proposed by Hermann Guentert, and objects that an audience could not have deduced that meaning without modern comparative philology. So the paper argues for the scream as the working sense of the name for its hearers, while conceding the field to the other etymology.
rungs.evidence: https://www.academia.edu/8766740/In_the_beginning_was_the_Scream_Conceptual_thought_in_the_Old_Norse_myth_of_creation for the paper's text and its abstract, which says the meaning of Ymir's name in conjunction with new interpretations of Ginnungagap and the Old Norse word yppa adds layers to the myth. The sentence about ymr was returned identically on two separate reads of that page. Venue, editors, place and year confirmed at http://sagaconference.org/SC12/SC12.html, the archive of the Twelfth International Saga Conference, Bonn 2003, edited by Rudolf Simek and Judith Meurer, where Kure's paper appears in the contents.
rungs.note: The conference archive lists the paper with a slightly different subtitle from the one on the author's own posting. Guentert's book is Der arische Weltkoenig und Heiland (Halle: Niemeyer, 1923); I confirmed the book exists but did not see its pages on Ymir, so the attribution here is Kure's, reported as his.

rungs.witness: Rudolf Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, English translation by Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), entry Ymir
rungs.date: 1993, translating the German Lexikon der germanischen Mythologie; cited by one of the sources below in a 1995 printing at page 485
rungs.reads: It derives the name from a word for twin, not from a word for sound. Two independent sources citing this entry give the same derivation: from Indo-European *iemo-, glossed twin and hermaphrodite, with Sanskrit Yama and the Latin Gemini as comparanda. Nothing in either citation mentions scream, roar or noise.
rungs.evidence: https://www.nordicnames.de/wiki/Ymir attributes to Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993) the derivation from Indo-Germanic *iemo- meaning twin, hermaphrodite, and separately attributes a derivation from Old Norse ymja, to whine, to cry, to Gulbrand Alhaug's Norwegian name lexicon of 2011. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuisto cites Simek at page 485 for Ymir from Proto-Indo-European *iemo-, twin or double.
rungs.note: Second-hand. I did not see Simek's printed page this session, only two independent works citing it to the same effect. Treat the wording as reported rather than quoted.

rungs.witness: Jan de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Woerterbuch, page 678a, as indexed in Gerhard Koebler's Altnordisches Woerterbuch
rungs.date: De Vries's dictionary in its second revised edition, Leiden: Brill, 1977. Koebler's index is a later online reference work; I read the index, not de Vries's printed page.
rungs.reads: It splits the word in two. Koebler's index records, both referred to de Vries page 678a: Ymir (1), an., M.: nhd. Urriese, with no cross-reference to any noise-word; and Ymir (2), an., M.: nhd. Laermer, Habicht; Hw.: s. ymja, that is a second Ymir meaning noise-maker and used as a name for the hawk, expressly cross-referred to the verb ymja. Alongside these stand ymja, sw. V., schreien, jammern, and ymr, st. M., Laerm. So a noise-formation Ymir does exist in Old Norse, and in this lexicography it is the bird, while the primeval giant is a separate lemma carrying no such link.
rungs.evidence: https://www.koeblergerhard.de/an/an_y.html, entries Ymir (1), Ymir (2), ymja and ymr, quoted above in Koebler's abbreviated German. Vr 678a is Koebler's siglum for de Vries's page. De Vries's own wording on that page was not seen this session.
rungs.note: This is the single most useful rung and also the one most easily misread. It does not say the noise reading is impossible. It says a noise-derived Ymir is attested for something else.

rungs.witness: Richard Cleasby and Gudbrand Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1874), page 726
rungs.reads: It confirms that the noise-words exist in Old Norse and it does not attach them to the giant. The page carries YMJA, glossed to whine, cry and to echo, resound, with the note that the present tense is ym, ymr; and ymr, m., glossed a humming sound, with citations from Helgakvida Hundingsbana, Atlakvida and Fornmanna sogur. It also carries ymta, to mutter, and ymtr, a muttering. The page runs from ylgja to YRKJA and includes proper names such as Yngvi, Yngvi-Freyr and Yrjar, but there is no headword Ymir on it. So the raw material for a noise reading is in the language, and the dictionary does not apply it to the giant.
rungs.evidence: http://lexicon.ff.cuni.cz/html/oi_cleasbyvigfusson/b0726.html, the digitised Cleasby-Vigfusson at the Charles University lexicon server. I asked for the full list of headwords on the page and read the YMJA and YMR entries as printed. Publication details confirmed against dealer and library records returned for the 1874 Clarendon Press first edition.
rungs.note: The gloss on ymr in this dictionary is a humming sound, and on ymja to whine, cry. Those are quieter English words than scream.

rungs.witness: The eddic poems Voluspa, Vafthrudnismal and Grimnismal, preserved in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, shelfmark GKS 2365 4to
rungs.date: Manuscript written in Iceland in the 1270s, now in the Arni Magnusson Institute for Icelandic Studies. The poems themselves are undated and may be considerably older. The text read here is Edward Pettit's edition and translation, The Poetic Edda: A Dual-Language Edition (Cambridge: Open Book Publishers, 2023), not the manuscript itself.
rungs.reads: The poems use the name repeatedly and never unpack it. Voluspa 3 opens Ar var alda, thar er Ymir bygdi. Vafthrudnismal 21 begins Or Ymis holdi var jord um skopud. Vafthrudnismal 28 to 31 run the Aurgelmir genealogy and ask hvadan Aurgelmir kom med jotna sonum fyrst, and the answer is about venom-drops from Elivagar, not about a name. On what the word Ymir means the poems are silent.
rungs.evidence: https://books.openbookpublishers.com/10.11647/obp.0308/ch1.xhtml for Voluspa 3 and https://books.openbookpublishers.com/10.11647/obp.0308/ch3.xhtml for Vafthrudnismal 21 and 28 to 31, both in Pettit's Old Norse text with facing translation. Pettit's footnote to Vafthrudnismal 29 glosses the -gelmir names as possibly 'Sheaf' or 'Roarer' compounds and cites R. D. Fulk's 1989 article in the Review of English Studies; he attaches no comparable etymological footnote to Ymir. Shelfmark, repository and 1270s dating taken from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Regius after handrit.is returned a 403.
rungs.note: Vafthrudnismal is also partly preserved in AM 748 I 4to. I did not consult that manuscript or its readings for these stanzas.

rungs.witness: Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning, chapter 5 (Upphaf Ymis ok hrimthursa)
rungs.date: Composed in Iceland about 1220. Not an object of that date: it survives in fourteenth-century and later Icelandic manuscripts, and the text read here is Gudni Jonsson's printed edition in digital form.
rungs.reads: It introduces the figure and supplies a second name, and it glosses neither. The sentence read was: ok vard manns likandi, ok var sa nefndr Ymir, en hrimthursar kalla hann Aurgelmi. Snorri elsewhere in the Edda is fond of explaining names, and at this point he explains nothing: he reports what the frost-giants call him and moves on to the cow Audumla. There is no scream, no noise and no etymology in the passage.
rungs.evidence: https://norroen.info/src/snorra/gj/2.html (Edda Snorra Sturlusonar, Gudni Jonsson's edition, chapter 5). The passage naming Ymir and Aurgelmir reads as transcribed above. Checked the surrounding chapters for any gloss of the name Ymir and found none.
rungs.note: Composition date and manuscript date are different things here. The catalogue entry is right to call the Prose Edda a thirteenth-century compilation, but the parchment we read it from is later.

chain.floor: Gylfaginning and the Codex Regius poems give the name Ymir and the frost-giants' name Aurgelmir, and offer no meaning for either; Snorri, who explains names elsewhere, does not explain this one. What survives underneath the claim is a real Old Norse word-family for sound, ymja to whine or cry and ymr a humming sound, and a separate attested Ymir meaning noise-maker that is a name for the hawk. Against that, the reference dictionaries consulted here derive the giant's name from a word for twin. The scream reading is a scholarly argument of 2003 about what medieval hearers would have associated with the name, not a gloss recovered from a medieval text, and it lost a good deal of its hedging on the way into popular circulation.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The Yemo/Manu complex
scholarlyNotes.body:
Ymir is one of the clearest surviving examples of a shared Indo-European root myth. Bruce Lincoln's work on the reconstructed *Yemo/*Manu complex traces a consistent pattern across Indo-European traditions: a primordial twin (*Yemo, "twin") is sacrificed by his brother (*Manu, "man") to build the world from his body. Ymir, killed by Odin, Vili, and Vé, and the Vedic Purusha, dismembered by the gods in the Rigveda's Purusha Sukta, are two of the best preserved branches of that same root myth. A possible third branch survives in the Roman legend of Remus.

The Mesopotamian creation myth in the Enuma Elish, where Marduk kills Tiamat and splits her corpse into sky and earth, follows the same "world built from a slain primordial body" pattern but is not part of this lineage. Akkadian and Babylonian traditions sit outside the Indo-European language family entirely, so the resemblance is convergent, not inherited. Separate cultures appear to have arrived at the same narrative solution independently, which arguably makes the pattern more interesting than a single shared origin would.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Etymology: twin, not scream
scholarlyNotes.body: Ymir's name is sometimes glossed as related to a word for "scream" or "roar," but this is not the mainstream philological reading. The more widely accepted etymology derives Ymir from Proto-Germanic *jumjaz, "twin," the same root reconstructed for *Yemo above, and cognate with the Vedic Yama and Avestan Yima, both twins in their respective traditions. The "scream" reading appears in some older scholarship but has not held up as the primary etymology.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Not simply a frost giant
scholarlyNotes.body: Ymir is conventionally described as a frost giant, but this framing may oversimplify the textual evidence. Ymir carries the alternate names Aurgelmir, Brimir, and Bláinn. Brimir in particular has been read as pointing toward brim, "surf" or "sea," rather than ice specifically, a reading noted in Edward Pettit's translation and commentary on the Poetic Edda. If Brimir and Bláinn point toward sea and stone rather than ice, the opposition sometimes drawn between Ymir and Surtr may be better described as "the sea and stone that predate order" against "the fire that ends it," rather than a clean ice-versus-fire binary. This fits Ymir's origin point in the Eddas: he rises from meltwater in Ginnungagap, a liminal, transitional substance rather than ice in a settled state.

scholarlySources: Bruce Lincoln, Death, War, and Sacrifice (Indo-European comparative mythology)
Edward Pettit, translation and commentary on the Poetic Edda
Prose Edda, Gylfaginning

handling.living: Modern heathenry (Ásatrú and related revivalist movements, including bodies like Iceland's state-recognized Ásatrúarfélagið) does draw on Ymir and the Eddas as scripture-adjacent material, but this is a modern, public, non-restrictive revival of a medieval literary corpus rather than an unbroken living faith with custodial authority over the myth. No community holds gatekeeping claims on the story the way a still-practising Indigenous tradition would; the Eddas have been open texts for scholarly and creative use for over a century.
handling.distortions: Popular retellings routinely turn Ymir into a straightforward villain slain by a heroic Odin, flattening a cosmology that is really about the gods committing kin-murder against their own ancestor to build the world from his corpse. A second common mangling harmonizes Snorri's tidy Prose Edda narrative with the stranger, contradictory Poetic Edda material (the unresolved Ymir/Aurgelmir identity, the ambiguous á lúðr vessel) into one clean origin story, erasing the genuine textual disagreement between sources written roughly two centuries after Iceland's conversion.
handling.take: This is freely usable public-domain material: the birth from Ginnungagap's meltwater, Auðumbla's licking, the murder by Odin, Vili and Vé, and the body-becomes-world construction are all fair game for direct adaptation. Be honest in a fiction or nonfiction context that Snorri Sturluson (writing c. 1220, two centuries post-conversion) is a systematizing Christian redactor, not a neutral transcriber, so his tidy version and the older, rougher Poetic Edda poems (Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál) can be blended or presented as alternatives, but shouldn't be silently harmonized as though there were one settled canonical account. Avoid asserting the Near Eastern flood-parallel (Bergelmir's escape) as proven borrowing; the scholarship treats it as unresolved.
handling.cite: Credit Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning, c. 1220) for the narrative version and the Poetic Edda's Vafþrúðnismál and Grímnismál for the older poetic layer; both are long in the public domain in multiple translations.

nephilim.fullDescription: The Nephilim appear in Genesis in three verses and are never explained. They are on the earth before the flood, born after the sons of God go in to the daughters of men, and the text calls them the mighty men of old, men of renown.
nephilim.mysteryNote: The text never measures them. That silence has filled libraries, and more than one forged photograph.
nephilim.fate: No fate is recorded: the text moves to the flood without one.

sections.story:
Genesis 6:1-4 is one of the strangest passages in the Hebrew Bible, partly because of what it says and mostly because of how quickly it stops saying it.

The sons of God see that the daughters of men are fair and take wives from among them. The Nephilim are on the earth in those days, and also afterward. The verses sit immediately before God's decision to destroy the world by flood, and the connection is implied but never stated.

Then the text moves on. No genealogy, no episode, no explanation of what the Nephilim were or what they did. The whole thing is four verses and it reads like a fragment of something much larger that the compiler either did not know or chose not to include.

The word itself is not translated. Nephilim is usually connected to the Hebrew root n-p-l, to fall, giving "the fallen ones": though whether that means fallen in status, fallen from heaven, or those who cause others to fall is not determinable from the word alone. The Septuagint translators rendered it gigantes, giants, and that decision shaped two thousand years of reading.

They reappear once, in Numbers 13:33, when the spies sent into Canaan report seeing the Nephilim and say that they seemed like grasshoppers beside them. This is a bad report given by frightened men, and the text frames it as such, but it establishes the image that stuck.

Later Jewish tradition, particularly the Book of Enoch, filled the silence with an enormous amount of material: named angels, taught forbidden knowledge, monstrous offspring, and a war in heaven.
sections.origins:
Genesis 6:1-4 and Numbers 13:33 are the whole of the biblical material.

The Book of Enoch, a non-canonical Jewish work whose earliest sections date from roughly the third to first centuries BCE, is the major expansion. Its Watchers narrative names the angels who descended, describes their teaching of metallurgy, cosmetics and sorcery, and makes their offspring devouring giants. Fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, confirming its currency in the Second Temple period.

The Book of Jubilees covers similar ground. The Septuagint's choice of gigantes carried the giant reading into Greek and then Latin Christianity.

Josephus, in Antiquities of the Jews I.3.1, refers to the tradition of angels who consorted with women and begat unjust sons, comparing them to those "whom the Grecians call Giants." The bones "still shown to this very day" are elsewhere: Antiquities V.2.3 (5.125), on the taking of Hebron, where he describes the race of giants and their remains.
sections.disputed:
What the sons of God are is the central unresolved question. The three main readings (divine or angelic beings, the righteous line of Seth intermarrying with the line of Cain, or dynastic rulers claiming divine descent) have each been the majority view at different periods, and the Hebrew supports all three.

Whether the Nephilim are the offspring of that union or simply present at the same time is grammatically ambiguous in the Hebrew. Most translations imply causation the text does not clearly state.

"And also afterward" in Genesis 6:4 is a genuine problem, since it appears to place them after a flood that killed everything. Explanations range from a second incursion to an editorial insertion harmonising with Numbers 13.

Modern claims that giant skeletons confirm the Nephilim are a distinct phenomenon with no scholarly standing. They rest on misidentified fossils, hoaxes and doctored photographs; no verified remains exist.

chain.claim: The nephilim of Genesis 6 were giants: enormous hybrid offspring born when the sons of God took human wives, whose kind the Israelite spies later saw and felt like grasshoppers beside.
chain.verdict: The giant reading is genuinely ancient and continuously attested, but it travels on translation and on expansion literature rather than on the wording of the Hebrew verse.

rungs.witness: Brian R. Doak, 'The Embarrassing and Alluring Biblical Giant', Bible and Interpretation, University of Arizona
rungs.date: December 2015
rungs.reads: Doak takes Genesis 6:1-4 as the parade example of biblical giants, and states that 'the exact size of the "Nephilim" does not appear in the passage'. He observes that giant stature has almost always been assumed, with Numbers 13:33 supplying the biblical support for it, and notes that 4QSam-a and the ancient Greek versions cut Goliath's height sharply against the Masoretic figure.
rungs.evidence: https://bibleinterp.arizona.edu/node/3280 returned the article by Brian R. Doak of George Fox University, dated December 2015, containing the sentence quoted above and the Numbers 13:33 and Goliath points.
rungs.note: A current specialist stating that the size is absent from the Genesis passage itself.

rungs.witness: Rashi, commentary on Genesis 6:4
rungs.date: northern France, about 1100 CE
rungs.reads: Rashi derives the name from the root n-p-l, saying they fell and caused the world to fall, and also records that the word denotes giants, citing Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer and Targum Yonatan. A medieval Jewish commentator therefore holds the etymology and the giant sense together rather than choosing between them.
rungs.evidence: https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/8171/showrashi/true returned the Hebrew of Gen 6:4 and Rashi's gloss, giving both the fell / caused to fall derivation and the statement that in Hebrew the word means giants, with the citations to Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer and Targum Jonathan.
rungs.note: Consulted in an online edition with English rendering, so the gloss is summarised rather than quoted.

rungs.witness: Leningrad Codex (Firkovich B 19 A), Hebrew Bible
rungs.date: colophon dates it to 1008 or 1009 CE, Cairo
rungs.reads: Carries the Masoretic Hebrew of Genesis 6:4: han-nephilim, then ham-gibborim, then anshei hash-shem, men of the name. The verse has no word meaning tall, huge or of great stature. Numbers 13:33 in the same tradition has han-nephilim twice and the comparison ka-chagavim, like grasshoppers, which is where size enters, inside a report the surrounding narrative frames as a bad one.
rungs.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_Codex gives the colophon date of AD 1008 or 1009 and Cairo. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleppo_Codex states the surviving Aleppo text begins with the last word of Deuteronomy 28:17, so it cannot supply Genesis. https://biblehub.com/interlinear/genesis/6-4.htm listed every word of Gen 6:4 with gloss and contained no term for height. https://biblehub.com/interlinear/numbers/13-33.htm listed han-nephilim twice and ka-chagavim. https://bible.streetwitnessing.org/dead-sea-scrolls-dss/torah-dss/genesis-dss records 6Q1 PaleoGenesis as containing Genesis 6:13-21 and shows Genesis 6:1-4 among no listed scroll; https://lexicon.qumran-digital.org/transcriptions/6Q1/2024-04-29/index.html confirms 6Q1 preserves 6:13-21.
rungs.note: For the Hebrew wording of this verse the surviving copies are medieval, because Genesis 6:1-4 is not among the Genesis passages recovered at Qumran.

rungs.witness: Codex Panopolitanus, the Akhmim Greek fragments of 1 Enoch
rungs.date: sixth century CE papyri, recovered at Akhmim in Egypt and published in 1892
rungs.reads: Contains portions of 1 Enoch chapters 1 to 32 in Greek, the span that holds the watchers narrative and the birth of the giants. It shows the Enochic giants tradition circulating in Greek in Christian Egypt. The complete text of 1 Enoch survives in Ethiopic copies of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and later.
rungs.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Enoch describes 'fragments of two 6th-century papyri containing portions of chapters 1-32 recovered by a French archeological team at Akhmim in Egypt and published five years later, in 1892', and dates the earliest Ethiopic manuscripts to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, naming the fifteenth-century Kebran Gabre'el Lake Tana MS. 9. It also quotes the Charles translation of 1 Enoch 7: 'And they became pregnant, and they bare great giants'.
rungs.note: I did not inspect the Greek of chapter 7 in this manuscript, only its stated chapter range, so no Greek is quoted from it here. The giants' height figure differs between the Ethiopic and Greek traditions, which is why no number appears in this ladder.

rungs.witness: Codex Alexandrinus, Greek Bible
rungs.date: fifth century CE
rungs.reads: A physical copy in which Greek Genesis 6 survives, and therefore an object that carries the gigantes wording. Its recorded Genesis defects are 1:20-25, 1:29-2:3, 14:14-17, 15:1-5, 15:16-19 and 16:6-9, so chapter 6 is not among the losses. Codex Vaticanus cannot serve here because its Genesis is lost as far as 46:28.
rungs.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Alexandrinus gives the fifth-century date and lists exactly those Genesis lacunae, with chapter 6 absent from the list. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Genesis states that Papyrus 911 matters textually 'due to the lacuna of Gen. 1:1-46:28a in Vaticanus'.
rungs.note: Roughly seven centuries separate the Greek translation from this copy of it.

rungs.witness: Jerome, Vulgate, Genesis 6:4
rungs.date: translated about 400 CE
rungs.reads: 'Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis'. Latin Christianity took the giant reading from the Greek. Jerome did not push it through the whole verse: the second Hebrew term becomes 'potentes a saeculo viri famosi', mighty men of old, men of renown, where the Septuagint had repeated gigantes.
rungs.evidence: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%206%3A1-4&version=VULGATE returned 'Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis: postquam enim ingressi sunt filii Dei ad filias hominum, illaeque genuerunt, isti sunt potentes a saeculo viri famosi.' The same Latin appeared independently at https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/jvl/genesis/6-4.html. Schmid Pfaendler (link above) makes the point that Jerome used gigantes at 6,4a but rendered the giborim phrase as 'potentes a saeculo viri famosi'.
rungs.note: I did not verify which surviving Latin manuscript carries this verse, so no shelfmark is claimed.

rungs.witness: Aquila and Symmachus at Genesis 6:4, as documented by Brigitta Schmid Pfaendler (2018)
rungs.date: Aquila about 130 CE, Symmachus later in the second century; their readings survive as Hexaplaric citations rather than as continuous manuscripts. Reported in Vulgata in Dialogue 2 (2018) 15-30
rungs.reads: Two Jewish Greek revisers declined the Septuagint's word. Schmid Pfaendler writes: 'Symmachus, der mit οἱ βίαιοι (die Gewalttaetigen) wohl eher das Gewaltpotential der Machthabenden hervorhebt und Aquila, der mit οἱ ἐπιπίπτοντες (die "Gefallenen", "Ueberfallenden") der anderen Konnotation aus der Wurzel נפל den Vorzug gibt.' Symmachus gives 'the violent ones', Aquila 'the fallen ones' or 'those who fall upon'. The same article records that Theodotion kept gigantes. Within Greek-reading Judaism the giant rendering was therefore contested.
rungs.evidence: https://vulgata-dialog.ch/ojs/index.php/vidbor/article/download/31/21/99 gave the author as Brigitta Schmid Pfaendler, the title 'Uebersetzungsvarianten der Schluesselbegriffe in Gen 6,4: Wie fuegen sich die Gigantes aus Genesis 6,1-4 in den Kontext der Hebraeischen Bibel?', Vulgata in Dialogue 2 (2018) 15-30, and the German sentence quoted above with the Greek forms. The same content was returned independently from https://jeac.de/ojs/index.php/vidbor/article/download/31/21, which also reported Theodotion's gigantes and Jerome's renderings.
rungs.note: Kind is scholarship, not manuscript: I verified these readings in a peer-reviewed journal article, not in Hexaplaric marginalia or in Field's edition. German umlauts are transliterated here.

rungs.witness: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 1.3.1, with 5.2.3
rungs.date: written about 93 to 94 CE; the Greek copies are eleventh century and later, and a Latin version was commissioned by Cassiodorus in the fifth or sixth century
rungs.reads: At 1.3.1, in Whiston's translation: 'For many angels of God accompanied with women, and begat sons that proved unjust, and despisers of all that was good, on account of the confidence they had in their own strength; for the tradition is, that these men did what resembled the acts of those whom the Grecians call giants.' Josephus reports a comparison with the Greek gigantes and emphasises strength and confidence rather than height. Separately at 5.2.3, about Hebron after Joshua's death: 'There were till then left the race of giants; who had bodies so large, and countenances so intirely different from other men, that they were surprising to the sight, and terrible to the hearing. The bones of these men are still shewn to this very day; unlike to any credible relations of other men.'
rungs.evidence: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/2848/2848-h/2848-h.htm returned the 1.3.1 sentence quoted above. https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/ant-5.html returned the 5.2.3 passage quoted above with the chapter and section reference. https://www.tertullian.org/rpearse/manuscripts/josephus_antiquities.htm lists the Greek copies of books 1 to 10: Vienna Codex Vindobonensis II. A 19 and Paris Codex Parisinus Graecus 1419 in the eleventh century, Venice Marcianus Gr. 381 in the thirteenth, Paris Codex Regius and Florence Laurentianus plut. lxix. 20 in the fourteenth, Oxford Bodleian miscell. graec. 186 in the fifteenth, and records the Latin version made by order of Cassiodorus.
rungs.note: There is no first-century object here. The gap between writing and surviving Greek copy is roughly a thousand years.

rungs.witness: Book of Jubilees 7:22
rungs.date: composed about 160 to 150 BCE; Hebrew fragments at Qumran, complete Ge'ez copies from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries
rungs.reads: In Charles's English the verse runs 'And they begat sons the Naphidim, and they were all unlike, and they devoured one another: and the Giants slew the Naphil, and the Naphil slew the Eljo, and the Eljo mankind, and one man another.' Jubilees supports a giants tradition attached to the watchers, but at this verse it sets Giants and Naphil side by side as distinct groups rather than simply identifying the two.
rungs.evidence: https://www.pseudepigrapha.com/jubilees/7.htm returned the sentence quoted above. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Jubilees gives the 160-150 BCE composition range, about fifteen Qumran Hebrew scrolls, and four Ge'ez copies of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries as the complete witnesses.
rungs.note: I checked an English translation, not the Ge'ez, and I did not establish that any Qumran Hebrew fragment preserves this particular verse.

rungs.witness: 4Q201 (4QEn-a), Aramaic Book of the Watchers, Qumran Cave 4
rungs.date: copy assigned palaeographically to the early second century BCE
rungs.reads: Does not use the word nephilim and does not comment on Genesis. It retells the Genesis 6 situation: the watchers descend, take wives, and the women conceive and bear offspring. The editors' text at that point reads 'And they became pregnant by them and bo[re giants]', with the bracket marking a restoration. So the tradition that the Genesis 6 union produced giants is attached to a physical object of this date, but the word 'giants' at that exact line is reconstructed rather than legible.
rungs.evidence: https://ms.fortresspress.com/downloads/9781451490329_Chapter%202%20excerpt.pdf lists the fragments of 4QEn-a as 1.1-6; 2.1-5.6; 6.4-8.1; 8.3-9.3, 6-8; 10.3-4; 10.21-11.1; 12.4-6, which brackets 1 Enoch 7, and dates 4QEn-a to the early second century BCE and 4QEn-b to the mid second century on Milik's palaeography. https://intertextual.bible/text/1-enoch-7.1-4q201-1 prints the fragment line quoted above. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Enoch dates the oldest Book of the Watchers fragments to 200-150 BC. https://sethlsanders.wordpress.com/2022/03/09/how-old-are-the-books-of-enoch/ reports Drawnel (2019) at late third or early second century BCE and Langlois (2008) at second century BCE, and argues against treating such datings as precise.
rungs.note: This is the load-bearing early rung: an object, not a reconstruction from later copies.

rungs.witness: Septuagint, Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33
rungs.date: Pentateuch translated into Greek in Alexandria in the third century BCE; the copies carrying these verses are centuries later
rungs.reads: Puts gigantes where the Hebrew has nephilim. Genesis 6:4 opens 'οἱ δὲ γίγαντες ἦσαν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις' and uses the same Greek word again later in the verse for the Hebrew gibborim, so two different Hebrew words are flattened into one Greek one. Numbers 13:33 reads 'καὶ ἐκεῖ ἑωράκαμεν τοὺς γίγαντας, καὶ ἦμεν ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ὡσεὶ ἀκρίδες'. This is the point at which 'giants' enters the transmission.
rungs.evidence: https://www.blueletterbible.org/lxx/gen/6/1/s_6004 returned the full Greek of Gen 6:4 quoted above, with γίγαντες twice. https://biblehub.com/sepd/numbers/13.htm returned the Greek of Num 13:33 quoted above, with γίγαντας and ἀκρίδες. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septuagint gives the early-to-mid third century BCE date for the Pentateuch translation and notes Vaticanus and Alexandrinus as the substantially intact copies.
rungs.note: The translation date is a composition date. No third-century BCE copy of Greek Genesis 6:4 survives.

chain.floor: Genesis 6:4 in Hebrew calls them nephilim and then gibborim, men of the name, and its vocabulary carries no term for height. 'Giants' is the word the Greek translators supplied, and Latin took it from the Greek. Great size attaches to these figures at Numbers 13:33, where nephilim are equated with the sons of Anak and the Israelites feel like grasshoppers, in a report the narrative presents as a bad one. The giant tradition itself is old and physically attested: an Aramaic scroll of the second century BCE already tells of watchers whose human wives bear giant offspring. So the claim stands on a translation decision, on a second biblical passage, and on the Enochic expansion, rather than on anything Genesis 6 says about stature.

scholarlyNotes.heading: What falls in Nephilim
scholarlyNotes.body:
Modern English versions usually leave the word untranslated, because the derivation is contested rather than plain. The starting point is the Hebrew root n-p-l, to fall, and that much is broadly shared: John Day and Ronald Hendel both work from it. Hendel, in "Of Demigods and the Deluge" (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1987), takes the falling to be death, which would make the Nephilim the war dead and set the word beside the gibborim of the same verse rather than against them. What the root cannot supply is height. The lexicon of Brown, Driver and Briggs records a proposed link to an Aramaic word for Orion, then dismisses the whole field: the suggested etymologies are "all very precarious".

Giant is therefore a translator's decision rather than a lexical fact. The Septuagint rendered the plural gigantes, the Vulgate kept gigantes, and English inherited the size from Greek. What kind of being is meant remains open. Ki-Eun Jang, writing in Religions in 2025, disagrees with Hendel and argues that the Nephilim are human in nature, pre-Israelite giants introduced in anticipation of the land promise and the conquest narrative rather than as a prelude to the flood.

scholarlyNotes.heading: How the Watchers material reaches us
scholarlyNotes.body: The entry is right that 1 Enoch fills the silence of Genesis, but the book arrives in pieces and in three languages, and the pieces do not all say the same thing. All five sections survive complete only in Ge'ez, preserved because the Ethiopian church kept the work as an authoritative writing. A substantial Greek witness covering roughly 1 Enoch 1 to 32 was found in a codex at Akhmim in Upper Egypt in 1886 to 1887 and published in the early 1890s. Aramaic fragments of the Watchers material were then recovered from Qumran Cave 4 and edited by J. T. Milik, with Matthew Black, as The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (Clarendon, 1976). Palaeographic dating places some of those copies in the early second century BCE, as Archie Wright sets out in The Origin of Evil Spirits (Fortress, revised edition 2015). Whether the Ethiopic translators worked from Greek alone or also had Aramaic in front of them is still argued. George Nickelsburg's 1 Enoch 1 (Hermeneia, 2001) is the commentary most often cited on these questions.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Mesopotamian sages or Greek models
scholarlyNotes.body: Where the Watchers story came from is a live comparative question, and the proposals divide by region. Amar Annus, in "On the Origin of Watchers" (Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha, 2010), derives the Watchers and their giant sons from the Mesopotamian apkallu, the antediluvian sages who taught humanity its crafts. His claim is that Jewish writers inverted the material: the sages became rebels, their instruction became forbidden knowledge, and Enoch displaced them as the legitimate holder of antediluvian wisdom. Annus adds that some Mesopotamian sources already treated the apkallu as capable of malice, so the inversion had something to work with. Ida Fröhlich, in The Watchers in Jewish and Christian Traditions (Fortress, 2014), works the same ground through the diviner-king Enmeduranki. Set against this are readings that look to Greece, taking the Watchers' teaching as modelled on Prometheus and Asael as a first inventor. Fröhlich concedes that "neither historical-sociological nor mythological models, including Greek images, can be ruled out", but objects that "observation of only one or two motifs of the narrative does not illuminate the background and meaning of the whole story".

scholarlySources: Ronald S. Hendel, "Of Demigods and the Deluge: Toward an Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4", Journal of Biblical Literature 106/1 (1987), 13-26
John Day, "The Sons of God and Daughters of Men and the Giants: Disputed Points in the Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4", Hebrew Bible and Ancient Israel 1/4 (2012), 427-447
Ki-Eun Jang, "The Problems of Sons of Gods, Daughters of Humans, and the Nephilim in Genesis 6:1-4: A Reassessment", Religions 16/8 (2025), article 972
Francis Brown, S. R. Driver and C. A. Briggs, A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, entry nephilim
J. T. Milik, with Matthew Black, The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976)
George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary on the Book of 1 Enoch, Chapters 1-36; 81-108, Hermeneia (Fortress Press, 2001)
Archie T. Wright, The Origin of Evil Spirits: The Reception of Genesis 6:1-4 in Early Jewish Literature, revised edition (Fortress Press, 2015)
Amar Annus, "On the Origin of Watchers: A Comparative Study of the Antediluvian Wisdom in Mesopotamian and Jewish Traditions", Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha 19/4 (2010), 277-320

Ida Fröhlich, "Mesopotamian Elements and the Watchers Traditions", in Angela Kim Harkins, Kelley Coblentz Bautch and John C. Endres (eds), The Watchers in Jewish and Christian Traditions (Fortress Press, 2014)

handling.living: The Nephilim appear in the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Numbers), scripture actively read, studied and prayed with today by living Jewish and Christian communities worldwide, so this is not inert literary material the way a dead pantheon is; it sits inside an active religious canon even though the passage itself has no ritual or liturgical use and is not a figure of devotion. The Book of Enoch material that elaborates the story is canonical scripture today specifically for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, a living church, though it is non-canonical (apocryphal/pseudepigraphal) for Judaism and most other Christian traditions.
handling.distortions: The single most common distortion is treating the four verses of Genesis 6:1-4 as if they contained the elaborate Watchers mythology (named fallen angels, taught forbidden arts, a war in heaven) that actually comes from the much later Book of Enoch, presenting later Second Temple-period expansion as if it were the biblical text itself. A second is the modern 'giant skeleton' conspiracy genre, which claims physical evidence for the Nephilim; this has no scholarly standing and rests on hoaxes and misidentified fossils, and treating it as a serious historical claim misrepresents both the text and the archaeology.
handling.take: The biblical text (Genesis 6:1-4, Numbers 13:33) and the Enoch/Jubilees expansions are public-domain ancient texts and fully citable and adaptable; the interpretive question of who the 'sons of God' are (angelic beings, Sethite line, or divine-descent-claiming rulers) is genuinely unresolved among scholars, so present it as an open question rather than picking one reading and asserting it as fact. Treat this as biblical/religious material with respect rather than as generic monster lore, it belongs to living Jewish and Christian scriptural traditions, and clearly separate the sparse canonical text from the much richer non-canonical Enoch elaboration so readers don't mistake one for the other; keep the modern giant-skeleton hoax material out of anything presented as factual.
handling.cite: Cite Genesis 6:1-4 and Numbers 13:33 (Hebrew Bible) for the canonical material, 1 Enoch (Book of the Watchers, chapters 6-16) and Jubilees 5 for the major Second Temple-period expansion, and Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews I.3.1, for the earliest interpretive gloss connecting them to 'Giants' in the Greek sense.

goliath.fullDescription: Goliath of Gath stands in the valley of Elah for forty days and challenges Israel to send one man against him. The armour is described piece by piece before the fight, which is how the story tells you what is about to be irrelevant.
goliath.mysteryNote: The brook in the Valley of Elah still runs. The stones there are ordinary. That is the whole point.
goliath.fate: Killed by a sling-stone from David, then beheaded with his own sword.

sections.story:
The Philistines and Israel face each other across the valley, each on a hill, neither willing to descend. Goliath proposes single combat to settle it: their champion against Israel's, winner takes the war.

1 Samuel 17 catalogues his equipment with unusual precision: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, greaves, a bronze javelin, a spear whose shaft is like a weaver's beam with a head of six hundred shekels of iron, and a shield-bearer walking ahead of him. The inventory is doing work. It establishes a system of warfare, comprehensively.

David is a boy delivering bread and cheese to his brothers. He hears the challenge and volunteers. Saul offers his own armour; David tries it, cannot walk in it, and takes it off. He goes down to the brook, chooses five smooth stones, and approaches with a sling.

Goliath is insulted: "Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?" David answers with a speech about whose battle it is. Then he runs at him, which is the tactical detail everyone forgets: he closes the distance while slinging rather than waiting to be reached.

The stone sinks into the forehead and Goliath falls face down. David takes the giant's own sword and cuts off his head. The Philistines break and run.

The story is not about strength. It is about a man who has optimised for one kind of fight meeting someone who declined to have it. A sling in trained hands was a genuine military weapon with real range: the mismatch is the reverse of how it looks.
sections.origins:
1 Samuel 17 is the main text. 1 Samuel 21:9 and 22:10 refer back to the sword kept at Nob.

The textual situation is complicated and important. The Septuagint version of 1 Samuel 17 is substantially shorter than the Masoretic Hebrew, usually put at around forty to forty-five per cent shorter rather than a clean half, and the two appear to preserve different stages of the story's development.

2 Samuel 21:19 states that Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath the Gittite. 1 Chronicles 20:5 adjusts this so that Elhanan kills Goliath's brother Lahmi: visibly a later harmonisation.

An inscription from tenth-to-ninth-century Tell es-Safi, the site generally identified as Gath, carries names close in form to Goliath. Aren Maeir reads both as resembling the biblical name; others are more cautious about how many names the sherd holds. What the sherd shows is that names like Goliath were in use at Gath in the right period. It does not by itself prove a securely Philistine etymology: proposed links run toward Anatolian and Egyptian forms as well, and the exact derivation remains disputed.
sections.disputed:
Goliath's height differs between manuscripts. The Masoretic text gives six cubits and a span, around 2.9 metres. The Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls fragment 4QSam-a and Josephus all give four cubits and a span, around 2 metres: tall but within human range. The six-cubit figure is not only Masoretic: the Vulgate (around 400) and Targum Jonathan also read six, so the taller number was already in Hebrew exemplars centuries before the medieval codices. Whether the larger figure is the later reading is argued both ways: J. Daniel Hays has treated six as secondary; Gurry and Meade (2022) conclude the reverse. It is a live text-critical dispute, not a settled result.

Who killed him is a real problem in the text, not a modern invention. The Elhanan attribution in 2 Samuel is difficult to explain away, and the Chronicles version reads as an attempt to fix it.

Suggestions that Goliath had a pituitary disorder producing gigantism and visual field defects are medically coherent but entirely speculative, and rest on treating a literary description as a clinical record.

chain.claim: Goliath of Gath stood six cubits and a span, about nine feet nine inches, or close to three metres.
chain.verdict: The height is a textual variant rather than a fixed number: the surviving copies of 1 Samuel 17:4 do not agree with each other, and the disagreement is ancient.

rungs.witness: Peter J. Gurry and John D. Meade, 'How Tall Was Goliath? A Textual Dilemma', Crossway, 24 October 2022, adapted from their book 'Scribes and Scripture'
rungs.date: 24 October 2022
rungs.reads: Two textual critics who come down the other way. They tabulate the witnesses as 'MT; the Three; Vulgate; Peshitta; Targum' for six cubits and '4QSama; LXXB L; Josephus, Antiquities 6.171' for four, then conclude: 'Although the six-nine Goliath has the earlier and perhaps better external evidence, the nine-nine Goliath is probably more likely original', on the reasoning that a scribe had a contextual motive to shorten Goliath.
rungs.evidence: Article read this session at https://www.crossway.org/articles/how-tall-was-goliath-a-textual-dilemma/ , including the witness lists, the concluding sentence and the byline and date.
rungs.note: A publisher's web article rather than peer-reviewed scholarship, which is why it is filed as press, but it is by the authors of a book on the transmission of the biblical text and it is the clearest statement of the case against the catalogue entry's conclusion.

rungs.witness: Omer Sergi, 'Goliath', Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception vol. 10 (Walter de Gruyter, Berlin and Boston, 2015)
rungs.reads: Sets out the split as reference-work consensus: 'The portrayal of Goliath is that of a legendary giant, six cubits and a span (about three meters height) according to the MT and four cubits and a span (about two meters height) according to LXX Codex Vaticanus and Lucianic textual tradition, 4QSamA and Josephus (Ant. 6.171).'
rungs.evidence: Offprint PDF read this session at https://courses.edx.org/asset-v1:IsraelX+BIBARC101+3T2019+type@asset+block/Goliath_EBR_online.pdf ; the bibliographic line on the offprint reads 'Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception vol. 10 (c) Walter de Gruyter, Berlin/Boston, 2015'.
rungs.note: Useful because it is a neutral reference work rather than a partisan in the JETS exchange.

rungs.witness: Clyde E. Billington, 'Goliath and the Exodus Giants: How Tall Were They?', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 50/3 (September 2007), 489-508
rungs.date: September 2007
rungs.reads: Defends the six-cubit reading, but not the nine feet nine figure. Billington rejects the 18-inch cubit, holding that 'common cubits were never standardized, varied greatly from person to person, and were by their very nature always considerably smaller than the royal cubit', and puts Goliath near 8 feet 11 inches. He explains the Greek away: 'The 4 cubits and a span reading found in the lxx is almost certainly a translation of the mt's common cubits into royal Egyptian cubits.'
rungs.evidence: PDF read this session at https://etsjets.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/files_JETS-PDFs_50_50-3_JETS_50-3_489-508_Billington.pdf .
rungs.note: Worth registering that even a defender of the six-cubit text does not defend nine feet nine.

rungs.witness: J. Daniel Hays, 'The Height of Goliath: A Response to Clyde Billington', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 50/3 (September 2007), 509-516
rungs.date: September 2007
rungs.reads: Restates that the Hebrew evidence from Qumran undercuts the cubit-conversion defence: 'The four cubits reading of 4QSama is a huge problem for Billington's thesis', and 'The fact remains that the earliest Hebrew text of 1 Sam 17:4 is 4QSama (part of the dss), which dates to 50-25 bc.'
rungs.evidence: PDF read this session at https://etsjets.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/files_JETS-PDFs_50_50-3_JETS_50-3_509-516_Hays.pdf .
rungs.note: In this piece Hays also writes 'Also, for this particular variant, Codex Alexandrinus follows the mt', which contradicts his own 2005 article. See the top-level note.

rungs.witness: J. Daniel Hays, 'Reconsidering the Height of Goliath', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48/4 (December 2005), 701-714
rungs.date: December 2005
rungs.reads: Argues that four cubits and a span is the likelier original and that six is a later enlargement. Supplies the arithmetic behind the popular figure: 'A cubit is approximately 18 inches, and a span is about 9 inches. Thus, in the MT Goliath is 9'9" tall.' Concludes: 'I suggest that we accept "four cubits and a span" as the most likely original reading.'
rungs.evidence: Full PDF read this session at https://etsjets.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/files_JETS-PDFs_48_48-4_JETS_48-4_701-714.pdf . Volume, issue, date and pagination confirmed against the JETS 48 contents page at https://etsjets.org/jets48/ .
rungs.note: This article is the main modern source for the claim that the taller Goliath is secondary.

rungs.witness: Masoretic Text of 1 Samuel 17:4 (Tiberian tradition, Aleppo Codex, about 920 CE)
rungs.date: The Aleppo Codex was written in the 10th century, about 920 CE. Its surviving portion runs from Deuteronomy 28:17 onward, with 2 Kings 14:21 to 18:13 among the losses, so 1 Samuel 17 is within the extant text.
rungs.reads: Six cubits and a span: 'גׇּבְה֕וֹ שֵׁ֥שׁ אַמּ֖וֹת וָזָֽרֶת', his height six cubits and a span. This is the reading behind 'nine feet nine'.
rungs.evidence: Hebrew read this session via the Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/I_Samuel.17.4 , version title 'Miqra according to the Masorah', which is a digital edition based on the Aleppo Codex and related manuscripts. Extant range and date of the codex from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleppo_Codex .
rungs.note: I read an Aleppo-based digital edition, not the codex leaf. The reading itself is not in doubt: it is the standard Hebrew text printed in every edition.

rungs.witness: Vulgate, 1 Samuel (1 Kings) 17:4, Latin
rungs.date: Jerome translated Samuel from the Hebrew in about 391 to 405 CE. Consulted here in a printed Latin Vulgate text online, not in an early codex.
rungs.reads: Six cubits and a span: 'Et egressus est vir spurius de castris Philisthinorum nomine Goliath, de Geth, altitudinis sex cubitorum et palmi'.
rungs.evidence: Latin text read at https://www.drbo.org/lvb/chapter/09017.htm this session. Gurry and Meade list the Vulgate among the six-cubit witnesses.
rungs.note: Jerome worked from a Hebrew text, so this is a witness to a Hebrew exemplar already reading six around 400 CE, well before the surviving Masoretic codices.

rungs.witness: Septuagint, 1 Kingdoms 17:4, in the Greek text carried by Codex Vaticanus (Vatican, Vat. gr. 1209)
rungs.date: Codex Vaticanus is 4th century CE. The Greek translation of Samuel is earlier and its date is estimated rather than known.
rungs.reads: Four cubits and a span: 'ὕψος αὐτοῦ τεσσάρων πήχεων καὶ σπιθαμῆς'.
rungs.evidence: Greek text read at https://www.blueletterbible.org/lxx/1sa/17/1/s_253001 this session; the same wording, τεσσάρων πήχεων καὶ σπιθαμῆς, is given at https://www.accordancebible.com/goliath-lxx/ . Attribution of this reading specifically to Vaticanus and to the Lucianic tradition from Omer Sergi's Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception entry, and from Gurry and Meade, who list the four-cubit witnesses as '4QSama; LXXB L; Josephus, Antiquities 6.171'. Brenton's 1851 English of the Septuagint, which follows Vaticanus, likewise reads 'his height was four cubits and a span' (https://biblehub.com/sep/1_samuel/17.htm).
rungs.note: I read printed and digital Greek editions plus scholarly attribution, not the Vaticanus leaf itself.

rungs.witness: Targum Jonathan to the Prophets, 1 Samuel 17:4 (Aramaic)
rungs.date: Composition uncertain and disputed, usually placed in the early centuries CE with later reworking. Read here in a printed Mikraot Gedolot text, not in a dated manuscript.
rungs.reads: Six cubits and a span: 'רוּמֵיהּ שִׁתָּא אַמִין וְזֵירְתָא', his height six cubits and a span.
rungs.evidence: Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Targum_Jonathan_on_I_Samuel.17.4 , read this session; version title given as 'Mikraot Gedolot'. Gurry and Meade list the Targum among the six-cubit witnesses.
rungs.note: The sort position is a rough placeholder. The date of Targum Jonathan is genuinely open, and this rung's value is that it puts the six-cubit reading in the Aramaic tradition, not that it dates it.

rungs.witness: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 6.171
rungs.date: Written about 93 to 94 CE. The Greek text survives in medieval copies: the oldest manuscripts for Antiquities books 1 to 10 are 11th century (Vienna, Vindobonensis hist. gr. II A 19, and Paris, Parisinus gr. 1419), with the main group 13th to 15th century. This is not a first-century object.
rungs.reads: Four cubits and a span. Whiston's standard English renders it 'for he was of four cubits and a span in tallness'.
rungs.evidence: Whiston's translation of Ant. 6.171 read at https://lexundria.com/j_aj/6.171/wst and confirmed against a second copy of the same translation at https://sacred-texts.com/jud/josephus/ant-6.htm , both giving 'four cubits and a span'. Manuscript sigla and centuries from https://www.tertullian.org/rpearse/manuscripts/josephus_antiquities.htm . Sergi in the Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception cites Ant. 6.171 for the four-cubit reading.
rungs.note: Whiston is an 18th-century translation. I did not check Niese's Greek.

rungs.witness: 4QSamuel-a (4Q51), Qumran Cave 4, Hebrew scroll of 1-2 Samuel
rungs.date: Copied in the middle of the first century BCE, commonly placed at about 50 to 25 BCE.
rungs.reads: Four cubits and a span, not six. The transcription printed by Accordance is 'א֯רבע[ א]מות וזרת', where the dot marks a damaged letter and the square brackets mark a restored one, so the word for 'four' is on the leather while part of 'cubits' is reconstructed.
rungs.evidence: J. Daniel Hays, JETS 48/4 (2005), PDF at https://etsjets.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/files_JETS-PDFs_48_48-4_JETS_48-4_701-714.pdf , read this session: 'Although some portions of the scroll are damaged, 1 Sam 17:3-6 is clear, and in this manuscript, by far our oldest Hebrew manuscript of this text, Goliath is listed as four cubits and a span'; and '4QSama, dating to the middle of the first century BC, is our oldest extant Hebrew manuscript that contains 1 Sam 17:4.' The Hebrew transcription with its damage marks is at https://www.accordancebible.com/goliath-lxx/ . Confirmed independently by Omer Sergi in the Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception offprint cited below.
rungs.note: I have not inspected the plate or the DJD XVII edition itself, only transcriptions and descriptions of it.

rungs.witness: Ostracon (inscribed bowl sherd) from Tell es-Safi/Gath, Israel
rungs.date: Stratified to the 10th to early 9th century BCE. Excavated 2005, published by A. M. Maeir, S. J. Wimmer, A. Zukerman and A. Demsky in the Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research 351 (2008), 39-71.
rungs.reads: Silent on height. It carries personal names only. The excavator reads two names close in form to Goliath; the Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception is more cautious and says it 'probably renders at least one name lwt (Alwat?)'. It shows such a name was current at Gath in roughly the right period. It says nothing about anyone's stature.
rungs.evidence: https://gath.wordpress.com/2006/02/16/comment-on-the-news-item-in-bar-on-the-goliath-inscription/ , the excavation director Aren Maeir's own post, read this session: he writes that 'The stratigraphic context of the sherd dates it to the 10th to the early 9th cent. BCE' and states flatly that 'the Goliath of the inscription from Gath is not the Biblical Goliath'. Cross-checked against https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_es-Safi_inscription for the find date, the 1000-925 BCE range and the BASOR 351 publication details, and against the Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception offprint at https://courses.edx.org/asset-v1:IsraelX+BIBARC101+3T2019+type@asset+block/Goliath_EBR_online.pdf for the cautious 'at least one name' reading.
rungs.note: This is the physical anchor the catalogue entry leans on, and it is worth being clear that it anchors the name, not the man and not the measurement.

chain.floor: A Hebrew scroll copied at Qumran in the middle of the first century BCE and the Greek text carried by a fourth-century codex both make Goliath four cubits and a span, roughly six feet nine. The six-cubit figure that yields nine feet nine is carried by the Masoretic Hebrew, by Jerome's Latin around 400 CE and by the Aramaic Targum. Both figures are therefore ancient, and specialists argue in both directions about which stood in the text first: Hays holds that four is original, Gurry and Meade hold that six is. Nine feet nine rests on one branch of the transmission and on an 18-inch cubit, not on an agreed text. Even a published defender of the six-cubit reading, Billington, arrives at about 8 feet 11 inches rather than nine feet nine.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A name that is not Hebrew
scholarlyNotes.body: Golyat has no accepted Semitic derivation. Omer Sergi, writing the Hebrew Bible section of the Goliath article in the Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception, volume 10 (de Gruyter, 2015), calls the name "clearly not Semitic" and adds that, although it is commonly identified as Anatolian, an identification his article credits to Caspari and Albright, its exact etymology remains much disputed. The long-standing suggestion links it to the Lydian royal name Alyattes. Mariona Vernet Pons argued in Kadmos 51 (2012) for the Carian personal name Wljat or Wliat instead, on the grounds that Alyattes itself lacks a secure etymology and that the Carian form accounts for the consonants and supplies a sense fit for a warrior, the strong one. She records support for the Lydian route from Albright, Kitchen and Singer, and an Egyptian alternative from Goerg. The Tell es-Safi sherd bears on the question without closing it. Aren Maeir, who directs the excavation there, wrote on the project's blog that both names on the sherd are "etymologically very close to Goliath", while stressing that the inscription does not mention the Goliath. Sergi reads the same object more cautiously, as probably rendering at least one name, lwt.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Six cubits, or four
scholarlyNotes.body: 1 Samuel 17:4 makes Goliath six cubits and a span in the Masoretic text, near 2.9 metres. Three other witnesses give four cubits and a span, near two metres: the Septuagint; the Qumran manuscript 4QSam-a, edited by Frank Moore Cross, Donald W. Parry, Richard J. Saley and Eugene Ulrich in Qumran Cave 4.XII: 1-2 Samuel, Discoveries in the Judaean Desert 17 (Oxford, 2005); and Josephus, whose Antiquities 6.171 has Goliath "of four cubits and a span in tallness" in Whiston's translation. Sergi's encyclopedia article sets out the same division of the evidence. J. Daniel Hays put the case for the shorter reading in "Reconsidering the Height of Goliath", Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48 (2005), 701-14, concluding that the text-critical evidence, external and internal, requires cutting Goliath from nine feet nine to six feet nine. Hays also makes the point of method that matters here: before the Qumran discoveries scholars were readier to treat the Greek Samuel as secondary to the Hebrew, and 4QSam-a stands roughly a millennium closer to the composition than the Masoretic manuscripts do. Which figure a reader inherits depends on which Bible is in front of them.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The long text and the short
scholarlyNotes.body: The Greek 1 Kingdoms 17-18 is far shorter than the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17-18, by something on the order of forty per cent. Absent from the Greek are, among other passages, David's introduction as the shepherd son of Jesse, Saul's question about whose son the boy is, and Jonathan's covenant with him. Whether a translator cut down a long text or the Hebrew grew out of a short one was argued out between named scholars in a single volume: Dominique Barthelemy, David W. Gooding, Johan Lust and Emanuel Tov, The Story of David and Goliath: Textual and Literary Criticism, Orbis Biblicus et Orientalis 73 (Fribourg and Goettingen, 1986). Reviewing it for Themelios, H. G. M. Williamson set out the division. Lust and Tov hold that the Greek rests on a shorter Hebrew text which stood earlier in the composition history than the Masoretic one. Barthelemy and Gooding hold that the Masoretic narrative is coherent as it stands and the Greek is a truncation of it, and therefore secondary. Both readings remain in circulation, and the choice decides whether the fuller story most readers know is the original or the expansion.

A. M. Maeir, S. J. Wimmer, A. Zukerman and A. Demsky, "A Late Iron Age I/Early Iron Age II Old Canaanite Inscription from Tell es-Safi/Gath, Israel: Palaeography, Dating, and Historical-Cultural Significance", Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research 351, 2008, 39-71

J. Daniel Hays, "Reconsidering the Height of Goliath", Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005, 701-14
