handling.living: Goliath appears in 1 Samuel, scripture shared by Judaism, Christianity and Islam (as Jalut in the Quran), and the David-and-Goliath story is actively read, taught and preached in living synagogues, churches and mosques today, not just studied as ancient literature. It is also the subject of ongoing archaeological work at Tell es-Safi/Gath, so this is simultaneously scripture with billions of adherents and a live scholarly research site.
handling.distortions: The commonest flattening is treating the story as a simple strength-versus-cunning underdog fable, which erases the text's own point that a trained slinger with range was a real tactical answer to a slow, over-armored close-fighter, not a lucky trick. Retellings also routinely present Goliath's nine-foot height and the Elhanan-killed-Goliath discrepancy (2 Samuel 21:19 vs. the harmonized 1 Chronicles 20:5) as settled or ignore them entirely, when both are genuine, unresolved text-critical problems rather than errors to silently fix.
handling.take: The narrative beats are freely retellable and have been retold for millennia across all three Abrahamic traditions, but because this is living scripture, not just folklore, avoid mockery or blasphemy-adjacent framing, and distinguish clearly between the biblical text itself and later folk or medical speculation (e.g. the popular pituitary-gigantism theory, which is medically coherent but has zero textual support and should be labeled as speculation, not read back into the story). The height and Elhanan discrepancies are worth keeping visible as genuine manuscript variation rather than resolving them into one "true" version.
handling.cite: Cite 1 Samuel 17 (Masoretic Text) alongside the notably shorter Septuagint version (1 Kingdoms 17) and the Dead Sea Scrolls fragment 4QSam-a for the height variant, plus Aren Maeir's Tell es-Safi/Gath excavation reports for the Philistine-name ostracon evidence.

og-of-bashan.fullDescription: Og, king of Bashan, is the last survivor of the Rephaim. Deuteronomy offers his iron bed as proof of his size, and notes that it can still be seen in Rabbah: a footnote that turns a king into an exhibit.
og-of-bashan.mysteryNote: No iron bed was ever dug from Rabbah with a museum label. Only the cubits remain: cold, exact, and unproven.
og-of-bashan.fate: Defeated by Israel at Edrei; only his iron bed is said to remain.

sections.story:
Og rules Bashan, east of the Jordan, with sixty fortified cities. Israel meets him at Edrei, defeats him, and takes the territory. As conquest narratives go it is brief.

What makes Og memorable is the aside. Deuteronomy 3:11 pauses to observe that he alone remained of the remnant of the Rephaim, and that his bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long and four wide, roughly four metres by two, and adds, almost conversationally, that it is still in Rabbah of the Ammonites.

That single verse does several things at once. It classifies him as the last of an older people. It gives a measurement of the object, not of Og: the verse nowhere states his height. And it points at something a reader could in principle go and look at, which is a form of evidence the Hebrew Bible rarely offers.

The Rephaim appear throughout the text as a pre-Israelite population of large stature, listed alongside the Anakim, the Emim and the Zamzummim: all named as earlier inhabitants displaced by later arrivals. Deuteronomy 2 is unusually systematic about this, working through which nation drove out which giants from which land.

Og's defeat becomes a fixed reference point. Psalms 135 and 136 name him in liturgical recitals of what God did for Israel, paired always with Sihon. He is remembered less as a person than as an item on a list of things overcome.

Later rabbinic tradition made him enormously larger. Niddah 61a says he was saved from the punishment of the generation of the flood; the familiar detail of his clinging to the outside of the ark is later midrashic elaboration rather than a line in the folio usually cited for the rest of the cycle.
sections.origins:
Numbers 21:33-35 records the battle at Edrei. Deuteronomy 3:1-13 gives the fuller account including the iron bedstead and the Rephaim classification. Joshua 12-13 lists the conquered territory.

Psalms 135:11 and 136:20 preserve him in liturgy, which indicates the tradition was well established.

The rabbinic expansions appear in the Talmud and in later midrash. Berakhot 54b carries the mountain-throwing; Niddah 24b the thighbone; Niddah 61a the flood survival. The ark-clinging detail is later midrashic. These make Og a figure of legendary scale and are clearly homiletic elaboration rather than historical claim.

The word rendered "bedstead" is read as a sarcophagus in some modern translations and commentaries. The ancient versions treat it as a bed: the Greek gives κλίνη, Jerome lectus, Onkelos ערסא. The sarcophagus reading is a modern preference, not an ancient consensus.
sections.disputed:
Whether the iron object was a bed or a basalt sarcophagus is a live question. Basalt is common in the Bashan region, dark and iron-like in appearance, and a large stone sarcophagus would fit both the dimensions and the "still to be seen" remark. On that reading Deuteronomy is describing a monument, not furniture.

Who the Rephaim were is contested. The term is used both for a living people and, elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible and in Ugaritic texts, for shades of the dead: a double sense that may indicate an ancient population remembered as ancestral spirits, or two unrelated words.

The dolmens and megalithic structures scattered across the Golan and Transjordan have often been linked to the Rephaim traditions. The association is plausible as a mechanism, unexplained large structures inviting explanation by large builders, but is not demonstrated.

chain.claim: Deuteronomy records that Og of Bashan's iron bed was nine cubits long and four wide, and that measurement proves Og himself stood about four metres, roughly thirteen and a half feet.
chain.verdict: The four metre figure is the length of an object, not a stated height: the verse measures the bed and leaves the man unmeasured, and the readers who converted bed into body disagreed with each other about how to do it.

rungs.witness: Laura Quick, 'Og, King of Bashan: Underworld Ruler or Ancient Giant?', TheTorah.com, 22 July 2020
rungs.date: 22 July 2020
rungs.reads: Defends the plain reading and states the inference the claim depends on: 'the term ʿereś barzel should be interpreted in line with its simple meaning, "iron bed"', and 'the text describes the dimensions of his bed, highlighting its, and thus his, enormous size.' She also names the funerary reading and its author: 'Timo Veijola has argued that ʿereś barzel refers to a dolmen, a funerary monument', and objects that 'nothing in the text connects Og or his rephaʾim to the living dead'. She cites Alan R. Millard for iron as a decorative overlay in a period when iron was rare and expensive.
rungs.evidence: https://www.thetorah.com/article/og-king-of-bashan-underworld-ruler-or-ancient-giant read twice this session, returning the byline, the date, the sentences quoted and the attributions to Veijola, Millard and the Harvard author of the CBQ piece.
rungs.note: Filed as press because it is a website essay rather than a peer-reviewed article, though the author is an academic. Note that even this defence infers 'enormous size' from the bed and stops short of naming a height.

rungs.witness: Zvi Ron, 'The Bed of Og', Jewish Bible Quarterly 40:1 (2012), 30-34
rungs.reads: Surveys several readings and treats the giant reading as one option among them. On Maimonides: 'Rambam similarly understands that Og was "six cubits tall, or a little more," "twice as long as an ordinary person," something that is "undoubtedly an exceptional height among men, but not quite impossible." This is based on Rambam's understanding that a bed is generally made a third longer than the person who is to sleep in it.' On the tomb reading: 'Many contemporary Bible commentators, particularly non-Jewish ones, prefer to translate the word eres as a tomb or sarcophagus.' Ron's own conclusion is that the eres is a cultic object and that its being on display at Rabbah means Og was still being worshipped there.
rungs.evidence: PDF read this session at https://jbqnew.jewishbible.org/assets/Uploads/401/jbq_401_og.pdf , returning the author, title, journal, volume, issue, year, pages and the sentences quoted above.
rungs.note: Useful because it is a survey rather than an advocacy piece, and because it shows the sarcophagus reading as a modern commentators' position rather than an ancient one.

rungs.witness: 'King Og's Iron Bed', The Catholic Biblical Quarterly 73 (2011), 477-492
rungs.reads: Argues the bed is a real bed and a battle trophy rather than a tomb, and points to a Mesopotamian bed of the same dimensions. The article quotes the Esagil Tablet on Marduk's bed as 'The bed, nine cubits (its long) side, four cubits (its) front', the same nine by four as Deuteronomy. It nonetheless reads the size as evidence of Og's stature: 'The hugeness of the bed (about thirteen feet long and six-and-a-half feet wide) attests to the great stature of King Og and supports Deuteronomy's claim that Og was one of the giant Rephaim.'
rungs.evidence: Academia.edu posting of the article, https://www.academia.edu/11641907/_King_Ogs_Iron_Bed_CBQ_73_2011_477_92 , read this session for the abstract, the Esagil Tablet quotation and the sentence on Og's stature, and for the journal, volume, year and pages.
rungs.note: The author's name is a loose end. The academia.edu posting gives Maria Metzler; Laura Quick, citing what is evidently the same piece, writes 'Dr Maria Lindquist of Harvard University'. I could not resolve which name is printed in CBQ. The article's content is what this rung rests on, and the Marduk parallel cuts against reading nine by four as a field measurement of a particular object.

rungs.witness: NET Bible, translators' notes on Deuteronomy 3:11
rungs.date: NET Bible first edition 2005. Notes read this session in the online edition.
rungs.reads: Renders the object as a sarcophagus rather than furniture and supplies the arithmetic behind the popular figure. The translation reads 'It is thirteen and a half feet long and six feet wide according to standard measure', and the note explains the Hebrew עֶרֶשׂ as most likely 'a basaltic (volcanic) stone sarcophagus of suitable size to contain the coffin of the giant Rephaite king', the iron-like appearance of the basalt accounting for the description. It takes the cubit here as the short cubit of about 18 inches.
rungs.evidence: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Deu+3%3A11%2C20%2C22 read this session, returning the verse text and the notes summarised above.
rungs.note: Thirteen and a half feet is 4.1 metres. That is where the four metre number comes from, and in this edition it is the length of a stone box.

rungs.witness: Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed, Part II, chapter 47
rungs.date: Written in Arabic in Egypt and completed about 1190. Read here in Michael Friedlander's English translation, and cross-checked against a Hebrew digital edition.
rungs.reads: Performs the bed-to-body calculation explicitly and gets a figure well under four metres. Friedlander: 'the bedstead ... is always greater than the person that sleeps therein; as a rule, is it by a third longer. If, therefore, the bed of Og was nine cubits in length, he must, according to this proportion, have been six cubits high, or a little more.' And: 'This is undoubtedly an exceptional height among men, but not quite impossible.'
rungs.evidence: Friedlander's English read this session at https://sacred-texts.com/jud/gfp/gfp134.htm , confirmed as Part II chapter 47 and returning the sentences quoted. The same calculation, six cubits or slightly more from a bed a third longer than its occupant, was returned independently from a Hebrew edition via https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Guide_for_the_Perplexed%2C_Part_2.47 .
rungs.note: Six cubits is roughly two and a half to three metres depending on the cubit used. This is a believer in a large Og arriving at a materially smaller number than the claim, from the same verse.

rungs.witness: Abraham Ibn Ezra, commentary on Deuteronomy 3:11
rungs.date: Twelfth century, Ibn Ezra died about 1167. Read here in a printed and digitised commentary text.
rungs.reads: Rejects the reading Rashi gives and rejects an outsized Og with it: 'באמת איש. באמת כל אדם והנה הוא כפול ולא יתכן להיות באמתו כי מה בא הכתוב ללמד ועוד שלא יהיה בצלם אדם כלל'. In my own English, not a published translation: by the cubit of a man means by the cubit of any man, and behold he is double, and it cannot be by his own cubit, for what would Scripture be teaching, and further he would then not be in human form at all.
rungs.evidence: Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Ibn_Ezra_on_Deuteronomy.3.11 , read this session, returning the Hebrew exactly as quoted. The English is my rendering; Sefaria's listed English versions (Strickman and Silver, Shachter) did not return text in the response I received.
rungs.note: The word כפול, double, is the size Ibn Ezra allows: about twice a man, not four times. He also states plainly that a larger figure would put Og outside human shape, which is an objection to the very inference the claim makes.

rungs.witness: Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), commentary on Deuteronomy 3:11
rungs.date: Written in northern France in the late eleventh century, Rashi died in 1105. Read here in a printed and digitised commentary text, not in a manuscript.
rungs.reads: Glosses the measuring unit as Og's own forearm: 'באמת איש. בְּאַמַּת עוֹג', on 'by the cubit of a man', by the cubit of Og. On that reading the bed is nine of Og's cubits, which makes the conversion to metres circular rather than fixed.
rungs.evidence: Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Deuteronomy.3.11 , read this session; Hebrew version 'Rashi on Deuteronomy, trans. M. Rosenbaum and A.M. Silbermann, 1929-1934'.
rungs.note: Rashi is not asserting a height. He is saying which ruler the verse is using, and his answer removes the fixed 18 inch cubit that the four metre figure depends on.

rungs.witness: Masoretic Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 3:11 (Tiberian tradition)
rungs.date: The Tiberian codices run from about 920 CE (Aleppo) to 1008 or 1009 CE (Leningrad B19a). The Aleppo Codex has lost most of the Torah, its surviving text beginning at the last word of Deuteronomy 28:17, so this verse is not in its extant leaves. Read here in a digital edition of the Tiberian text.
rungs.reads: 'כִּ֣י רַק־ע֞וֹג מֶ֣לֶךְ הַבָּשָׁ֗ן נִשְׁאַר֮ מִיֶּ֣תֶר הָרְפָאִים֒ הִנֵּ֤ה עַרְשׂוֹ֙ עֶ֣רֶשׂ בַּרְזֶ֔ל הֲלֹ֣ה הִ֔וא בְּרַבַּ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן תֵּ֧שַׁע אַמּ֣וֹת אׇרְכָּ֗הּ וְאַרְבַּ֥ע אַמּ֛וֹת רׇחְבָּ֖הּ בְּאַמַּת־אִֽישׁ׃'. The feminine suffixes on 'אׇרְכָּהּ' and 'רׇחְבָּהּ', its length and its width, refer to the bed. The verse supplies no noun and no number for Og's own stature.
rungs.evidence: Full unpunctuated-free Hebrew read this session via https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Deuteronomy.3.11 , version 'Miqra according to the Masorah'. Word-by-word parsing of ʿarso, ʿeres, barzel, tesha, ammot, orkah, rochbah and be-ammat ish checked at https://biblehub.com/text/deuteronomy/3-11.htm . The extent of the Aleppo Codex and its start at Deuteronomy 28:17 checked at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleppo_Codex .
rungs.note: Because the Aleppo Codex is missing here, the Tiberian text for this verse rests on other manuscripts. I read a digital edition, not a codex leaf. The reading itself is not in dispute: it is the standard printed Hebrew.

rungs.witness: Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 24b
rungs.date: Same body of material and same transmission as the preceding rung. Read here in the Sefaria digital edition.
rungs.reads: Abba Shaul reports chasing a gazelle three parasangs inside what he was afterwards told was the thigh bone of Og king of Bashan: 'וְרַצְתִּי אַחֲרָיו שָׁלֹשׁ פַּרְסָאוֹת, וּצְבִי לֹא הִגַּעְתִּי, וְקוּלִית לֹא כָּלְתָה. כְּשֶׁחָזַרְתִּי לַאֲחוֹרַי, אָמְרוּ לִי: שֶׁל עוֹג מֶלֶךְ הַבָּשָׁן הָיְתָה'. A femur measured in parasangs is on a different scale from a bed measured in cubits.
rungs.evidence: Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Niddah.24b , read this session, returning the Hebrew and Aramaic quoted above.
rungs.note: Filed as a second witness to the same point because it comes from a different tractate and a different named tradent.

rungs.witness: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 54b
rungs.date: The Bavli reached substantially its present form in late antiquity, conventionally by about the sixth to seventh century CE; complete manuscripts are medieval. Read here in the William Davidson digital edition.
rungs.reads: Abandons the bed's arithmetic entirely and makes Og far larger than nine cubits. Og 'went, uprooted a mountain three parasangs long, and brought it on his head'. The passage then asks 'How tall was Moses? He was ten cubits tall. He took an axe ten cubits long, jumped up ten cubits, and struck Og in the ankle and killed him.' That places Og's ankle around thirty cubits above the ground, which is more than three times the length of the bed.
rungs.evidence: Sefaria API, https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Berakhot.54b and https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Berakhot.54b?version=english , read this session; English version title given as 'William Davidson Edition - English'. The Aramaic returned includes 'אֵיזֵיל וְאֶיעֱקַר טוּרָא בַּר תְּלָתָא פַּרְסֵי'.
rungs.note: The rabbinic Og is not derived from the bed. If the bed were read as a height gauge, this passage would be impossible.

rungs.witness: Vulgate, Deuteronomy 3:11 (Latin)
rungs.date: Jerome translated the Pentateuch from the Hebrew in the 390s CE. Read here in a printed Latin Vulgate text online, not in an early codex.
rungs.reads: Bed again, and a race of giants: 'Solus quippe Og rex Basan restiterat de stirpe gigantum. Monstratur lectus ejus ferreus, qui est in Rabbath filiorum Ammon, novem cubitos habens longitudinis, et quatuor latitudinis ad mensuram cubiti virilis manus.' Og is 'de stirpe gigantum', of the stock of giants, which is a classification, and the measurements attach to the 'lectus ferreus', the iron bed. No height is stated.
rungs.evidence: Latin read this session at https://www.drbo.org/lvb/chapter/05003.htm , which returned the sentence exactly as quoted.
rungs.note: Jerome's 'de stirpe gigantum' is where the English word giant enters this verse. The Hebrew has Rephaim, a people name, not a size word.

rungs.witness: Septuagint, Deuteronomy 3:11 (Greek)
rungs.date: The Greek Pentateuch is conventionally placed in the third century BCE. The complete Greek codices carrying Deuteronomy are fourth century CE and later. Consulted here in digital editions of the Greek and in Brenton's 1851 English, not in a manuscript.
rungs.reads: Bed, not tomb: 'ἡ κλίνη αὐτοῦ κλίνη σιδηρᾶ', his bed a bed of iron, with 'ἐννέα πηχῶν τὸ μῆκος' and 'τεσσάρων πηχῶν τὸ εὖρος' and the unit 'ἐν πήχει ἀνδρός'. Brenton's English: 'the length of it is nine cubits, and the breadth of it four cubits, according to the cubit of a man'. No height is given for Og.
rungs.evidence: Greek read this session at https://www.blueletterbible.org/lxx/deu/3/1/s_156001 ; Brenton's English of the same verse read at https://biblehub.com/sep/deuteronomy/3.htm , which returned the full sentence quoted above. I did not inspect a Septuagint codex, so this rung is filed as a printed witness.
rungs.note: The Greek translators read the Hebrew ʿereś as a bed. That is relevant because the sarcophagus reading is often presented as if it were the plain sense.

rungs.witness: Targum Onkelos, Deuteronomy 3:11 (Aramaic)
rungs.date: Composition conventionally placed in the early centuries CE, with the date genuinely open. Read here in vocalised printed and digital editions, not in a dated manuscript.
rungs.reads: Gives the same nine by four cubits but changes the measuring unit. Where the Hebrew ends 'בְּאַמַּת־אִֽישׁ', by the cubit of a man, Onkelos ends 'בְּאַמַּת מְלַךְ', by the cubit of a king. It also renders Rephaim as 'גִּבָּרַיָּא', mighty ones. The bed is 'עַרְסָא דְפַרְזְלָא', a bed of iron.

rungs.note: This matters for the arithmetic. A royal cubit and a common cubit are not the same length, so the Aramaic tradition and the Hebrew tradition do not yield the same number of metres from the same number of cubits. I did not attempt to fix a value for either unit.

rungs.witness: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 4.98
rungs.date: Written about 93 to 94 CE. The Greek survives in medieval copies, and what was read this session is William Whiston's English translation of 1737, not a manuscript.
rungs.reads: Treats the bed as an index of Og's bulk while giving no figure for his height. Whiston: 'And men could easily guess at his strength and magnitude when they took his bed at Rabbath, the royal city of the Ammonites; its structure was of iron, its breadth four cubits, and its length a cubit more than double thereto.' The length is therefore nine cubits, as in Deuteronomy, and the inference Josephus draws is 'strength and magnitude', not a number.
rungs.evidence: https://lexundria.com/j_aj/4.98/wst read this session, giving the sentence quoted above. The immediately preceding sections were checked at https://lexundria.com/j_aj/4.96/wst and https://lexundria.com/j_aj/4.97/wst to confirm the bed passage sits at 4.98 and not at 4.96 or 4.97. The same wording appears in Whiston's Book 4, chapter 5, at https://sacred-texts.com/jud/josephus/ant-4.htm .
rungs.note: This is the point at which the bed is on record as being used to argue about Og's size. It is worth noticing what Josephus does not do, which is state a height.

chain.floor: The witnesses reached this session leave a measured object and an unmeasured man. Deuteronomy 3:11 in the Tiberian Hebrew, and in the Greek, Latin and Aramaic versions consulted here, gives nine cubits by four for the thing at Rabbah and attaches no figure to Og's body. Nine cubits at an 18 inch cubit is thirteen and a half feet, about 4.1 metres, so the four metre number is the length of the object, and the NET Bible prints that number for what it translates as a sarcophagus. Josephus, writing about 94 CE and surviving in later copies, already reasons from the bed to Og's 'strength and magnitude', which shows the inference is old, but he supplies no height either. Readers who did convert bed into body reached different answers: Maimonides worked from a bed a third longer than its occupant to six cubits and a little more, Rashi took the cubit to be Og's own while Ibn Ezra rejected that and allowed roughly double an ordinary man, and the Talmudic passages drop the bed's arithmetic and put Og's ankle at about thirty cubits and his thigh bone at three parasangs. Whether the object was furniture is contested in print, and a 2011 study in the Catholic Biblical Quarterly quotes a Babylonian text describing Marduk's bed at the same nine cubits by four, which suggests the figures may be a literary measure rather than a survey of a particular piece.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Bed, or basalt box
scholarlyNotes.body: Deuteronomy 3:11 says that Og's 'eres was an 'eres barzel, an iron 'eres, nine cubits long and four wide, lying in Rabbah of the Ammonites. Scholarly translations do not agree on the noun. The Revised JPS Tanakh of 2023 keeps the furniture: "His bedstead, an iron bedstead, is now in Rabbah of the Ammonites; it is nine cubits long and four cubits wide, by the standard cubit!" The NET Bible reads a burial container instead, "his sarcophagus was made of iron", and its translators' note argues that 'eres here denotes a basaltic stone box, the dark iron-like rock of the region supplying the description of it as iron. That note sends readers to a 1990 discussion by A. R. Millard in Bible Review. The difference decides what the verse is doing. On the sarcophagus reading it points at a funerary monument a traveller could be shown, which suits the challenge in the Hebrew, is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites. On the bedstead reading it is a trophy and a measure of the man. Both translations take the closing qualification as a standard cubit rather than a giant's; NET converts the figures to thirteen and a half feet by six.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Rephaim, rpum, and two towns
scholarlyNotes.body: Og is what remained of the Rephaim in Deuteronomy 3:11, a living population listed in Deuteronomy 2 alongside the Anakim, Emim and Zamzummim. The same word names the dead elsewhere. At Isaiah 26:14 rephaim stands in parallel with metim, and the Revised JPS gives "Shades, they can never rise". Ugaritic has a matching term, rpum. Whether Hebrew preserves one word whose sense moved between a people and their ancestral shades, or two words that fell together, has been argued since the Ras Shamra tablets were published. Conrad l'Heureux, "The Ugaritic and Biblical Rephaim", Harvard Theological Review 67 (1974), 265-274, and Jonathan Yogev, The Rephaim: Sons of the Gods (Brill, 2021), which opens with a long survey of the Ugaritic material, are two places to watch the argument run. One detail keeps it alive. Deuteronomy 1:4 places Og at Ashtaroth and at Edrei; a Ugaritic text catalogued as KTU 1.108 attaches those two place names to a figure called Rapi'u. Matthew McAffee took the pairing up in 2022, under the title "Biblical King Og and the Ugaritic Deity Rapi'u: Sorting Out Two Figures in Light of the Rephaim and the Toponyms Ashtaroth and Edrei". The title states the caution: two figures, joined by geography and vocabulary, not one.

scholarlyNotes.heading: How Og got bigger
scholarlyNotes.body: The colossal Og of popular retelling is largely rabbinic, and two Talmudic passages carry most of it. Berakhot 54b has him try to crush the Israelite camp: "He went, uprooted a mountain three parasangs long, and brought it on his head." God sends grasshoppers, which pierce the peak so that it drops round his neck, and Moses, "ten cubits tall", takes "an axe ten cubits long", jumps ten cubits and strikes the ankle. Niddah 24b arrives at the same scale from the other end, through Abba Shaul the gravedigger, who chased a deer three parasangs inside a thighbone without reaching the end of it and was told by the Sages whose it had been. Niddah 61a makes Og and Sihon brothers, sons of Ahijah son of Shamhazai, and refers to Og as one "who was saved from the punishment of the generation of the flood". These passages are homiletic and read as such: they are arguments about Moses, merit and fear, not reports of measurement. Quotations follow the English translation on Sefaria.

handling.living: Og of Bashan appears in the Hebrew Bible (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Psalms) and is a fixture of the Babylonian Talmud and later midrash, so he sits within scripture and rabbinic literature actively studied today by living Jewish communities (and read as scripture by Christians), unlike a dead pantheon figure. He has no independent cult, festival, or devotional status of his own; he functions within liturgical recital (Psalms 135-136) and as a stock figure of rabbinic legend expansion (Berakhot, Niddah) rather than as an object of belief in himself.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening is presenting the vastly exaggerated rabbinic legend material (surviving the Flood by clinging to the ark, hurling mountains at Israel, a thighbone requiring days to traverse) as if it were in the Torah text itself, when the actual biblical account is a brief conquest narrative with one aside about an iron bedstead of stated dimensions and no stated height for Og. A second distortion is asserting confidently that the iron object was 'really' a basalt sarcophagus rather than a bed, treating a plausible modern scholarly proposal as settled fact when the ancient versions (Septuagint, Vulgate, Targum Onkelos) all read it as a bed.
handling.take: The biblical text and the rabbinic expansions are both public-domain ancient sources and freely usable, but keep them distinct in your telling: attribute the bedstead-at-Rabbah account to Deuteronomy 3, and attribute the flood-survival, mountain-throwing and giant-thighbone material explicitly to the Talmud and midrash as later homiletic elaboration, not as scripture. Treat this as Hebrew Bible and Talmudic material with the same respect you'd give any actively-studied religious text, present the bed-vs-sarcophagus question as genuinely open rather than resolved, and avoid overstating what's known about the Rephaim, whose status as a historical people versus a term for ancestral shades is itself contested.
handling.cite: Cite Deuteronomy 3:1-13 and Numbers 21:33-35 for the core narrative, Psalms 135:11 and 136:20 for the liturgical afterlife, and Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 54b, Niddah 24b and Niddah 61a for the rabbinic legendary expansion, clearly marked as later elaboration rather than the biblical account.

atlas.fullDescription: Atlas, a Titan of the generation before the Olympians, stands at the western edge of the world holding the sky away from the earth. The punishment is the portrait: he is remembered almost entirely as a posture.
atlas.mysteryNote: If he ever shrugs, the stars will fall. The mountains have not yet moved. Neither, it seems, has he.
atlas.fate: Still holds up the sky at the world's western edge, in the older telling.

sections.story:
The Titans lost. That is the fact everything about Atlas follows from.

When Zeus and the Olympians broke the older gods, most of the defeated were thrown into Tartarus. Atlas was given something more specific. Hesiod places him at the world's western limit, holding up the wide sky with his head and tireless hands, and the word he uses carries the sense of unrelenting necessity: not a sentence with an end date, but a job that is now simply how the cosmos is arranged.

Later tellings soften the geometry. He becomes the bearer of a sphere rather than only the separator of sky from earth. The sphere is ancient: Apollodorus has Heracles take the celestial sphere from Atlas, and the Farnese Atlas (about 150 CE) shows a constellation-marked globe. What is post-classical is the terrestrial globe and the use of "atlas" for a book of maps, from Mercator's Atlas of 1595. The older image remains a man keeping sky and earth apart.

Two visitors interrupt him. Heracles, sent for the golden apples of the Hesperides that grow in Atlas's own country, offers to take the weight while Atlas fetches them. Atlas returns with the apples and no intention of resuming the load, and Heracles asks him to hold it briefly while he pads his shoulders: then walks away. The strongest figure in the story is beaten by the oldest trick in it.

Perseus arrives with the head of Medusa and receives no hospitality, so he uses it, and Atlas becomes the mountain range in north-west Africa that still carries the name. That version and the sky-holding version cannot both be true, and the tradition never tried to reconcile them.
sections.origins:
Hesiod's Theogony, composed around 700 BCE, is the earliest full account: Atlas as son of the Titan Iapetus, stationed at the world's edge under harsh compulsion. The detail is brief and assumes an audience that already knows him.

Homer's Odyssey mentions him differently: Book 1 calls him the one who knows the depths of every sea and holds the pillars that keep earth and sky apart. Pillars, not shoulders. The image was still moving.

The apples episode is developed by later mythographers, most usefully Apollodorus in the Bibliotheca, a systematising handbook probably of the first or second century CE that survives as our most complete narrative source for much of this material. Ovid's Metamorphoses IV supplies the petrification by Perseus.

The Atlas Mountains and the Atlantic Ocean both take their names from him, which means the geography is repeating a story every time it is written down.
sections.disputed:
Whether Atlas began as a Greek figure at all is an open question. The name has no secure Greek etymology, and proposals ranging from a pre-Greek substrate word to a North African or Near Eastern origin have all been argued without resolution.

The relationship between the sky-bearer and the mountain is unresolved in a different way. It is not clear whether the mountain was named after the myth, the myth grew out of a way of talking about the mountain, or the two traditions were independent and later joined. Ancient authors already disagreed.

Sky-bearing itself is not distinctively Greek (Egyptian, Vedic and other traditions arrange the heavens by similar means), but the resemblance is loose enough that it may show a common way of solving an obvious problem rather than any shared inheritance.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Etymology: the bearer, or not Greek at all
scholarlyNotes.body: Greek speakers themselves heard the name as transparent, connecting it with tlenai, to bear or endure. The standard Indo-European analysis follows that instinct: copulative a- prefixed to the root *telh2-, to uphold or support, reshaped as an nt-stem, giving roughly the one who bears. Robert S. P. Beekes rejects this in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Brill, 2010), classing the name as Pre-Greek and pointing to the -ant- ending as characteristic of the substrate vocabulary he reconstructs. That verdict cannot be taken on its own, because the category it rests on is itself under argument: Oliver Simkin, reviewing the dictionary in The Classical Review 61 (2011), and Miles Beckwith in Classical World 105 (2012), both credit the work while objecting that Pre-Greek is reached for too readily across the whole dictionary. A third proposal, which circulates without a settled proponent, takes the name from Berber adrar, mountain, which would make the sky-bearer secondary to the range rather than its source. None of the three has carried the field, and the entry is right to leave the question open.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The pillar and the mountain
scholarlyNotes.body: The entry notes that the image was still moving, and the two ancient poets differ in a way worth being precise about. At Odyssey 1.52-54, in Walter Shewring's rendering, Atlas knows the depths of all the seas and guards "the tall pillars that keep the sky and earth apart": he attends the pillars, he is not one. Hesiod puts the load on the body. At Theogony 517-520 he "upholds the wide heaven with unwearying head and arms", standing at the borders of the earth before the Hesperides, and the same posture returns at 746-748, before the house of Night. The pillar language survives outside poetry. Herodotus, at Histories 4.184, describes a mountain in north-west Africa called Atlas, small in circuit, rounded, and so lofty its summits are never clear of cloud, and reports that the people living around it call it "the pillar of the heaven" and are themselves called Atlantes. Whether Herodotus preserves a local Libyan usage or a Greek name already exported onto the range is exactly the question the entry leaves unresolved.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The sphere is not a Renaissance invention
scholarlyNotes.body: The globe on Atlas's shoulders is older than the entry allows, though what he carries in antiquity is a celestial sphere and not the earth. Apollodorus, at Bibliotheca 2.5.11, has Prometheus advise Heracles to relieve Atlas of the celestial sphere and send him for the apples rather than go himself. The Farnese Atlas, a marble of about 150 CE in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, shows him stooped under a sphere roughly 65 cm across carved with constellation figures. What that sphere records is disputed. Bradley E. Schaefer argued in the Journal for the History of Astronomy 36 (2005) that the constellation positions derive from Hipparchus's lost star catalogue; Dennis W. Duke replied in the same journal, 37 (2006), that the figures disagree too sharply with Hipparchus's surviving work to carry the claim. What is genuinely post-classical is the terrestrial globe, and the use of the name for a bound collection of maps: Gerardus Mercator's Atlas of 1595, which he named for Atlas king of Mauretania, whom he took for an early geographer, rather than for the Titan.

Oliver Simkin, review of Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, The Classical Review 61.1 (2011), 1-3
Miles Beckwith, review of Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, Classical World 105.4 (2012), 558-560

Dennis W. Duke, 'Analysis of the Farnese Globe', Journal for the History of Astronomy 37.1 (2006), 87-100

handling.living: As of the 2020s Atlas belongs to no living faith and no community holds custodial claims on him; ancient Greek religion has no continuous practising body with authority over its myths. He survives instead as common cultural stock: the word for a book of maps, the name of a mountain range and an ocean, an architectural motif, and a byword for carrying weight.
handling.distortions: The commonest mangling is the terrestrial globe: retellings put the whole Earth on his shoulders, when the classical burden is the sky, and the Earth-globe habit descends from Renaissance cartography after Mercator titled his 1595 map book an Atlas. A second mangling is smoothing the tradition into one biography, when the Heracles episode and the petrification by Perseus flatly contradict each other and ancient authors never reconciled them.
handling.take: Take anything: the tireless sky-bearing, the golden apples trick and its shoulder-padding reversal, the petrification, the mountain, the name itself. Decide consciously which burden you mean, since sky and Earth produce different images and different physics, and the contradiction between the Heracles and Perseus versions is itself usable material rather than an error to fix. The one thing to leave is any confident claim about where the figure originally came from; the name has no secure Greek etymology and scholarship has not settled the question, so rooting him firmly in any single pre-Greek or North African source outruns the evidence.
handling.cite: The primary texts are the credit: Hesiod, Theogony 517-520 for the punishment, Apollodorus, Bibliotheca II.5.11 for the apples, and Ovid, Metamorphoses IV.627-662 for the petrification, all long in the public domain in multiple translations.

polyphemus.fullDescription: Polyphemus, son of Poseidon and the nymph Thoosa, keeps flocks on a wild island and knows no assembly, no law and no planted field: only the cave, the cheese-racks, the sheep, and his own hunger.
polyphemus.mysteryNote: The stone still fits some cave mouths along that coast. No one has tried the old seal. Wisdom, or fear: the island does not say.
polyphemus.fate: Blinded by Odysseus; survives, and curses him to Poseidon.

sections.story:
Odysseus goes ashore with twelve men, expecting the exchange that governs the civilised world: a stranger arrives, is fed, and leaves with a gift. He finds a cave stacked with cheeses and lambs and decides to wait for the owner.

The owner arrives, rolls a stone across the entrance that no twenty wagons could shift, and asks who they are. Told about guest-right, he answers that the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus, and eats two of the men. He eats two more in the morning. The trap is complete: kill him in his sleep and the survivors starve behind a door they cannot move.

So Odysseus gives his name as Nobody, gets the giant drunk on unmixed wine, and drives a sharpened olive stake into the single eye. Polyphemus roars for help and the other Cyclopes gather outside. Who is hurting you? Nobody. They leave. In the morning he opens the cave to let the sheep out to pasture and feels along their backs for escaping men, and the men leave underneath, roped beneath the bellies.

Then Odysseus makes his mistake. Safe offshore, he cannot resist shouting his real name. Polyphemus prays to his father, and Poseidon grants it, and ten years of sea follow.

A separate tradition gives him a wholly different life: in Theocritus and later in Ovid he is a lovesick herdsman singing badly to the sea-nymph Galatea, pitiable rather than terrifying. Both versions were current at once.
sections.origins:
Homer's Odyssey Book 9 is the source everything else answers to, and it was already old when it was written down: late eighth or seventh century BCE on many estimates, drawing on oral material of uncertain age.

The pastoral Polyphemus belongs to a later Hellenistic taste. Theocritus, writing in the third century BCE, makes him a comic lover in Idylls VI and XI; Ovid reworks the same triangle of Polyphemus, Galatea and Acis in Metamorphoses XIII, where the jealous giant crushes his rival with a boulder.

Euripides had meanwhile put the Homeric episode on stage as the satyr play Cyclops, our only complete surviving example of the form.

Hesiod's Cyclopes are a different set entirely: Brontes, Steropes and Arges, smiths who forge Zeus's thunderbolt. The tradition has at least two unrelated groups of one-eyed beings under one name.
sections.disputed:
The blinded-ogre story is not exclusive to Homer. Versions in which a trapped hero blinds a one-eyed cave-dweller and escapes among the flock have been recorded across Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, and folklorists catalogue them as a single international tale type.

Whether these descend from Homer, feed into him from older oral tradition, or represent independent tellings of the same situation has been argued for over a century without settlement. The escape-under-the-sheep detail appears in versions with no plausible route from Greek literature, which has been the main argument that Homer was working with existing material rather than inventing it. Because that escape is itself part of the standard type description (AaTh 1137), using its presence as proof is close to circular, and sceptics (among them O'Sullivan 1987 and Gousopoulos 2025) attack exactly that inference.

A sharper split runs between the blinding and the false name. Comparative study since Nyrop has treated them as separable. Hackman found Homer's form of the name trick in only one folk variant (from Anjou), and there in a tale without a Cyclops. On that reading Homer's distinctive move is not the ruse under the sheep but the substitution of Nobody for Self, so the pun survives in the third person.

A long-standing suggestion that the Cyclops was inspired by dwarf elephant skulls found in Sicilian caves, the central nasal opening read as an eye socket, is popular but has no ancient support and is not accepted by most scholars.

chain.claim: The trick in Odyssey 9, where Odysseus gives his name as Nobody and then blinds the Cyclops and escapes under the sheep, was invented by Homer for the poem, and the folk versions collected later across Europe and Asia are descendants of it.
chain.verdict: The surviving documents split the claim rather than settling it: the blinding and the escape under the flock are attested in traditions that scholars have long declined to derive from the poem, while the false name is argued about on separate grounds, and recent work warns against reconstructing what stood behind Homer at all.

rungs.witness: Dimitrios Gousopoulos, Homer's Polyphemus and Modern Tales: A Fresh Reading of Old Arguments, Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 65 (2025) 291 to 321
rungs.reads: The most recent voice, and the one closest to the claim, though it does not reach it. It reports Denys Page's position that the Odyssey episode is a fusion of two separate folk tales, one an ogre who eats men and is blinded and one a hero who escapes by giving a false name, typically Myself, and that the drunkenness and the name trick were Homer's own additions. Gousopoulos himself is sceptical that anything can be reconstructed behind the poem, quoting Burgess that no monolithic pre-Homeric tale type can be reconstructed on the basis of the modern folktales, and holds that Homer produced an original amalgamation. Scepticism about reconstructing the source is not the same as evidence that there was none.
rungs.evidence: Fetched https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/17108/7608/23277, which returned the title, author, journal, volume 65, year 2025, pages 291 to 321, the Page summary, the Burgess quotation and the Nyrop footnote.
rungs.note: This article was reached through a page fetching tool, not downloaded and read line by line, because the host refuses direct connections from this machine. I have kept quotation marks off its running prose for that reason and quoted only the short Burgess phrase it reproduces. The Nyrop citation it gives matches Hackman's independently, which is a check on both.

rungs.witness: Oskar Hackman, Die Polyphemsage in der Volksuberlieferung, academic dissertation, Helsingfors 1904
rungs.reads: The largest test of the claim, and it comes out against both halves, with reservations he states himself. On the blinding: he opens by saying the whole character of the Homeric telling shows plainly that it, "wie viele andere Episoden der Odyssee, aus der Volkssage geschöpft ist", and that no researcher so far has doubted that not all the folk tellings can go back to the epic as their only source. On the false name: he concludes that the epic borrowed it from a separate folktale, "Aus diesem Märchen hat aller Wahrscheinlichkeit nach das homerische Epos seine Niemandepisode entlehnt, die ja, wie im vorigen Kapitel dargetan wurde, den rein volkstümlichen Varianten der Polyphemsage unbekannt ist", the tale in question being the one where the trickster calls himself Self. He also records that the Homeric form of the name appears in only one folk variant he accepts as genuine, an Anjou fairy tale where the answer is Personne, and he leaves the question open at the end: "Möglich ist es ja übrigens immerhin, dass neben dem Selbst auch das Niemand schon seit Alters in der Volksüberlieferung vorkam." Against himself he sets out that the shouting Cyclopes in five variants may be a residue of the Nobody episode, in which case either it did belong to the folk groundform or those variants go back partly to the poem.

Sebillot, Contes des provinces de France, Paris 1884, no. 28, page 171 following. The variant numbers run to N:r 221.
rungs.note: Quotations are from an optical reading of a 1904 print. I have silently normalised the scan's quotation marks and the one place it renders dass as däss; the words themselves are as printed. Hackman's Anjou variant is worth knowing about: it has the answer Personne but it is not a Polyphemus story at all, it is a burned fairy tale, which is exactly his point.

rungs.witness: Kristoffer Nyrop, Sagnet om Odysseus og Polyphem, Nordisk Tidsskrift for Filologi, new series volume 5, pages 216 to 255
rungs.reads: It is the first study to separate the two halves of the claim. Nyrop greatly enlarged the body of variants and argued that the Nobody episode did not originally belong to the Polyphemus story at all but to a different circle of tales. Hackman states his contribution as: "dass die Niemandepisode ursprünglich nicht der Polyphemsage, sondern einem andern Märchenkreise angehört hat."
rungs.evidence: Hackman 1904, printed page 3, read verbatim in /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/bub_gb_cIHYAAAAMAAJ.pdf, with the footnote giving the journal as Nordisk Tidsskrift for Filologi, Ny raekke V, pages 216 to 255. The same article is cited as "K. Nyrop, 'Sagnet om Odysseus og Polyphem,' Nord.Tidsskr.Filol. 5 (1880) 216–255" in Gousopoulos 2025, fetched from https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/17108/7608/23277.

The year does not read cleanly in the Hackman scan, where the digits come out as 1831; I have taken 1880 from the 2025 citation, and the surrounding argument in Hackman, who places Nyrop two decades after Grimm's 1857 paper and shortly before Krek's of 1887, fits 1880.

rungs.witness: Wilhelm Grimm, Die Sage von Polyphem, Abhandlungen der koniglichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, philosophisch-historische Classe, 1857
rungs.date: 1857, reprinted in Grimm, Kleinere Schriften IV (Gutersloh 1887) pages 428 to 462
rungs.reads: The first study to treat the tale as a comparative problem. Grimm assembled ten variants, pressed the point that the story is spread far too widely to be derived from the Greek poem, and reported Diez's Oghuz version, though he did not accept Diez's own explanation of how Homer would have met it. He is silent on the false name as a separable element.

An 1857 printed copy is scanned at https://archive.org/details/diesagevonpolyp00unkngoog, whose title page names the Abhandlungen of the Berlin academy for 1857.

rungs.witness: Heinrich Friedrich von Diez, Der neuentdeckte oghuzische Cyklop verglichen mit dem homerischen, Halle and Berlin 1815
rungs.reads: It publishes the Dresden Oghuz giant and argues against the claim directly, treating Depegoz as the model behind Homer's Polyphemus rather than a descendant of him. That is the first published statement that the Greek poem is not the origin of the story.

Diez, Der neuentdeckte oghuzische Cyklop verglichen mit dem homerischen, Halle u. Berlin 1815". A scan is held at https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_nAK6AAAAIAAJ and a catalogue record at https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/006188372. Diez's position is recorded here on the authority of the Dresden library's reception page and of Hackman's and Grimm's use of him, not on the authority of his own words.

rungs.witness: Kitab-i Dedem Korkut, Dresden, Sachsische Landesbibliothek, shelfmark Mscr.Dresd.Ea.86
rungs.date: 16th century copy of Oghuz Turkic material of older and disputed date
rungs.reads: It carries the story of the one-eyed giant Depegoz, or Depe Ghoz, killed by Basat. In the summary that reached western scholarship the hero is blinded by nothing: the giant is blinded, with a heated slaughtering knife driven into his single eye, and the hero then escapes by wrapping himself in the fleece of a ram he has killed and passing between the giant's legs. There is no false name in it.
rungs.evidence: Shelfmark and date checked at https://www.slub-dresden.de/en/explore/manuscripts/kitab-i-dedem-korkut which gives Mscr.Dresd.Ea.86, dates the manuscript to the 16th century and states that it contains 12 tales. The content of the giant episode was read in Hackman 1904, variant N:r 118, at /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/bub_gb_cIHYAAAAMAAJ.pdf printed pages 99 to 101, which gives the blinding with the glowing Schlachtmesser, the hiding among the sheep, the ram fleece, the ring and the beheading, and no name trick at any point.
rungs.note: I did not read this manuscript. What I verified is that it exists under that shelfmark with that dating, and what a chain of published summaries says its giant episode contains. Hackman notes at printed page 101 that the Oghuz work in which the tale sits was placed by Grimm in the 13th or 14th century.

rungs.witness: Homer, Odyssey IX (Greek text, book 9 lines 105 to 566)
rungs.date: Composed probably 8th to 7th century BCE. Not a surviving object of that date: the poem reaches us through Ptolemaic papyri and medieval manuscripts, and the text consulted here is A. T. Murray's printed Greek (Loeb Classical Library, London and New York 1919) in the Perseus digital edition.
rungs.reads: It tells the trick and says nothing whatever about where the trick came from. It makes no claim of novelty. What it does carry is a pun that only functions in Greek: Odysseus says his name at 9.366, the neighbouring Cyclopes ask their question at 9.405 to 406 with the words me tis, Polyphemus answers at 9.408, and at 9.414 Odysseus credits his own metis. The blinding stands at 9.375 onward and the ram escape at 9.425 to 435. On the question of invention the poem is silent.
rungs.evidence: Downloaded https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit/master/data/tlg0012/tlg002/tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2.xml to /tmp/od.xml. The TEI header names the editor as Augustus Taber Murray and the source as The Odyssey with an English Translation, London, William Heinemann, and New York, G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1919, Loeb Classical Library. Extracting book 9 gave, verbatim: line 366 Οὖτις ἐμοί γʼ ὄνομα· Οὖτιν δέ με κικλήσκουσι ; line 406 ἦ μή τίς σʼ αὐτὸν κτείνει δόλῳ ἠὲ βίηφιν; ; line 408 ὦ φίλοι, Οὖτίς με κτείνει δόλῳ οὐδὲ βίηφιν. ; line 414 ὡς ὄνομʼ ἐξαπάτησεν ἐμὸν καὶ μῆτις ἀμύμων. ; line 433 τοῦ κατὰ νῶτα λαβών, λασίην ὑπὸ γαστέρʼ ἐλυσθεὶς.
rungs.note: The same line 408 is quoted by Hackman in 1904 as Odyssee IX 408, which lets the two witnesses be checked against each other.

chain.floor: Odyssey 9 tells the trick and says nothing about where the trick came from. The poem makes no claim to have invented anything, and it is not an object of its own age: it reaches us through papyri and medieval copies, and what I read was a printed Greek text of 1919. What the Greek itself carries is a pun that works only in Greek. Odysseus gives his name at 9.366, the Cyclopes outside frame their question with me tis at 9.405 to 406, Polyphemus answers at 9.408 with the same sound as a name, and at 9.414 Odysseus credits his metis. That is a solid reason to think the wording of the name was shaped in Greek, by a Greek poet, for Greek ears. It is not a reason to think the situation was: a man trapped in a cave by a one-eyed eater of men, blinding him and leaving under the animals. On that, the poem gives no evidence in either direction, and everything the argument turns on has to be brought in from outside it.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Much spoken of, and Nobody
scholarlyNotes.body:
Polyphemos is transparent Greek: polys, much, and pheme, speech or report. Liddell-Scott-Jones separates three senses, and the Odyssey supplies two of them. At 22.376 the adjective describes Phemios the singer, glossed there "abounding in songs and legends"; at 2.150 it describes the agore, the assembly, "many-voiced, wordy". The third sense, "much spoken of, famous", LSJ finds in Parmenides, where a road is polyphemos. Which sense the Cyclops carries is not settled, and the name was not coined for him: Homer gives the same formula, antitheon Polyphemon, to a Lapith at Iliad 1.264 and to the Cyclops at Odyssey 1.70.

The pseudonym is sharper in Greek than in English. Odysseus says his name is Outis, Nobody (9.366). When the giant shouts that Outis is killing him (9.408), the Cyclopes outside answer with the other Greek negative, me tis (9.410), and me tis sounds like metis, cunning. Homer sets the two together himself at 9.414, where the name and the faultless metis share a line. Naming in the poem is the subject of Norman Austin, "Name Magic in the Odyssey", California Studies in Classical Antiquity 5 (1972).

scholarlyNotes.heading: One tale type, and a hundred and seventy years of argument
scholarlyNotes.body: Folklorists file the blinded-ogre story as type 1137, which the Aarne-Thompson catalogue titles "The Ogre Blinded (Polyphemus). Escape under ram's belly", so the detail the entry singles out is written into the type description itself. The argument begins with Wilhelm Grimm, Die Sage von Polyphem (Berlin 1857), who derived the European versions from a proto-tale independent of Homer, and turns on the corpus built by the Finnish folklorist Oskar Hackman, Die Polyphemsage in der Volksueberlieferung (Helsinki 1904), which assembled 221 related stories. Denys Page, The Homeric Odyssey (Oxford 1955), argued from that corpus that Homer fused existing folk material, and Justin Glenn takes the pre-Homeric tale as his starting point in Greece and Rome 25 (1978) 141-155. The other side is as old. J. N. O'Sullivan, "Observations on the Kyklopeia", Symbolae Osloenses 62 (1987) 5-24, dismantled Page's criteria, and Dimitrios Gousopoulos, "Homer's Polyphemus and Modern Tales", Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 65 (2025) 291-321, restates the case that the modern versions descend from Homer and that Hackman's catalogue is methodologically unsound. Julien d'Huy has meanwhile run the variants through phylogenetic software and argued for a prehistoric date; Gousopoulos treats that reconstruction as speculative.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The elephant skull
scholarlyNotes.body:
The fossil explanation has an author and a date. The Austrian palaeontologist Othenio Abel proposed in Die Tiere der Vorwelt (1914) that skulls of the Sicilian dwarf elephant Palaeoloxodon falconeri lay behind the one-eyed giant, the large central nasal opening that carried the trunk being read as a single socket. Adrienne Mayor's The First Fossil Hunters (Princeton 2000, revised 2011) carried the idea to a general readership, and it now circulates in popular writing, and in press coverage of screen adaptations, as though it were established.

Classicists have been cooler. Mercedes Aguirre and Richard Buxton, in Cyclops: The Myth and Its Cultural History (Oxford 2020), object that the proposal is unfalsifiable, and that what is missing is a chain of argument connecting the skulls to the stories rather than a bare resemblance between them. That is the shape of the objection generally. Nobody disputes that the dwarf elephants existed, that Greeks could have dug up their skulls, or that the skulls look startling. The gap is between the skull and the poem, and it has not been closed.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Polyphemus belongs to no living faith and no community holds custodial claims on him; ancient Greek religion has no continuous practising body with authority over its myths. He survives as classical literature and as raw material for the international "blinded ogre" folktale type (AaTh 1137), both fully in the public domain.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening collapses the two wholly separate Polyphemus traditions into one figure: the murderous cave-dwelling Cyclops of Homer and the lovesick, comic herdsman of Theocritus and Ovid are different characters serving different genres, and blending them muddies both. Retellings also routinely present the Nobody trick and the escape-under-the-sheep as Homer's own invention, when comparative folklore scholarship treats these as part of a much older and wider international tale type that Homer was drawing on, not originating.
handling.take: Everything is freely usable: the guest-right violation, the blinding, the Nobody pun, the escape beneath the flock, and separately the pastoral lover-of-Galatea tradition, each treated as its own distinct strand rather than merged into a single "true" version. Present the folktale-type question (whether Homer invented or inherited the trick) as a genuinely open, long-argued scholarly debate rather than settling it, and specifically avoid citing the escape-under-the-sheep detail as proof of Homer's originality, since scholars note that inference is close to circular. The dwarf-elephant-skull theory for the one-eye motif is popular but has no ancient support and should be flagged as speculative if mentioned at all.
handling.cite: Cite Homer's Odyssey IX.105-566 as the anchor text, with Euripides' Cyclops, Theocritus's Idylls VI and XI, and Ovid's Metamorphoses XIII.750-897 for the separate traditions; for the folktale-type scholarship, note the AaTh 1137 classification and the Nyrop/Hackman comparative tradition along with more recent critiques (O'Sullivan 1987, Gousopoulos 2025).

enceladus.fullDescription: Enceladus is one of the Giants who rose against the Olympians and lost. He is buried under Sicily, and Mount Etna is what he does about it.
enceladus.mysteryNote: Etna breathes in the night. The old story says it is not only the mountain that breathes.
enceladus.fate: Buried alive under Sicily by Athena; Etna is his breath.

sections.story:
The Gigantomachy is the second war of the Greek cosmos. The Titans had already been beaten; now Gaia, the earth herself, brings forth the Giants to avenge them. They are born from her, they are enormous, and in the older sources they are not snake-legged monsters but armoured warriors: the reptilian lower body is a later artistic convention.

Prophecy holds that the gods cannot finish the Giants alone. A mortal must strike the final blow, so Heracles is brought into the fight, and the Olympians pair off against their opponents.

Enceladus is assigned to Athena. Accounts differ on the manner of it, but the outcome is consistent: she throws the island of Sicily on top of him. He is not killed. He is pinned.

Everything Sicily does afterwards is explained by him. The fire of Etna is his breath, forced up through the rock. Earthquakes are him shifting his weight against a burden he cannot lift. When the mountain rumbles, the giant has turned over. In some versions the eruption is his blood.

The value of this is that it is checkable. Etna is among the most active volcanoes on earth and has been erupting throughout recorded history, so the story is not something told about the distant past: it is a running commentary on an event people were watching. The myth stays alive because the mountain keeps confirming it.
sections.origins:
Apollodorus gives the fullest surviving narrative of the Gigantomachy in Bibliotheca I.6, including the pairings and Athena's use of Sicily.

Euripides refers to Enceladus in passing, and Virgil supplies the most influential poetic version in Aeneid III.578-582, where the giant lies half-burnt beneath Etna and the whole of Sicily trembles when he turns. Roman poets after Virgil repeat and elaborate the image; Claudian gives it a late and vivid treatment.

The Gigantomachy was a major subject in art before it was fixed in prose. The frieze of the Pergamon Altar, built in the second century BCE and now in Berlin, is the most spectacular surviving depiction and shows Athena in combat with a giant usually identified as Alcyoneus rather than Enceladus: an indication of how fluid the assignments were.

Hesiod's Theogony 185 mentions the Giants' birth from Gaia but does not narrate the war.
sections.disputed:
Which giant lies under which volcano is not stable. Enceladus is the usual occupant of Etna, but the mountain is also assigned to Typhon, a wholly different and much more dangerous monster, and the two traditions coexist without reconciliation. Polybotes gets Nisyros by the same logic.

The Giants' relationship to the Titans is likewise inconsistent. Later authors, including Roman ones, frequently conflate the two revolts, and some modern retellings inherit that confusion. In the older Greek scheme they are separate generations fighting separate wars.

Whether the volcano explanations are original to the myth or were attached to an existing set of defeated giants is not determinable from the sources. The pattern of pinning an enemy under a landmark is widespread, and Greek tradition applied it more than once.

handling.living: As of the 2020s this is classical heritage, not a living faith: nobody worships Enceladus or holds his story restricted. He survives as a literary and scientific namesake, most visibly in Saturn's moon Enceladus, and the giant-under-Etna image persists as Sicilian volcano lore rather than belief.
handling.distortions: The commonest mangling is merging the Gigantomachy with the Titanomachy, so the Giants become Titans and the wars collapse into one; Roman authors started this and modern retellings inherit it. The snake-legged body is a later artistic convention, and Enceladus is often swapped for or blended with Typhon, a different monster assigned to the same mountain.
handling.take: Everything here is free: the pinning under Sicily, Athena as his opponent, the breath as Etna's fire, the earthquakes as the giant turning over. The only care needed is internal accuracy, not permission: keep the Giants distinct from the Titans if you want the older Greek scheme, and know that giving Etna to Typhon instead is an equally attested choice, not an error. You may also exploit the fluidity itself, since the ancient sources never settled which giant lies where.
handling.cite: Credit Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.6 for the narrative and Virgil, Aeneid III.578-582 for the poetic image, and see the Pergamon Altar frieze in Berlin for the visual tradition.

antaeus.fullDescription: Antaeus, son of Poseidon and Gaia, wrestles every traveller who crosses his country in Libya, kills them all, and roofs a temple to his father with their skulls. He cannot lose while he is touching the ground.
antaeus.mysteryNote: Sertorius measured bones. History lost the skeleton and kept the number: as it so often does.
antaeus.fate: Lifted off the earth and crushed by Heracles, mid-air.

sections.story:
The rule is simple and it is the whole story. Antaeus is the son of the earth, and while any part of him is in contact with his mother he cannot be exhausted or overcome. Throw him down and he gets up stronger. Every fall is a resupply.

This makes him undefeatable in the ordinary way, and a great many travellers found that out. The skull-roofed temple is the detail that fixes him as something other than a sportsman.

Heracles comes through on his way to the golden apples, is challenged, and wrestles. He throws Antaeus and Antaeus rises renewed. He throws him again with the same result. Somewhere in the repetition Heracles works out what is happening, and this is the part the vase painters loved, lifts him clear of the ground, holds him in the air, and crushes him while he weakens.

It is a rare Greek monster-killing that requires no weapon and no divine assistance, only observation. Heracles wins by noticing a pattern.

The story had a long afterlife. Dante puts Antaeus among the giants ringing the ninth circle, where he lifts Dante and Virgil down into the pit: a giant used as an elevator. Renaissance sculptors returned repeatedly to the moment of the lift, because it is a physically legible image: one man holding another off the floor, and the floor being the point.
sections.origins:
Pindar refers to Antaeus in the fourth Isthmian ode, which makes the story current in the fifth century BCE and probably older.

Apollodorus gives the compact narrative version in Bibliotheca II.5.11, placing him in Libya as a stop on the way to the Hesperides. Lucan expands the episode considerably in Pharsalia IV, where the wrestling is described at length and Antaeus is given a genuinely alarming pedigree.

The scene is common in Greek vase painting from the sixth century BCE onward, generally at the moment Heracles hoists him. Its popularity in art suggests audiences knew it well before the surviving literary treatments were written.

Plutarch (Sertorius 9) reports that the Roman general Sertorius, at Tingis in what is now Morocco, disbelieved the Libyans' claim about Antaeus's remains, had the tomb dug open himself, and only then stood dumbfounded: active scepticism, not a guided display. It is still an early instance of large bones being enlisted as proof.
sections.disputed:
The Libyan setting is not securely explained. It may reflect real Greek contact with North Africa, or it may be the standard practice of placing monsters at the edge of the known world; the two are hard to separate.

Whether the earth-contact rule is original is also uncertain. Pindar mentions Antaeus without it, and it is possible that the detail which now defines him was a later narrative refinement of a simpler wrestling story.

The Tingis skeleton Plutarch describes was almost certainly a fossil, large Miocene mammal remains occur in the region, but the report is secondhand and no examination is possible. It is a clean early example of a myth being retro-fitted with physical evidence, whatever the bones actually were.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Ἀνταῖος: a position, not a person
scholarlyNotes.body:
The name is not originally a name. Ἀνταῖος is an ordinary Greek adjective built on ἄντα, "against, opposite". Liddell, Scott and Jones give two main ranges of sense: "set over against, right opposite", used of a wound taken in the front of the body in Sophocles and in Euripides, and "opposed to, hostile", as of a creature hostile to mortals in Aeschylus, Choephori. Read that way the giant's name states his function rather than his identity: the one who stands facing you, the one you have to get past. The feminine Ἀνταία is separately a cult title of Hecate, which the same lexicon glosses as besought with prayers and cites from Apollonius Rhodius and the Orphic Hymns, so the word was never reserved for the wrestler.

What the Greek does not explain is the North African setting. Roman geography ties Antaeus to Punic harbour towns: Pliny has Tingi founded by him at Natural History 5.2, and puts his royal seat, his fight with Hercules and the gardens of the Hesperides at Lixus at 5.3. A transparently Greek adjective attached to a figure rooted at Phoenician sites is worth noticing, though nothing in the sources settles which came first.

scholarlyNotes.heading: When the earth-contact rule enters the record
scholarlyNotes.body:
Pindar's fourth Isthmian brings Herakles to the house of Antaios in the fifth century BCE, and the line usually quoted for it says little more than that. The rule that now defines him is secure in the mythographers of the imperial period. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.11, calls Antaeus a son of Poseidon who killed strangers by forcing them to wrestle, and has Heracles lift him aloft, break him and kill him, because when he touched the earth he grew stronger; Apollodorus then adds that this was why some said he was a son of Earth. The order of that sentence repays attention. There the earth-contact is the evidence and the parentage is the inference drawn from it, not the other way round.

Lucan works the same material at length in Pharsalia 4, where Antaeus goes down on purpose and rises with renewed strength, and Hercules answers by lifting him clear of the ground and holding him there. Philostratus the Elder, describing a painting at Imagines 2.21, gives Ge an active part: she arches herself up and heaves her son back onto his feet. Three imperial authors, three slightly different mechanisms for one rule.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The tomb at Tingis, and Strabo's refusal
scholarlyNotes.body:
Plutarch, Life of Sertorius 9, is more particular than the story usually told. Sertorius was not shown a skeleton. Having taken Tingis he was told the Libyans buried Antaeus there, disbelieved them because of the size of the tomb, and had it dug open; on finding a body of sixty cubits he was dumbfounded, performed a sacrifice, and had the tomb filled in again. Plutarch then gives the local genealogy: the widow Tinga consorted with Heracles and bore Sophax, who named a city for his mother, and Sophax's son Diodorus ruled many Libyan peoples. Plutarch does not report this neutrally. He says the tale must be put down to a wish to gratify King Juba, whose ancestors were said to descend from Sophax and Diodorus.

Strabo has the same episode at 17.3.8, taken from the Roman historian Gabinius, and files it among the marvellous stories told of Maurusia that he declines to credit. He also places the tomb near Lynx, that is Lixus, rather than at Tingis, and the Loeb translation renders his measurement as sixty feet against Plutarch's sixty cubits. The bones were disputed evidence in antiquity, before any modern reading of them.
