When the towns were finished there was stone left over, and rather than waste it they built one more. That is Hum, which now advertises itself as the smallest town in the world.

After the work they rested at Kotli, where the water falls in steps and where people still walk today.

Dragonja's son Gorazd is said to be in the forests of the Istrian highlands still, watching them.

Set him beside Daidarabotchi in Japan. Both are giants who made a real, named, walkable landscape by working on it while they were alive, which is the opposite of Ymir, who had to die first.
sections.origins:
This is local place-legend from the Mirna valley in central Istria, tied to named ground rather than to any medieval text: the rivers Mirna and Dragonja, the hill towns above them, the water steps at Kotli.

Nineteenth-century collecting in Istria concentrated on song. The circle around the newspaper Naša sloga gathered oral material from 1879, printed as Hrvatske narodne pjesme što se pjevaju po Istri i Kvarnerskih otocih in 1880, and Jakov Volčić recorded songs, tales and proverbs. Prose legend was the poorer relation. Carlo De Franceschi (1809 to 1893), historian of Istria and secretary of the Istrian Diet from 1861 to 1876, is the name cited for giant traditions from the Motovun district.

Systematic prose collecting came in the 1950s, when the Institut za narodnu umjetnost in Zagreb, now the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research, worked across the peninsula. Maja Bošković-Stulli edited the result as Istarske narodne priče (Zagreb, 1959), the first volume of the series Narodno stvaralaštvo Istre, with her introduction and commentary.

The tradition now travels largely through local tourism, which has an interest in it.
sections.disputed:
The most famous Istrian giant, Veli Jože, is not folk tradition in the strict sense. He comes from Vladimir Nazor's novel of 1908, which draws on Istrian material but is an authored work written with a national awakening in mind. He is frequently presented online and in tourist copy as an ancient figure of the coast. He is not. The novel is literary, dated, and attributable.

That does not empty the landscape of giant tradition. Local stories of large builders and land-shapers still attach to hills and caves in Istria and the Croatian littoral, and this entry treats those as the folk layer. Veli Jože is kept out of the account of origins for that reason: mixing him in would smuggle a twentieth-century novel into a medieval and oral dossier. Readers who meet him first should know which century he belongs to.

handling.living: Dragonja is heritage place-legend, not living faith: there is no religious community or custodial body attached to him, and the tradition today is carried mainly by regional tourism (Motovun, Hum, the water-steps at Kotli) and by academic folklore archives such as Maja Bošković-Stulli's Istarske narodne priče (1959). The one thing to watch is that the tourism industry has a commercial stake in the story, which shapes how it's presented but doesn't make it a living cult.
handling.distortions: The biggest hazard is confusing Dragonja with Veli Jože, the far more famous Istrian giant, who is not folk tradition at all but a 1908 authored novel by Vladimir Nazor; tourist copy routinely presents Veli Jože as ancient folklore, and a writer could easily import his beats into Dragonja's entry by mistake. A second distortion is smoothing the giants' hilltop-building into a single unified myth-cycle, when the record is local place-legend attached town by town rather than one coherent narrative.
handling.take: The landscape material is freely usable: Dragonja cutting the furrow that becomes the river, the giants building the hill towns and passing stone between hilltops, Hum built from the leftover stone, the rest at Kotli, and the son Gorazd said to still watch from the highlands. Keep Veli Jože entirely out of this entry since he belongs to a different, dated, attributable twentieth-century author, and don't backdate him into the oral record. The De Franceschi/Bošković-Stulli chain is thin compared to song-collecting from the same region, so avoid overstating how much prose documentation actually exists.
handling.cite: Credit Maja Bošković-Stulli's Istarske narodne priče (Zagreb, 1959) and Carlo De Franceschi's nineteenth-century recording of Motovun-district giant traditions; credit Vladimir Nazor by name and date (1908) if Veli Jože is discussed at all, to keep the literary figure clearly separated from the oral one.

daidarabotchi.fullDescription: Mount Fuji is the soil he dug out of one province. Lake Biwa is the hole he left in another.
daidarabotchi.mysteryNote: No one records a single word he said. Everything known about him is the shape he left in the ground: a lake, a mountain, and a plateau where he lay down.
daidarabotchi.fate: No death: he is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.

sections.story:
Daidarabotchi is a giant of the Kantō and Chūbu regions, known also as Deidarabotchi, Derabotchi and Daidarabō depending on where the story is told. That spread of names is itself evidence: separate local traditions arriving at the same figure.

He built Fuji from earth he scooped out of Kai Province, which is why the land around the mountain is a wide basin. When he needed more he dug again in Ōmi, and that pit filled with water and became Lake Biwa, the largest lake in Japan. He once picked up Fuji and Tsukuba to weigh them against each other and split Tsukuba's summit doing it.

Senba Lake in Ibaraki fills a single one of his footprints. The Takabocchi Plateau in Nagano is where he lay down to rest his back. The towns of Daita and Daitakubo carry his name. The earliest textual trace is in the eighth-century *Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki*, which records a giant seated on a hill eating clams from the beach and piling the shells into mounds.

Unlike almost everything else in this catalogue, he is not a threat. In Ibaraki he is remembered warmly, as a giant who shifted mountains to make life easier for the people below. He is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.
sections.origins:
The oldest written trace is the Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, one of the provincial gazetteers ordered by the edict of 713 and compiled in the decade after it. Its Naka district notice describes a giant on the hill at Ōkushi who reached from the hilltop to the shore for clams, the discarded shells becoming the hill itself. That hill is the Ōgushi shell mound at Shiozaki in Mito, a real Jōmon midden, protected as a national historic site since 1970. The giant there is called only ōhito, a great person. The Harima no Kuni Fudoki carries a comparable figure whose footprints filled with water and became marshes.

The name Daidarabotchi belongs to later oral tradition. Ryūtei Tanehiko noted the word in his miscellany Yōshabako, printed in 1841. The scattered local legends were first gathered as a single body of material by Yanagita Kunio in "Daidarabō no ashiato", published in Chūō Kōron in April 1927 and collected in Hitotsume Kozō sono ta (Koyama Shoten, 1934).
sections.disputed:
The etymology is unsettled. Ryūtei Tanehiko, in his miscellany Yōshabako of 1841, took the word as an insult aimed at large men, the inverse of Issun-bōshi, the one-inch boy. Yanagita derived it from Daitarō-hōshi and read the tara element as an old term of respect for a person of rank. Minakata Kumagusu took daida as a contraction of the personal name Daitarō. A separate proposal, recorded in the Nipponica encyclopedia beside Yanagita's own, links tara to tatara, the foot-bellows of iron smelting, and reads the giant as a trace of the spread of smiths.

What he originally was is also argued. Watanabe Shōgo's Nipponica article on giant legends treats him as a land-making god degraded into a comic figure as belief fell away, in company with oni and tengu. The reverse account, a yōkai tradition swelling into a giant one, also has currency.

The fudoki giants are not named Daidarabotchi. They are ōhito, great people, and the Hitachi text survives only in an abridged recension.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Daidarabotchi is public folklore in Japan, not faith: he survives in place names, in local affection in Ibaraki, and in a 15-metre commemorative statue at Ogushi Kaizuka Park in Mito, and he is familiar nationwide because the night form of the Forest Spirit in Princess Mononoke (1997) carries the name Deidarabotchi. No community claims restricted or sacred status over the material.
handling.distortions: The common manglings are recasting a benevolent land-maker as a rampaging kaiju, and importing the Ghibli Night-Walker's powers over life and death, which belong to the film and not the folklore. A subtler one is flattening dozens of separate regional legends, first assembled by Yanagita in 1927, into a single canonical giant with one fixed biography.
handling.take: The land-shaping deeds are free: building Fuji, digging Lake Biwa, footprint lakes, shell mounds, weighing mountains, and the whole spread of regional name variants. Leave two things: do not name the eighth-century fudoki giants Daidarabotchi, because those texts call them only ohito and the name is centuries later, and do not present the tatara iron-smelting etymology as settled fact, because it is one proposal among several. Keep his temper; the benevolence is the distinctive feature, and a hostile Daidarabotchi is a different giant wearing his name.
handling.cite: Credit Yanagita Kunio's 1927 collection of the footprint legends; for an English-language reference, Matthew Meyer's illustrated yokai database at yokai.com.

baqbaq-devi.fullDescription: Cut off a devi's head and another grows. So the hero did not bring a sword. He brought a riddle.
baqbaq-devi.mysteryNote: Cut one head and another answers. So the hero came carrying a question instead, and kept asking until the last head slept.
baqbaq-devi.fate: Stabbed through the heart by Amirani, after a riddle contest put every head to sleep.

sections.story:
The devi are the giants of the Georgian mountains. They are many-headed, and a severed head simply grows back, which is why Georgian heroes do not win these fights by force. They win by outthinking them, or by striking at the heart.

They live underground or high in the remote Caucasus peaks, usually as a family of seven or nine brothers in a castle with their wives, their children and their hoard. When the ground shakes and a hillside tears loose, that is them.

The strongest of all of them was Baqbaq-Devi, the one the other giants deferred to. Amirani, the great Georgian culture hero, could not beat him in a straight fight and did not try. He challenged the giant to a contest of riddles instead, and used the rhythm of his own voice to put the many heads to sleep one after another. Then he stabbed him through the heart.

The word itself has travelled a long way. Georgian *devi* is kin to the Persian *div* and behind that the Zoroastrian *daeva*, the old Indo-Iranian word for a hostile spirit. The same word surfaces in South Slavic as *div* and in Albanian as *div* and *dif*. One name for a hostile giant, carried along the corridor between the Caspian and the Adriatic.

In one tale Amirani threw a devi into a ravine, and a lake formed where he fell. It is called Devi Lake. In drought the villagers still go there, throw stones into the water, and ask for rain.
sections.origins:
The devi belong to the oral tradition of the Georgian highlands rather than to any single book. The literary trace begins with *Amiran-Darejaniani*, a prose romance attributed to Mose Khoneli and usually placed in the twelfth century, though its surviving manuscripts are seventeenth and eighteenth century copies and it was not printed until Zakaria Chichinadze's edition of 1896.

Systematic collection began in the nineteenth century. Teimuraz Batonishvili published variants of the Amirani legend in 1848 and was the first to link them with Prometheus.

Marjory Wardrop's *Georgian Folk Tales* (London, David Nutt, 1894) carried devi stories into English, translated from the Aghniashvili collection *Khalkhuri Zghaprebi* (Tiflis, 1891) and from Mingrelian and Gurian collections printed at St Petersburg.

Mikheil Chikovani assembled sixty-eight recorded versions of the chained Amirani, taken down across Georgia between 1848 and 1945.
sections.disputed: Amirani, who killed Baqbaq-Devi, was himself chained to a Caucasus peak for bringing fire and metalworking to humanity, with an eagle at his liver by day and the liver regrowing by night, and a dog wearing the chain thin until smiths renew it each year. That is the Prometheus myth point for point. The Greeks placed Prometheus's rock in the Caucasus. Some scholars argue the Georgian version is older, or arose independently, which would put the famous Greek story downstream of this one. The question is open.

handling.living: As of the 2020s the devi are stock antagonists of Georgian folk tales, told to children and printed in school anthologies, while Amirani stands as a national hero whose name Georgians give to football clubs and businesses. This is living national folklore in a Christian country, not worship and not restricted knowledge; no community protocol governing its use is known to this codex, and none is likely, since Georgia has published and exported these tales since the nineteenth century.
handling.distortions: Retellings flatten the devi into dumb ogres who die by the sword, which erases the actual mechanic of the tradition, that severed heads regrow and heroes must win by wit or a strike to the heart. The other common mangle, inherited from the Prometheus parallel, is presenting Amirani as a Georgian copy of a Greek original, when the direction of borrowing is an open scholarly question.
handling.take: The regrowing heads, the riddle contest, the families of seven or nine brothers in mountain castles, and the earthquake explanation are all free; this is published folk literature, in English since Wardrop in 1894. Treat the chained Amirani complex with more care, because it functions as Georgia's national epic, so name it as Georgian rather than folding it into Greek myth. The Devi Lake rain rite is a reported village practice tied to real places; use the motif if you like, but do not attach it to invented Georgian geography as if it were documentation.
handling.cite: Start with Marjory Wardrop, Georgian Folk Tales, London, David Nutt, 1894, which is in the public domain and freely readable at the Internet Archive; for the Amirani scholarship the reference collection is Mikheil Chikovani's corpus of recorded variants.

gigantes.fullDescription: The Greek giants may not have been giants. In the earliest art they are painted as ordinary armed men.
gigantes.mysteryNote: The oldest painters gave them helmets, shields and spears, and nothing stranger than that. The snakes grew later, once losing to gods seemed to require a different sort of body.
gigantes.fate: Defeated by the Olympians and buried under volcanoes. Every eruption is one of them moving.

sections.story:
They were born out of violence. When Cronus castrated Ouranos, the blood fell on Gaia, and from it came three things: the Erinyes, the Meliai, and the Gigantes. In Theogony 185 the adjectives are distributed: Earth bears the strong Erinyes and the great Giants with gleaming armour and long spears. "Great" is theirs; "strong" belongs to the Erinyes. The same line arms them as hoplites, which is more useful than a bare size word.

In archaic and classical art they are shown as hoplites, man-sized and fully human, fighting in armour like anyone else. The snake legs everyone pictures do not appear until after roughly 380 BCE. The defining trait in the earliest material is strength and aggression, not stature.

Alcyoneus was immortal, but only inside his own country, so Heracles dragged him over the border and killed him there. Porphyrion attacked Heracles and Hera, and Zeus made him burn with desire for Hera instead, which was enough of a distraction to finish him. Ephialtes took an arrow in the left eye from Apollo and one in the right from Heracles.

The defeated were buried under volcanoes. Every eruption and every earthquake since is one of them moving.
sections.origins:
Hesiod's Theogony, composed around 700 BCE, gives the earliest surviving account of their birth, at line 185. Homer's Odyssey mentions them three times, as a mortal race in the far west, with no war against the Olympians attached.

There was probably an archaic epic Gigantomachia, now lost. Xenophanes, in the sixth century BCE, lists the battles of Titans, Giants and Centaurs among the stock subjects of symposium song. Pindar supplies early detail, placing the fight at Phlegra and naming Porphyrion as king.

Much of the transmission is visual rather than textual: the north frieze of the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi around 525 BCE, the east metopes of the Parthenon, the peplos woven for Athena at the Panathenaia, and the great frieze of the Pergamon Altar, raised under Eumenes II between roughly 166 and 156 BCE, excavated by Carl Humann from 1878 and now in Berlin.

The fullest connected narrative is late: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.6, compiled in the first or second century CE.
sections.disputed: The war is younger than the giants. Homer knows a savage race in the far west, ruled by Eurymedon, wiped out by their own king for their insolence toward the gods, and knows nothing whatever about a battle with the Olympians. Hesiod gives them a birth but not a war. The Gigantomachy comes later, and later writers went on to confuse the Gigantes with the Titans, an earlier and separate generation. Much of what is now assumed about them is a late assembly.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Earth-born, or simply unexplained
scholarlyNotes.body: Hesiod makes the Giants children of Gaia, born when the blood of the castrated Ouranos fell on the earth, and ancient readers took the name to say as much: gigas was tied to gaia or ge, and the Giants were called gegeneis, earth-born. That derivation is still reprinted in reference material: the etymological note attached to the entry for the Greek word at lsj.gr derives it from gaia, ge, with a possible link to gignomai, to be born. Modern etymology is less confident. The Online Etymology Dictionary, under "giant", states that the Greek word is "of unknown origin, probably from a pre-Greek language", and adds that "Derivation from gegenes 'earth-born' is considered untenable". The disagreement matters beyond philology. If the name means earth-born, the parentage follows from the word. If the word came into Greek from somewhere else and was already opaque, then descent from Gaia is an explanation the Greeks supplied for a name they had inherited and could no longer read.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Armed men first, snakes later
scholarlyNotes.body: Hesiod's Giants arrive equipped. Evelyn-White's Loeb translation of Theogony 176-187 has Earth bear "the strong Erinyes and the great Giants with gleaming armour, holding long spears in their hands": the poet gives them hoplite gear before he gives them anything monstrous. The images were catalogued by Francis Vian, whose Repertoire des gigantomachies figurees dans l'art grec et romain (Klincksieck, 1951) and La guerre des Geants: le mythe avant l'epoque hellenistique (Klincksieck, 1952) are still the base texts. Reviewing Geants et gigantomachies entre Orient et Occident (Centre Jean Berard, 2017), Christopher Smith writes that the new volume "refreshes Vian's admirable early work" rather than displacing it, and notes how unstable the Giants are as a visual type: "many of the early Attic giants are barely identifiable as such except by context". Snake legs are one late option among several, and other hybrid forms stayed regional. In the same volume Linant de Bellefonds treats winged Giants as rare, appearing as an opponent of Athena in Tarentine material of the fourth century.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Who wrote Bibliotheca 1.6, and how it reaches us
scholarlyNotes.body: The connected account at Bibliotheca 1.6 is effectively anonymous. The manuscripts name an Apollodorus, and that name was long attached to Apollodorus of Athens, the scholar born around 180 BCE; chronology rules him out, so the author is conventionally called Pseudo-Apollodorus and the compilation is dated to the first or second century CE. The transmission is narrow. The surviving manuscripts descend from a fourteenth-century codex now in the Bibliotheque nationale de France, and the text breaks off in the Theseus material, the rest being known through two summaries that James George Frazer conflated for his Loeb edition of 1921. The Gigantomachy sits inside the continuous portion and is not touched by that loss. It repays reading against Hesiod, because the birth is not the same. Frazer renders 1.6.1: "But Earth, vexed on account of the Titans, brought forth the giants, whom she had by Sky." No blood of Ouranos, and a motive the earlier account does not give: anger over the Titans.

scholarlySources: Hesiod, Theogony 176-187, translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library 57, 1914
Apollodorus, The Library 1.6.1-2, translated by James George Frazer, Loeb Classical Library 121-122, 1921
Homer, Odyssey 7.56-60 and 7.205-206, translated by A. T. Murray
Francis Vian, Repertoire des gigantomachies figurees dans l'art grec et romain, Klincksieck, 1951
Francis Vian, La guerre des Geants: le mythe avant l'epoque hellenistique, Klincksieck, 1952

Francoise-Helene Massa-Pairault and Claude Pouzadoux (eds), Geants et gigantomachies entre Orient et Occident, Centre Jean Berard, 2017, reviewed by Christopher Smith, Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2018.10.31
Francois Queyrel, L'autel de Pergame: images et pouvoir en Grece d'Asie, Picard, 2005, reviewed by Brunilde Ridgway, Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2005.08.39
Online Etymology Dictionary, entry "giant"
lsj.gr, entry for the Greek headword gigas (LSJ, Pape and Mantoulidis etymological notes)

handling.living: As of the 2020s the Gigantes belong to no living faith; ancient Greek religion has no continuous practising body with authority over the Gigantomachy. They survive purely as literary and art-historical material, most visibly through the Pergamon Altar frieze now in Berlin, which is a museum object and cultural-heritage subject, not a cult site.
handling.distortions: The most common mangling is retrojecting the familiar snake-legged, mountain-sized image back onto the earliest material: archaic and classical sources and art show them as human-scaled hoplites, and the serpent legs only appear in art after roughly 380 BCE. A second is treating Gigantes and Titans as interchangeable, which later antiquity already did but Hesiod's texts keep them as separate generations, and treating the Gigantomachy as an original, unified war-story rather than a later assembly built up from Homer's very different "savage western race" and Hesiod's bare birth notice.
handling.take: Take anything: the birth from Ouranos's blood, the individual death-stories (Alcyoneus dragged over his own border, Porphyrion undone by lust for Hera, Ephialtes blinded by twin arrows), the volcano-burial etiology, the whole Gigantomachy as assembled by Apollodorus. Be deliberate about which visual tradition you're using, since hoplite Gigantes and serpent-legged Gigantes are different images with different eras behind them, and don't silently harmonize Homer's version with the later war-narrative, the discontinuity is real and worth keeping visible rather than smoothing over.
handling.cite: Credit Hesiod's Theogony (line 185) for the birth, Apollodorus's Bibliotheca 1.6 for the fullest connected narrative, and the Pergamon Altar frieze (2nd century BCE, Berlin) for the classic visual Gigantomachy, all long public domain.

patagonian-giants.fullDescription: Fifteen feet in 1520. Four inches taller than a sailor in 1773. Nothing in Patagonia changed. Only who was doing the measuring.
patagonian-giants.mysteryNote: Magellan's men sailed home with a story that held Europe for three centuries. Two of the people in it were taken aboard, and neither reached Spain.
patagonian-giants.fate: Ended by measurement: Bougainville found the tallest at five feet nine in 1767.

sections.story:
The first account comes from Antonio Pigafetta, who chronicled Magellan's voyage in the 1520s. Near what is now Puerto San Julián in Argentina they saw a man on the shore, naked, dancing and singing and throwing sand over his head. Magellan sent a crewman toward him with instructions to dance and sing the same way, to show they meant no harm. The man came, and was afraid, and pointed upward.

From that meeting the giants of Patagonia entered European imagination and stayed for close to three hundred years. Francis Drake's nephew, compiling The World Encompassed in 1628, did not simply repeat the claim: he gives about seven and a half feet and treats earlier reports as exaggerated. Later accounts still put them at twelve feet, then fifteen, then higher.

The collapse came from measurement. Bougainville's Voyage autour du monde (published 1771) reported the tallest Patagonian he met at five feet nine French feet, roughly six English feet and an inch or two. The official account of the Byron voyage in 1773 found them roughly four inches taller than the tallest men in the crew. Europeans of that period averaged around five feet, which accounts for nearly all of it.

The people underneath the story were real: the Tehuelche, from a Mapudungun word meaning fierce people, and possibly the Selk'nam. Both were genuinely taller than the men writing them down.

Magellan took two of them aboard to bring back to Spain. They died on the voyage home.
sections.origins:
This is a European textual tradition rather than an indigenous one, and it is carried in voyage narratives and their reprintings.

Antonio Pigafetta wrote his account of the Magellan expedition in the mid 1520s. It survives in four manuscripts, three in French and one in Italian, the Italian copy in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan. Giovanni Battista Ramusio printed a version in his Navigationi et Viaggi from 1550, and Carlo Amoretti published the Ambrosiana manuscript in 1800.

The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake, London 1628, was compiled by Drake's nephew from the notes of the expedition's chaplain Francis Fletcher and other papers.

The eighteenth-century revival ran through the periodical press: a report in the Gentleman's Magazine in 1766, then Charles Clerke's letter to the Royal Society on the very tall men seen near the Strait of Magellan, printed in the Philosophical Transactions in 1767. Bougainville's Voyage autour du monde followed in 1771, and John Hawkesworth's official Account of the Voyages in 1773.
sections.disputed:
Even the name is uncertain. Patagonia is often read as the land of the big foot, which fed the European legend of oversized people at the southern tip of the Americas. But Magellan may simply have taken the name from Patagón, a character in the sixteenth-century Spanish romance Primaleón, which he had probably read. Explorers of that period named places after their reading habits: California came out of another Spanish romance in the same way.

If the toponym is literary, the "big foot" folk etymology is a later gloss that made the legend feel inevitable. The voyage accounts still describe tall people; the Tehuelche and related groups were genuinely taller than many European sailors of the age. The dispute is not whether anyone large was met, but how a romance name, a real stature difference and three centuries of exaggeration braided into a single European giant myth.

chain.claim: The Patagonians were a race of giants twelve to fifteen feet tall, first met by Magellan's crew at Port San Julian in 1520 and reported by European voyagers for the next two and a half centuries.
chain.verdict: The voyage narratives that carry this story describe unusually tall people, but where they give numbers at all the numbers are much smaller than twelve to fifteen feet, and the figures shrink further once anyone measures.

rungs.witness: Helen Wallis, 'The Patagonian Giants', appendix to Robert E. Gallagher (ed.), Byron's Journal of his Circumnavigation 1764 to 1766, Hakluyt Society, 1964
rungs.reads: A survey of the reports from Pigafetta to Darwin by the British Museum Map Room. It concludes that the Patagonians were somewhat above average human height, and does not sustain any giant race.
rungs.evidence: The review of Gallagher's edition in the Hispanic American Historical Review, https://read.dukeupress.edu/hahr/article/45/3/482/158782/Byron-s-Journal-of-his-Circumnavigation, states: 'An entertaining feature of the appendix is an article, "The Patagonian Giants," by Dr. Helen Wallis of the British Museum Map Room', and that 'Dr. Wallis, after reviewing reports by travellers from Magellan's Pigafetta to Charles Darwin, inclines to agree that the Patagonian Indians are somewhat above the average human height.'
rungs.note: Checked through the review rather than the volume itself, so the appendix's page range is not established here.

rungs.witness: John Hawkesworth, An Account of the Voyages undertaken by the order of His present Majesty, London 1773, three volumes, Strahan and Cadell, containing Byron's narrative
rungs.reads: The official English account keeps the language of giants but drops the arithmetic: of one man it says 'it could not be much less than seven feet', and of the group that 'these people may indeed more properly be called giants than tall men . . . the shortest of whom were at least four inches taller' than an officer of six feet two inches. That puts the shortest at roughly six feet six.
rungs.evidence: Both quotations read at https://static-prod.lib.princeton.edu/visual_materials/maps/websites/pacific/magellan-strait/patgonian-giants.html. Publication details confirmed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Account_of_the_Voyages: 1773, three volumes, William Strahan and T. Cadell, covering Byron, Wallis, Carteret and Cook. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagon gives the same 1773 revision as six feet six inches.
rungs.note: So the 1773 volume is not a clean recantation. It halves the numbers while keeping the word giants.

rungs.witness: Louis-Antoine de Bougainville, Voyage autour du monde, Paris 1771
rungs.date: encounter 1766 to 1767, published 1771
rungs.reads: Gives a range rather than a marvel: of the Patagonians seen, none was below about five pieds five or six pouces, and none above five pieds nine or ten pouces. In French measure of the day that is roughly five feet ten inches to six feet two inches English.
rungs.evidence: The French sentence 'Ces hommes sont de belle taille: parmi ceux que nous avons vus, aucun n'etait en dessous de cinq pieds cinq a six pouces, ni au-dessus de cinq pieds neuf a dix pouces' was read at https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagons, which cites it to Bougainville. https://patlibros.org/frm/index.php?fun=myth&lan=eng quotes the journal of Bougainville's captain Duclos-Guyot in the same vein: 'We measured the shortest of them, and my brother found him 5 feet 7 inches high French measure', and states that Pernety's giant claims are not supported by the captains' journals.
rungs.note: The catalogue dates this to 1767 and gives five feet nine as an English figure. The book is 1771 and the units are French.

rungs.witness: Charles Clarke (Clerke), 'An Account of the Very Tall Men, Seen Near the Streights of Magellan, in the Year 1764, by the Equipage of the Dolphin Man of War, under the Command of the Hon. Commodore Byron; in a Letter from Mr. Charles Clarke, Officer on Board the Said Ship, to M. Maty, M. D. Sec. R. S.', Philosophical Transactions vol. 57 (1767), pp. 75 to 79
rungs.reads: The high water mark of the eighteenth century revival, put before the Royal Society by a serving officer. Reported as claiming that no man seen was under about eight feet and that some exceeded nine, with women around seven and a half to eight feet. Still short of twelve to fifteen.
rungs.evidence: Title, author, volume 57, year 1767 and pages 75 to 79 confirmed from the scan record at https://archive.org/details/philtrans04718283. The height figures were checked in two independent secondary accounts, https://www.sydhav.no/giants/patagonia.htm ('none of the men were lower than eight feet, and that some even exceeded nine', women 'from seven feet and a half to eight feet') and Robert Silverberg's essay at https://asimovs.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Reflections_StrangeCase-Dec11.pdf ('Some of them are certainly nine feet, if they do not exceed it').
rungs.note: The article itself was behind a paywall at the Royal Society and the archive.org plain text would not load, so the figures rest on two secondary readings that agree, not on the printed page.

rungs.witness: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake, London 1628, printed by Nicholas Bourne and compiled by Drake's nephew from Francis Fletcher's notes and other papers
rungs.reads: Argues the Patagonians had been overstated. On size it gives 'the name Pentagones, Five cubits viz. 7. Foote and halfe, describing the full height (if not some what more)'. That is roughly half the claimed figure, from a book published a century after the Magellan voyage.
rungs.evidence: Quotation taken from Princeton University Library's exhibit page, https://static-prod.lib.princeton.edu/visual_materials/maps/websites/pacific/magellan-strait/patgonian-giants.html, which reproduces the 1628 spelling and adds that the book called the Patagonians 'nothing so monstrous' as reported. Publication details confirmed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Encompassed_by_Sir_Francis_Drake: London 1628, Nicholas Bourne, compiled by Drake's nephew from the uncle's journal and Fletcher's notes.
rungs.note: This cuts against the catalogue entry, which says the 1628 book repeated the giant claim.

rungs.witness: Anthony Knivet's narrative, printed in Samuel Purchas, Hakluytus Posthumus or Purchas his Pilgrimes, London 1625
rungs.reads: Reports Patagonian dead bodies of great length. The figures are given in spans rather than feet, and modern renderings of the passage vary: roughly thirteen to fourteen spans, converted by different writers to anything from about nine and a half feet to twelve feet.
rungs.evidence: https://assets.cambridge.org/97811070/90910/excerpt/9781107090910_excerpt.pdf confirms the narrative was first published in London in 1625 in Purchas his Pilgrimes as 'The admirable adventures and strange fortunes of Master Anthonie Knivet', and that the modern edition is by Vivien Kogut Lessa de Sa for Cambridge University Press. The span figures were checked at https://www.sydhav.no/giants/patagonia.htm ('fourteen spannes long', 'thirteen spans tall') and https://dubioushistory.github.io/articles/patagonian-giants (3 to 3.2 m); https://hoaxes.org/patagonia.html renders the same passage as bodies 'measuring over twelve feet in length'.
rungs.note: I did not read the 1625 printed text itself this session. The rung is included for the document and its date; the conversion into feet is where the twelve foot figure enters, and the conversions disagree with each other.

rungs.witness: Antonio Pigafetta, account of Magellan's voyage
rungs.date: composed about 1524 to 1525; the wording checked here is from Lord Stanley of Alderley's translation of a French manuscript, Hakluyt Society, 1874
rungs.reads: Describes a giant on the shore at Port Saint Julian, dancing and singing and putting sand and dust on his head. On height it says only: 'He was so tall that the tallest of us only came up to his waist.' It gives no measurement in feet, and nothing approaching twelve to fifteen feet. It records that Magellan gave the people a name from which Patagonia derives.
rungs.evidence: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage and https://whalesite.org/RV/TIERRA/TEXTS/PIGAFETTA.htm both reproduce the Stanley translation and both carry the waist sentence and the sand and dust sentence. https://archive.org/details/firstvoyageround00piga confirmed the title page: The First Voyage Round the World by Magellan, translated by Lord Stanley of Alderley, Hakluyt Society, 1874. https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagons gives the same sentence in French, 'etait tant grand que le plus grand de nous ne lui venait qu'a la ceinture'.
rungs.note: Pigafetta wrote in the 1520s but no autograph survives in print from that decade; what survives is manuscript copies and later editions. I did not verify the manuscript count or the Ambrosiana shelfmark this session, so the entry's claim of four manuscripts is untested here.

chain.floor: Pigafetta, at the foot of the ladder, leaves standing a man on a beach at Port San Julian who was taller than the Europeans looking at him, described by where the top of their heads reached and not by any number. The figure of twelve to fifteen feet is not in that account.

handling.living: The "Patagonian giants" is a European legend about a real Indigenous people, not a story belonging to or told by that people: the Tehuelche (and possibly Selk'nam) are living peoples with descendant communities in Argentina and Chile today, but the giant myth itself is a colonial-era European misreading of their genuinely above-average stature, generated and sustained entirely in voyage narratives and the European press. There is no Tehuelche or Selk'nam tradition to consult here because the myth was never theirs; the people who need to be centered are the historical Tehuelche and Selk'nam themselves, including the trauma of specific events like Magellan's abduction of two men who died in transit to Spain.
handling.distortions: The commonest distortion is treating this as a straightforward "giant race" fantasy entry like Cyclopes or Fomorians, which erases that real, named, living-descended peoples are the actual subject and effaces the violence involved (measurement-as-spectacle, abduction, death in custody). A second distortion is repeating the exaggerated heights (twelve or fifteen feet) as if they were sincerely-held ancient belief rather than a three-century inflation that collapsed the moment Europeans of the era, themselves shorter on average, actually measured people carefully.
handling.take: The documented European textual history is freely usable and well worth telling accurately: Pigafetta's 1520s account, the inflation through Drake's-nephew and eighteenth-century voyage narratives, and the collapse via Bougainville's and Byron's more careful measurements. Do not write the Tehuelche or Selk'nam themselves as fantasy giants, and do not stage the Magellan abduction or any encounter scene as adventure color; center the story explicitly as a European perception problem and name the real peoples, since flattening them into interchangeable "giant natives" repeats the original colonial error rather than critiquing it. If the piece touches the abduction, treat the deaths of the two Patagonian men taken aboard with the same weight a true account of a death in custody deserves, not as an incidental detail.
handling.cite: Cite Antonio Pigafetta's account of the Magellan voyage (via the Ramusio 1550 or Amoretti 1800 editions), The World Encompassed (1628), Bougainville's Voyage autour du monde (1771) and the official Byron voyage account (1773) for the European record; for the Tehuelche and Selk'nam themselves, defer to contemporary ethnographic and community sources on those peoples rather than the voyage literature.

katallani.fullDescription: One eye, and no knees. He ate people, but he could not bend his legs to chase them.
katallani.mysteryNote: He cannot kneel and he cannot run. Every story about him is built on the small distance that gives you.
katallani.fate: No single death: Albanian tradition keeps him as a type, named across the ground rather than killed in one story.

sections.story:
The Katallani is the one-eyed giant of Albanian tradition, and the detail that sets him apart from every other cyclops in this catalogue is that he has no knees. A man-eater who cannot bend his legs is a different sort of danger from one who can run you down, and the stories are built around that difference.

In southern Albania he goes by Syqenhenjeri, which is glossed as the eye that eats people.

Albanian does not really have one word for him. It has a family of them, and most describe the eye rather than the body: Symadh, big-eye. Syqorr, blind-eye. Syqen, dog-eye. Syklysh. Syqenhenjeri. Alongside these sit Vigan, Gjigant, Katalla, Lutran, Gavell, Garravell, Dragumn, and among the Arbëresh of Greece, Reks. And, twice over, Div and Dif.

That last pair matters. The same word that gives the Georgian devi and the Persian div turns up here in a language belonging to neither family.

His name is on the ground at Shllak, in the field called Fusha e Katallajve and the graves called Vorret e Katallajve, and in the stream Përroi i Vigjanit near Mullens. It survives as a surname too: an M. Catalano recorded at Bar in 1517, and Catalano families among the Arbëresh of Italy in the fifteenth century.

Giants appear in the first book ever printed in Albanian. Gjon Buzuku's *Meshari* of 1555 names the gjigantë, phantoms of great height and warlike nature, and the modern Albanian word vigan descends from it.
sections.origins:
The written record begins with Gjon Buzuku's Meshari of 1555, the first book printed in Albanian, which names the gjigantë. It survives in a single incomplete copy in the Vatican Library, noticed in 1740 and rediscovered in 1909.

The folkloric material was collected far later. Gustav Meyer, the nineteenth-century lexicographer of Albanian, records katalla in a pagan sense. Shtjefën Gjeçovi (1874 to 1929), the Franciscan priest usually called the father of Albanian folklore studies, worked among the northern highland tribes between 1905 and 1920 and identified the figure with Homer's Polyphemus.

Eqrem Çabej returned to the popular-belief figures in Diana dhe Zana (1942) and Disa figura të besimeve popullore shqiptare (1972).

The name is also carried by documents and by the ground: a surname recorded at Bar in 1517, Arbëresh families in Italy in the fifteenth century, and the field and graves called Katallajve at Shllak. Azem Qazimi's Fjalor i mitologjisë dhe demonologjisë shqiptare gathers the modern summary.
sections.disputed: Whether the Balkan cyclops is Greek at all. A number of researchers have argued for the independence of the one-eyed giant among the non-Greek peoples of the Balkans, the Illyrians included, rather than treating it as a borrowing from Homer. The catalogue holds four of these traditions within a few hundred kilometres of each other: Polyphemus, the Katallani, the one-eyed giants of Brač and Paklenica, and further out Balor. Whether they are independent, a shared inheritance older than all of them, or later borrowings is not settled.

handling.living: As of the 2020s the Katallani belongs to no living cult or faith; Albanian folk belief in one-eyed man-eating giants is heritage folklore surviving in place-names, surnames and scholarly collection rather than active practice. Albania is a secular state with no institutional body governing this material, and the tradition is studied rather than observed.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening is reading the Katallani as simply a borrowed or garbled Polyphemus, when the actual scholarly question (independent Balkan/Illyrian origin versus Homeric borrowing versus older shared inheritance) is genuinely unsettled and worth preserving rather than resolving by fiat. A second distortion is losing the kneeless-leg detail, the single most distinctive feature that separates this figure from every other Balkan cyclops, in favor of a generic one-eyed giant. A third is treating the sprawling family of Albanian names (Symadh, Syqorr, Syqen, Vigan, Div/Dif, etc.) as synonyms for one fixed figure rather than as a genuinely plural naming tradition.
handling.take: This is freely usable folklore material: the kneeless cyclops, the man-eating theme, the toponymic traces at Shllak, and the wider Div/Dif terminology are all documented and safe to adapt. Preserve the genuine scholarly uncertainty about the figure's relationship to Polyphemus rather than flattening it into either "it's just Homer" or "it's wholly independent"; both are live positions in the literature. Treat Gjeçovi's early-twentieth-century identification with Polyphemus as one influential interpretation, not settled fact.
handling.cite: Cite Gjon Buzuku's Meshari (1555) for the earliest gjigantë reference, Shtjefën Gjeçovi's early-twentieth-century highland fieldwork, Eqrem Çabej's Diana dhe Zana (1942) and Disa figura të besimeve popullore shqiptare (1972), and Azem Qazimi's Fjalor i mitologjisë dhe demonologjisë shqiptare for the modern summary.

waligora-wyrwidab.fullDescription: Almost every giant in this catalogue is something to be survived. These two are the heroes.
waligora-wyrwidab.mysteryNote: One brother moved the mountain, the other pulled up the oak. Between them they killed a dragon without ever drawing a weapon.
waligora-wyrwidab.fate: No death: they killed the dragon, married the king's daughters, and divided the kingdom between them.

sections.story:
A hunter's wife went into the forest to pick berries and gave birth to twin boys there. She died at once. No woman came to nurse them, so a she-wolf fed one and a she-bear fed the other.

The wolf's foster-son was Waligóra, the mountain-feller. The bear's was Wyrwidąb, the oak-tearer. Their names are their strength and nothing else: one pushes mountains out of the way, the other pulls up the oldest oaks the way a man pulls ears of grain.

They went out together to see the world. A mountain blocked the road and Waligóra shouldered it half a mile aside. A great oak blocked the road and Wyrwidąb tore it up by the roots and threw it in the river. They met a small man with shoes that covered a mile at a step and two at a jump, and a carpet that flew, and he carried them to a kingdom where a dragon was eating people daily.

They killed it between them. Waligóra pinned the tail under a boulder so the thing could not move, and Wyrwidąb crushed the head with an oak. The king gave them his two daughters and princely titles, and when he died they divided the kingdom and ruled it together.

In Gliński's version the dragon is the Wawel dragon and the king holds Kraków, which ties the brothers into the city's foundation story. The Panieńskie Rocks there are named as traces of Wyrwidąb's work.
sections.origins:
The tale was first printed by Kazimierz Władysław Wójcicki (1807 to 1879) in *Klechdy, starożytne podania i powieści ludu polskiego i Rusi*, two volumes, Warsaw 1837. Wójcicki described gathering his material at the fireside, listening to spinners and household servants. The third edition of 1876, illustrated by Michał Elwiro Andriolli, carried the collection into wide circulation and into Czech, French, German and Russian translation.

Antoni Józef Gliński (1817 to 1866) printed his own version in *Bajarz polski, czyli zbiór baśni, powieści i gawęd ludowych*, four volumes, Wilno 1853, reissued repeatedly through the century (a corrected third edition appeared at Wilno in 1881).

Julian Krzyżanowski's Polish tale-type catalogue, *Polska bajka ludowa w układzie systematycznym*, carries this material as T 300B, *Smok i Waligóra*, inside the dragon-slayer group.

In Poland the tale has stayed in print as a children's and school text ever since.
sections.disputed:
Twins abandoned in the wild, suckled by animals, who grow up to rule a kingdom, is the Romulus and Remus shape. Whether that is inheritance from a common source, borrowing across languages, or two traditions independently reaching the same idea is not something the sources can settle. The parallel is noted because readers will see it; it is not offered as a proof of transmission.

Note also that this is a baśń, a folk tale, not a podanie, a local legend tied to a place. That distinction matters in Polish genre terms and is discussed under the Milžinai entry as well. A baśń can travel and reshape itself; a podanie claims a hill or a ruin. This pair of brothers belongs to the travelling kind. Treating them as a pinned local etiology would misread the type of story they are.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Waligóra and Wyrwidąb belong to no living faith and no community holds custodial claims on them; nineteenth-century Polish folk religion has no continuous practising body, and the tale has instead become a fixture of Polish national children's literature, kept in print continuously since Wójcicki's 1837 collection. It survives as heritage/literary material, reinforced by school editions and the Wawel dragon tie-in to Kraków's civic founding legend, not as living devotional practice.
handling.distortions: The commonest flattening treats the pair as a fixed local etiology (a podanie) pinned to Kraków and the Wawel dragon, when Krzyżanowski's tale-type catalogue (ATU 300B) classifies them as a travelling baśń that different collectors and regions attach to different settings; Gliński's Wawel/Kraków version is one localization, not the tale's origin point. A second distortion is over-reading the Romulus-and-Remus resemblance (animal-suckled twin founders) as proven inheritance or borrowing, when the sources only note the parallel without being able to settle its cause.
handling.take: This is freely usable public-domain literary folklore: the wolf- and bear-raised twins, the mountain-shouldering and oak-uprooting feats, the dragon-slaying partnership, and the divided kingdom are all fair game for retelling and expansion. Be explicit about which version you're using, since Wójcicki's 1837 text and Gliński's 1853 text differ (only Gliński ties the dragon to Kraków's Wawel and the Panieńskie Rocks), and avoid asserting a direct genetic link to the Romulus and Remus myth as fact rather than as a noted resemblance. Treat it as a baśń that travels rather than a podanie fixed to one place, unless you are specifically retelling the Gliński/Kraków localization.
handling.cite: Credit Kazimierz Władysław Wójcicki, Klechdy, starożytne podania i powieści ludu polskiego i Rusi (Warsaw, 1837) and Antoni Józef Gliński, Bajarz polski (Wilno, 1853) as the two primary printed versions, and Julian Krzyżanowski's Polska bajka ludowa w układzie systematycznym (tale type T 300B) for its classification.

milzinai.fullDescription: In local legend they are the ancestors and they are respected. In fairy tales the same beings are monsters to be beaten. The difference is not the region. It is which kind of story is being told.
milzinai.mysteryNote: Ask what raised the hill and one village says giants, the next says the Swedes. The ground keeps its own counsel.
milzinai.fate: Buried in the mounds that carry their name, the milzinkapiai.

sections.story:
Lithuanian folklorists group the milžinai material by genre, and the split is stark. In *padavimai*, local legends tied to real places, the milžinai are the old people, the ancestors of the humans who came after, and they are treated with respect. In *pasakos*, fairy tales, they are adversaries, and the point of the story is to outwit or destroy them.

There is a second layer to this. In tales structurally identical to the giant stories, the giant is swapped out for a witch, for *bėda* which means trouble itself, for the devil, and even for a grass snake. The giant is not always a character. Sometimes he is a slot that any large obstacle can fill.

Their graves are on the map. Čižiūnų Milžinkapis, Girgždūtės kalnas, Džiugo kalnas, Medvėgalis, Raktuvė, Karaimų kalnas, Lylavėnų Milžinkapiai. The archive holds an account explaining Medvėgalis as a mound piled up by giants, and another explaining the same hill as the work of the Swedes.

Folklore mapping shows where they cluster. The giants belong to the hills and to the odd shapes in the ground. Lake spirits belong to the lake country, devils to the most broken terrain. Geographically, a giant is an answer to strange ground.
sections.origins:
There is no medieval text behind the milžinai. The material is oral, taken down from named villagers, and it reaches print through the collecting institutions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The Lithuanian Science Society, founded in Vilnius in 1907 under Jonas Basanavičius, had gathered some 72,000 folklore items by 1940. The Lithuanian Folklore Archive was established at Kaunas in 1935 under Jonas Balys, who published his catalogue of motifs in Lithuanian narrative folklore in 1936. Those holdings passed through the Academy of Sciences and now form the manuscript archive of the Institute of Lithuanian Literature and Folklore in Vilnius.

Bronislava Kerbelytė (1935 to 2024) worked that archive for fifty years. Her collection Milžinai lietuvių padavimuose ir pasakose (Vytautas Magnus University, Kaunas, 2019) prints sixty-two texts, each carrying a classification number, an informant name and a variant count. It follows her Žemės atmintis: lietuvių liaudies padavimai (1999) and the four-volume Lietuvių pasakojamosios tautosakos katalogas (1999 to 2009).
sections.disputed:
What can be recovered from this material is contested. Algirdas Julien Greimas read Lithuanian folklore for a lost pre-Christian mythology in Apie dievus ir žmones (1979), translated as Of Gods and Men (Indiana University Press, 1992). Reviewing it in Metmenys 40 (1980), Eglė Viktorija Žygaitė preferred the positivism of Norbertas Vėlius and called his hypotheses poetic and his method, in Greimas's own description, like solving crosswords. Daiva Vaitkevičienė argued in 2017 that the Lithuanian Greimas is read in isolation from the French one. Loreta Mačianskaitė sets out that reception in Semiotika 17 (2022).

The graves raise a separate question. Milžinkapiai are real burial monuments, some of them Bronze Age barrows in western Lithuania. The legends attached to such sites are mobile: Manvydas Vitkūnas has documented mounds credited to Swedes, to the French, to Napoleon. Salvijus Kulevičius (2014) argues that padavimai preserve mythologised rather than historical memory. On that reading a giant at a site is not a memory of who built it.

handling.living: As of the 2020s the milžinai belong to no living faith; pre-Christian Lithuanian religion has no continuous practising body, and the surviving material is archival oral folklore held in institutions like the Institute of Lithuanian Literature and Folklore in Vilnius. There is a live scholarly community working the material (Kerbelytė's archive-based collections through 2019, ongoing debate over Greimas's structuralist readings), but no religious or Indigenous custodial claimants restrict its use the way an active tradition would.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening is collapsing the genre split the folklorists themselves insist on: treating the milžinai uniformly as either noble ancestors or monstrous adversaries, when Lithuanian tradition keeps these as two distinct registers (padavimai local-legend ancestors vs. pasakos fairy-tale antagonists) that do different work. A second distortion is over-reading the barrow graves (milžinkapiai) as literal evidence of a giant race rather than folklore attached after the fact to real Bronze Age burial mounds, and a third is importing Greimas's structuralist 'lost mythology' as settled fact rather than one contested interpretive framework among several.
handling.take: The recorded motifs are free to use: giants as respected ancestors in place-legends, as tricked or defeated adversaries in fairy tales, the giant-graves at named sites like Medvėgalis, and the genre-slot flexibility where a giant can be swapped for a witch, the devil, or trouble itself. Keep the genre distinction visible in your own telling rather than smoothing it away, and don't present the mound-builder folklore as history, the same mounds get attributed to Swedes or Napoleon in other tellings, which is itself good material. If you lean on a 'lost pre-Christian mythology' reading, flag it as Greimas's interpretation, which Lithuanian folklorists like Vėlius and Žygaitė have pushed back on.
handling.cite: Credit Bronislava Kerbelytė's Milžinai lietuvių padavimuose ir pasakose (Vytautas Magnus University, Kaunas, 2019) for the primary text collection, and Algirdas Julien Greimas's Of Gods and Men (Indiana University Press, 1992) for the interpretive framework, noting it is contested by Norbertas Vėlius and later reviewers.

troll-iceland.fullDescription: Half the strange rocks in Iceland are trolls who misjudged the sunrise.
troll-iceland.mysteryNote: Every one of them stopped exactly where the light found it. That is why the country is full of them.
troll-iceland.fate: Caught by sunrise and turned to stone, which is where most of them still stand.

sections.story:
In Icelandic, tröll is not a species. It is a superlative. The word covers every being larger than a human in some capacity and generally ill-disposed toward them, and it sits alongside jötnar, risar and þursar as overlapping names for the same broad class. The jötnar of the Eddas and the trolls of Icelandic farm legend are not quite the same tradition, and the second is younger.

The rule that governs them is the sun. A troll caught out at dawn turns to stone and stays there, which means the tradition is anchored to real places all across the country.

At Rauðhólar near Reykjavík there are two small mounds called Tröllabörn, the Troll Children, caught by the light. Drangey, the island rising out of Skagafjörður, is a troll cow that was petrified as her family crossed the fjord by night. In the Ölfusá at Selfoss there is a lone rock mid-river with a single pine on top, called Jóruklettur. It is named for Jóra, who threw a boulder into the river and used it as a stepping stone and became a giantess in the act, at the place still called Tröllkonuhlaup, the Giantess's Leap. She took a cave near Hengill and preyed on travellers until she was killed with a silver axe at sunrise, and that killing is said to have given the Öxará in Þingvellir its name.

The word kerling, a petrified troll-woman, names rock pillars and peaks the length of the country, including a sea stack off Drangey and the whole Kerlingarfjöll range in the highlands.

They are usually greedy and ferocious and fond of stray livestock and lone travellers, and the legends worked as warnings to keep children from wandering. But not always. Some stories give them kindness, or wisdom, or loyalty to a person who treated them decently.
sections.origins:
Icelandic troll legends are a post-medieval oral tradition, written down systematically only in the nineteenth century.

The foundation text is Jón Árnason's Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og æfintýri, printed in Leipzig by J. C. Hinrichs in two volumes, 1862 and 1864. Jón had begun collecting with Magnús Grímsson in 1845, and their small Íslenzk æfintýri appeared in Reykjavík in 1852 to little notice. The German scholar Konrad Maurer, visiting Iceland in 1858, pressed them to continue and undertook to find a German publisher. Magnús died in 1860. Guðbrandur Vigfússon, then in Copenhagen, read and corrected the material as it passed through.

Jón did not travel to collect. He circulated a written appeal and drew on a network of clergy, schoolmates and friends across the country who wrote the legends down where they lived.

The legends are now mapped by place in Sagnagrunnur, begun by Terry Gunnell in 1999 and hosted at the Árni Magnússon Institute.
sections.disputed:
What the word tröll denotes is the live argument. Lotte Motz, in "The Families of Giants" (Arkiv för nordisk filologi 102, 1987), tried to show that jötnar, risar, þursar and tröll were four distinct kinds. Ármann Jakobsson rejects that as unsupported, treating tröll as a term for the monstrous and the paranormal rather than a species (Saga-Book 32, 2008; The Troll Inside You, 2017). Katja Schulz's Riesen (2004) collapses the terms. Tom Grant, in Gripla 30 (2019), breaks with that consensus and argues that risar and jötnar are consistently distinguished in the sagas.

Petrification at dawn is older than the farm legends. It is in the Eddic Alvíssmál, and in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar Hrímgerðr is held in flyting until daylight takes her. How much of the nineteenth-century material descends from that literature is not settled.

Nor are the printed texts neutral witnesses: the relation between the collectors' manuscripts and Jón Árnason's published versions is under active examination.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Icelandic troll legends are folklore and landscape heritage rather than an active belief system; no living faith holds custodial authority over them, though the tales remain part of everyday Icelandic culture, place-naming and tourism. Modern heathenry (Asatru, state-recognised in Iceland) centres on the Eddic gods and jötnar rather than on farm-legend trolls specifically, and in any case makes no restriction-based claim over this material.
handling.distortions: Global pop culture, especially post-Tolkien fantasy and platforms like the Trolls franchise, imports a fixed "troll" species with stable traits, when Icelandic tröll is better understood as a broad, overlapping superlative term for large ill-disposed beings that sits alongside jötnar, risar and þursar, and scholars actively disagree about whether these were ever meant as distinct kinds. A second distortion is treating the sunlight-petrification rule and the specific named landscape sites (Drangey, Jóruklettur, Kerlingarfjöll) as generic fantasy tropes divorced from place, when the entire tradition's structure is that it is anchored to real, nameable Icelandic locations.
handling.take: The landscape material is freely usable and is arguably the most distinctive asset here: the sunrise-petrification rule, and the named sites, Rauðhólar's Tröllabörn, Drangey as a petrified troll-cow, Jóruklettur and the Giantess's Leap, the kerling rock formations. Feel free to note trolls are not always villainous, some legends give them kindness or loyalty, rather than defaulting to pure-menace framing. Avoid asserting a single fixed taxonomy of tröll versus jötunn versus risi versus þurs as settled fact; that is a live, unresolved scholarly argument (Motz versus Jakobsson versus Schulz versus Grant), and avoid presenting Jón Árnason's nineteenth-century printed collection as an unmediated transcript, since the relationship between collectors' manuscripts and the published text is still under active study.
handling.cite: Cite Jón Árnason, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur og æfintýri (1862-64, with Guðbrandur Vigfússon), as the foundational printed collection, and Sagnagrunnur (Terry Gunnell, Árni Magnússon Institute) for the mapped legend-and-landscape database; for the scholarly debate on troll taxonomy, Ármann Jakobsson's Saga-Book 32 (2008) article and The Troll Inside You (2017).

kalev-kalevipoeg.fullDescription: In Estonian, the word kalev simply means giant. His wife's tears became the lakes.
kalev-kalevipoeg.mysteryNote: In Estonian the word for giant is simply his name. What she wept became water, and the water is still there.
kalev-kalevipoeg.fate: Kalev died, and Linda's tears for him became the lakes of Estonia.

sections.story:
Kalev, Kaleva or Kalevi and his sons run through Estonian, Finnish and Karelian tradition as giants who lived in the land before people arrived. A stone-throwing giant is called Kalevanpoika in southwest Finland and Kalevipoeg in Estonia, the same figure across a language border.

The attestations are genuinely old. Mikael Agricola listed the Caleuanpojat, Kaleva's sons, among the giants of Finnic pagan belief in the sixteenth century. A seventeenth-century chronicle names an Estonian giant Kalliweh. The Old English poem *Widsith* mentions a Finnic ruler called Caelic, which some read as the same name again.

Linda, Kalev's wife, wept for him, and her tears are the lakes of Estonia.

There is an object in the churchyard at Untamala in Laitila, over two and a half metres tall, known locally as the whetstone Kaleva's son used on his scythe. It is a medieval tombstone. That correction is not a debunking. It is the clearest small example of the process this catalogue keeps running into: a community finds something in the ground that does not fit the scale of the people around it, and gives it to a giant.
sections.origins:
Mikael Agricola's list of Finnic pagan deities, printed in 1551 in the verse preface to his Finnish Psalter, is the earliest secure attestation: the Caleuanpoiat stand there among the gods of Häme. Heinrich Stahl's Leyen Spiegel, printed at Tallinn in 1641, carries the Estonian form Kalliweh.

The Finnish material survives mainly as place-names and as legends attached to boulders and hills, concentrated in the south-west around Kalanti. Mikko Heikkilä set out the onomastic evidence in SKY Journal of Linguistics 25 (2012).

On the Estonian side, Friedrich Robert Faehlmann proposed an epic built from Kalevipoeg legends to the Learned Estonian Society in 1839. Kreutzwald's second version, 19,087 verses with a German translation, was issued serially by that Society between 1857 and 1861, with a shorter popular edition printed at Kuopio in 1862.

The oral legends were gathered in the nineteenth century by Jakob Hurt and Matthias Johann Eisen, and are held in the Estonian Folklore Archives in Tartu.
sections.disputed:
The Estonian national epic Kalevipoeg was compiled by Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald between 1857 and 1861, modelled on the Finnish Kalevala. It is built from genuine oral material, runic song gathered from singers, but the assembly, the shaping and much of the connective tissue are nineteenth century and were done with national awakening in mind. It is folk material. It is not folklore in the sense of a single continuous oral epic that already existed in that shape.

The distinction is worth keeping for this entry. When the codex cites Kalevipoeg for landscape deeds or for the brothers as a race of giants, it is citing a literary construction that embeds older song, not a pure field recording. Readers who want only the pre-Kreutzwald layer will not find it cleanly separated here; the epic is how most of the tradition now arrives. Treating the epic as if it were medieval chronicle would be a category error.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Kalev and Kalevipoeg belong to no living cult; Finnic paganism has no continuous practising body. What is genuinely living is the national-epic status of Kalevipoeg in Estonia (the poem is a cornerstone of nineteenth-century national awakening and still taught and referenced culturally, much as the Kalevala is in Finland), and the ongoing scholarly custodianship of the underlying oral material at the Estonian Folklore Archives in Tartu. There is no Indigenous-custodianship issue here comparable to the Pacific or North American entries; this is European literary heritage material.
handling.distortions: The commonest mangling is treating Kreutzwald's Kalevipoeg (1857-1861) as a straight transcription of ancient oral epic, when it is a nineteenth-century literary composition built from genuine runic song but shaped, connected and completed with a national-awakening agenda, on the explicit model of Lönnrot's Kalevala. A second distortion is collapsing the Finnish Kalevanpoika, the Estonian Kalevipoeg and the Karelian material into one figure with one biography, when they are related but distinct regional traditions linked mainly by the shared name. A third is the tombstone-at-Untamala problem in miniature: taking a folk explanation (a giant's whetstone) as literal history rather than recognizing the pattern of communities assigning outsized objects to giants.
handling.take: The pre-nineteenth-century attestations (Agricola's 1551 list, Stahl's 1641 Kalliweh, the Widsith reference) and the general shape of the stone-throwing giant motif are free to use as folklore. Kreutzwald's Kalevipoeg itself is public domain and freely adaptable as a work of literature, but it should be credited as such, a compiled national epic, not presented as pristine ancient myth; if a piece needs the pre-Kreutzwald layer specifically, that requires going to the Jakob Hurt/Eisen archive material rather than the epic. Keep the Finnish and Estonian strands distinguished rather than merging them into a single pan-Finnic giant.
handling.cite: Credit Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald's Kalevipoeg (1857-1861) as a compiled national epic, Mikael Agricola's 1551 Psalter preface for the earliest attestation, and the Estonian Folklore Archives (Tartu, built on Jakob Hurt and Matthias Johann Eisen's collections) for the underlying oral material; Mikko Heikkilä's onomastic work (SKY Journal of Linguistics 25, 2012) is the relevant modern scholarship on the Finnish side.

suur-toll.fullDescription: He was king of the island. He lived as a farmer.
suur-toll.mysteryNote: A king who kept farming. The rocks he threw are still lying where they fell, and the island still knows which ones are his.
suur-toll.fate: No death recorded here: he stayed on Saaremaa, its king and its farmer at once.

sections.story:
Suur Tõll is the giant of Saaremaa, and he lived at Tõlluste on the coast with his wife Piret. He threw enormous rocks, mostly at Vanatühi, the Devil, who was his standing enemy, and at anyone else who threatened the islanders.

The detail that carries the whole figure is that he was king of Saaremaa and lived like an ordinary farmer anyway. Not a giant who ruled from a hall on a hill. A giant who worked his land and happened to be in charge.
sections.origins:
The first extended account of the Saaremaa giant in print is August Wilhelm Hupel's, in the third part of Topographische Nachrichten von Lief- und Ehstland, published at Riga by Johann Friedrich Hartknoch in 1782.

Martin Georg Emil Körber (1817 to 1893), a Saaremaa pastor, gave a longer connected treatment in Oesel einst und jetzt, whose first volume appeared at Arensburg in 1887. Four years earlier the schoolmaster Peeter Süda (1830 to 1893) had published at Kuressaare Väikene vana varanduse vakk ehk Saaremaa vägimees Suur-Tõll (1883), assembled, its subtitle says, from the mouths of the Saaremaa people over twenty years.

The manuscript record sits in the Estonian Folklore Archives, founded at Tartu in 1927 around Jakob Hurt's collection and now part of the Estonian Literary Museum. Fieldwork through the 1950s, and a mapping of Tõll sites and plot distributions carried out on Eduard Laugaste's initiative, fed the standard edition: Muistendid Suurest Tõllust ja teistest, edited by Laugaste, Ellen Liiv and Erna Normann, Tallinn, 1963.
sections.disputed:
Which stories are properly Tõll's is not fixed. Estonian scholarship publishes him inside a single corpus of hiiu- ja vägilasmuistendid, legends of giants and strongmen: the Kalevipoeg volume (1959), the Suur Tõll volume (1963) and the Vanapagan volume (1970) are three parts of one series. In his foreword to the first, Eduard Laugaste writes that the three cycles are closely interdependent, that motifs of the different giant-heroes became mixed, and that Kalevipoeg took over material earlier attached to Tõll or to Vanapagan. He allows that the distinction he takes from Matthias Johann Eisen, between the hiid and the vägilane, blurs in the legends themselves.

Peeter Süda's 1883 book is a second problem. He arranged separate stories into a continuous whole, meant as Saaremaa's local answer to Kalevipoeg, and later retellings, including Rein Raamat's 1982 animated film, descend from it.

The further claim that Tõll preserves the memory of a real early ruler of Saaremaa rests on the name and is not demonstrated.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Suur Tõll belongs to Estonian national folklore rather than to any living faith or custodial community; Estonia has no continuing religious tradition organised around him, and he functions as regional heritage, taught in schools and celebrated as a symbol of Saaremaa. The material survives through published folklore-archive scholarship rather than oral practice with living authority over the stories.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening is treating Peeter Süda's 1883 literary arrangement, and its descendants like Rein Raamat's 1982 animated film, as if it were the folk tradition itself, when it is one author's continuous narrative stitched from separate legends and modelled on Kalevipoeg. A second distortion is presenting Tõll, Kalevipoeg and Vanapagan as cleanly separate figures with fixed distinct stories, when Estonian scholarship itself documents that motifs migrated between the three giant-hero cycles and the categories blur in the source legends.
handling.take: The core material is freely usable: the farmer-king who lives on his land rather than ruling from a hall, the wife Piret, the running feud with Vanatühi/the Devil, and the stone-throwing. Feel free to draw on Süda's continuous narrative shape as a storytelling model, but be transparent that it is a nineteenth-century literary synthesis rather than a single ancient tale, and avoid asserting that Tõll preserves the memory of a real historical ruler of Saaremaa, since that rests on the name alone and is not demonstrated.
handling.cite: Credit the Estonian Folklore Archives (Estonian Literary Museum, Tartu) and the standard scholarly edition, Muistendid Suurest Tõllust ja teistest, ed. Eduard Laugaste, Ellen Liiv and Erna Normann (Tallinn, 1963), alongside Peeter Süda's 1883 Väikene vana varanduse vakk ehk Saaremaa vägimees Suur-Tõll as the source of the popular continuous narrative.

fomorians.fullDescription: They banned the teaching of poetry and law. That is what the sources remember about their rule, before anything about their size.
fomorians.mysteryNote: They ruled by tribute and by silence, forbidding the poets and the druids to teach. What was in the teaching that made it worth forbidding is not recorded.
fomorians.fate: Their rule ended at the second battle of Mag Tuired, when Lugh killed Balor, his own grandfather.

sections.story:
The Fomorians are the adversary race of Irish tradition. In the oldest layer they come from under the sea or under the earth. Later they are recast as sea raiders and giants, and later still as pirates from somewhere else entirely.

For a period they ruled. They took tribute from the Tuatha Dé Danann and from the Nemedians before them, and they forbade the scholars, the bards and the druids to teach. A giant race that suppresses education is a more interesting occupier than one that simply smashes things.

Their fall is a family matter. Balor, their commander, gave his daughter Ethne to Cían of the Tuatha Dé Danann. The child of that marriage was Lugh, who led the overthrow of Fomorian rule and killed Balor himself. The great enemy is destroyed by his own grandson.
sections.origins:
Cath Maige Tuired, the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, carries the fullest account: a Middle Irish narrative resting on earlier material, surviving in London, British Library, Harleian MS 5280, written by Giolla Riabhach Ó Cléirigh in the early sixteenth century. Whitley Stokes edited it in 1891, Elizabeth A. Gray for the Irish Texts Society in 1982.

Lebor Gabála Érenn supplies the other frame, setting the Fomorians against each people that reaches Ireland. It exists in several recensions rather than as one text, compiled from the eleventh century onward and edited by R. A. S. Macalister for the Irish Texts Society between 1932 and 1942.

Lebor na hUidre, written at Clonmacnoise around 1100, once held a copy of Lebor Gabála. Those leaves are now lost.

Mícheál Ó Cléirigh made his own recension in 1631 and led the Annals of the Four Masters at Bundrowes, County Donegal, from 1632 to 1636. Geoffrey Keating completed Foras Feasa ar Éirinn around 1634; it circulated in manuscript, unprinted until 1723.
sections.disputed: The *Lebor Gabála Érenn* is a pseudo-history. It was compiled by Christian scribes in the eleventh century to give Ireland an origin story comparable to the biblical one, folding surviving oral material into a scheme running from the Flood forward. It is a real and valuable source and it is not a neutral record of pagan tradition. Where it disagrees with itself about who the Fomorians were and when they arrived, that is the seam showing.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Under the sea, or under something worse
scholarlyNotes.body: The first element is agreed: Old Irish fo, meaning under or beneath. The second is not. Medieval Irish writers took it as muir, sea, which yields something like those under the sea, and which is where the seagoing Fomorians of popular retelling ultimately come from. A second proposal reads mór, great, giving the great ones below. A third connects it to a reconstructed Old Irish word for a spectre, the same element proposed in the name of the Morrígan and compared with Old English mære, the mare still audible in nightmare. Whitley Stokes set out the spectral reading in the notes to his 1891 edition of Cath Maige Tuired, and Rudolf Thurneysen carried it into his 1921 survey of Irish heroic and royal saga. It has attracted the most support since, though none of the three is settled, and the choice matters: sea dwellers and nether phantoms are different kinds of enemy. Keep the name question apart from the narrative one. Where the texts place the Fomorians is evidence about the stories, not about the word.

scholarlyNotes.heading: The Harley 5280 text and the passages Stokes left out
scholarlyNotes.body: The medieval narrative reaches us through London, British Library, Harleian MS 5280, written in the first half of the sixteenth century by Giolla Riabhach mac Tuathail Ó Cléirigh. Whitley Stokes edited and translated it in Revue Celtique 12 (1891), 52-130, but passed over the rosc or retoiric passages, the compressed rhetorical speeches. Rudolf Thurneysen printed those separately in Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 12 (1918), 400-406, and John Carey re-edited the Morrígan's prophecy of the end of the world in Studia Celtica 24-25 (1989-90), 66-69. Elizabeth A. Gray's edition, Irish Texts Society volume 52 (1982), is the working standard. On date, Gerard Murphy took the surviving text to be the work of an eleventh- or twelfth-century redactor drawing mainly on ninth-century material (Éigse 7, at p. 195). A separate Early Modern Irish account of the battle survives in Royal Irish Academy MS 24 P 9. Brian Ó Cuív edited it in 1945, and Mícheál Hoyne has argued it was composed around 1398 for a branch of the Mac Diarmada family. The two are related but they are not one text.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Lebor Gabála behaves like a tradition, not a book
scholarlyNotes.body: R. A. S. Macalister's edition for the Irish Texts Society, five volumes issued between 1932 and 1942, prints several recensions rather than one work, and his sigla (R1, R2, Míniugud, R3, with Mícheál Ó Cléirigh's 1631 version as R4) now sit beside a second set introduced by R. Mark Scowcroft (a, b, m, c). Scowcroft's two-part study in Ériu 38 (1987), 79-140 and Ériu 39 (1988), 1-66 splits the problem in two: the growth of the text, and the growth of the tradition behind it. A.
