G. van Hamel had gone at the same question in Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 10 (1915), 97-197, and John Carey later edited a volume of studies titled Lebor Gabála Érenn: Textual History and Pseudohistory (Irish Texts Society, Subsidiary Series 20, 2009). For the Fomorians this is the practical consequence. When the recensions disagree about who they were and when they arrived, the disagreement is a property of the compilation rather than damage to some single lost original.

scholarlySources: Elizabeth A. Gray (ed. and trans.), Cath Maige Tuired: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired, Irish Texts Society 52, 1982
Whitley Stokes (ed. and trans.), The Second Battle of Moytura, Revue Celtique 12, 1891, 52-130 and 306-308
Rudolf Thurneysen, Zu irischen Texten, Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 12, 1918, 398-407
Rudolf Thurneysen, Die irische Helden- und Königsage bis zum siebzehnten Jahrhundert, 1921
John Carey, Myth and mythography in Cath Maige Tuired, Studia Celtica 24-25, 1989-1990, 53-69
Gerard Murphy, Notes on Cath Maige Tuired, Éigse 7, 1953-1955, 191-198
Brian Ó Cuív (ed.), Cath Muighe Tuireadh: The Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh, Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1945
Mícheál Hoyne, The political context of Cath Muighe Tuireadh, the Early Modern Irish version of the Second Battle of Magh Tuireadh, Ériu 63, 2013, 91-116
R. A. S. Macalister (ed. and trans.), Lebor Gabála Érenn, 5 vols, Irish Texts Society 34, 35, 39, 41 and 44, 1932-1942
R. Mark Scowcroft, Leabhar Gabhála, Part I: the growth of the text, Ériu 38, 1987, 79-140
R. Mark Scowcroft, Leabhar Gabhála, Part II: the growth of the tradition, Ériu 39, 1988, 1-66
A. G. van Hamel, On Lebor Gabála, Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 10, 1915, 97-197
John Carey (ed.), Lebor Gabála Érenn: Textual History and Pseudohistory, Irish Texts Society Subsidiary Series 20, 2009

handling.living: The Fomorians belong to medieval Irish literary mythology with no living faith community or custodial body; pre-Christian Irish religion has no continuous practising tradition, and the surviving texts (Cath Maige Tuired, Lebor Gabála Érenn) are Christian-era compilations of older material rather than scripture of an ongoing religion. Modern Celtic reconstructionist and neopagan groups sometimes draw on this material, but they are recent, small, non-unified movements without any claim to exclusive custodianship comparable to an unbroken Indigenous tradition.
handling.distortions: Popular retellings tend to flatten the Fomorians into generic "evil giants/monsters" opposing the heroic Tuatha Dé Danann, losing the more interesting detail that they are remembered as suppressing education (forbidding scholars, bards, and druids to teach) rather than as simple destroyers. A second distortion is treating Lebor Gabála Érenn as a straightforward record of pagan belief, when it is an eleventh-century Christian pseudo-history deliberately built to give Ireland a biblical-style origin narrative, so its internal contradictions about who the Fomorians were are evidence of its compiled, constructed nature rather than errors to smooth over.
handling.take: The narrative material is freely usable public-domain myth: the Fomorians as an adversary sea/earth race, their tribute-taking and suppression of learning, Balor's daughter Ethne, Cían, and Lugh's overthrow and killing of his own grandfather Balor. Keep the sourcing honest about layering, the oldest strand casts them as chthonic/undersea beings, later texts recast them as sea-raiders and giants, still later as generic pirates, and don't present one version as the "original." Treat Lebor Gabála Érenn's internal disagreements as a genuine textual seam rather than resolving them into a single clean genealogy.
handling.cite: Cite Cath Maige Tuired (ed. Elizabeth A. Gray, Irish Texts Society, 1982; also Whitley Stokes's 1891 edition) and Lebor Gabála Érenn (ed. R. A. S. Macalister, Irish Texts Society, 1932-1942) as the primary texts, noting Lebor Gabála's status as a compiled pseudo-history rather than a direct pagan source.

bendigeidfran.fullDescription: His head is buried under London, facing France, still on duty.
bendigeidfran.mysteryNote: The head faced France for as long as the ground over it stayed shut. The tradition remembers who opened it, and why.
bendigeidfran.fate: Killed in the war on Ireland. His severed head was buried at White Hill in London, facing France.

sections.story:
Bendigeidfran, Brân the Blessed, is a giant king of Britain in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. He waged a war against Ireland and it destroyed almost everyone involved, including him.

What happened after is the part worth telling. His severed head was carried to London and buried at White Hill, the site that later became the Tower of London. It was set facing France, so that no invasion could come from that direction while it lay there.

A giant who keeps working after death, from underneath the capital, defending a border he can no longer see.
sections.origins:
The Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, is the source. It is a Middle Welsh prose tale, surviving complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382 to 1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6, dated by Daniel Huws to the second half of the thirteenth century. The composition is older than any surviving copy.

The collective title is modern. William Owen Pughe applied Mabinogion to the tales in 1795, and Lady Charlotte Guest's translation, published in parts between 1838 and 1845, fixed it in English. The form rests on a scribal plural of mabinogi that occurs once in the manuscripts.

The buried head travels outside the tale in the Welsh Triads, edited by Rachel Bromwich as Trioedd Ynys Prydein (Cardiff, 1961). They count the concealment of the head at the White Hill in London, facing France, among the Three Fortunate Concealments, and name Arthur as the one who disclosed it.
sections.disputed:
The date is unsettled. Ifor Williams, in Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930), proposed about 1060. T. M. Charles-Edwards argued for roughly 1050 to 1120. Andrew Breeze places the Four Branches in the 1120s or early 1130s and attributes them to Gwenllian ferch Gruffudd, a proposal the surviving evidence neither confirms nor refutes. Simon Rodway has argued on linguistic grounds that a later twelfth-century date cannot be ruled out.

Whether Bendigeidfran was once a god is not demonstrable. W. J. Gruffydd's reconstructions of a lost mythological cycle behind the Four Branches are now generally read as speculation.

The affinities of the tale are argued too. Proinsias Mac Cana, in Branwen Daughter of Llŷr (1958), made the case for Irish literary influence. Alaric Hall, in Cambrian Medieval Celtic Studies 42 (2001), set Icelandic analogues beside it, notably from Hrólfs saga kraka.

The ravens at the Tower of London are not evidence of him. Boria Sax and Geoffrey Parnell have found no reference to ravens kept there before the late nineteenth century.

handling.living: Medieval literature belonging to a living national tradition: as of the 2020s the Mabinogi is promoted by the Welsh Government as core heritage, retold in film, opera and graphic novels, and read in a language, Welsh, that is spoken and taught. It is public and celebrated, not restricted.
handling.distortions: Retellings routinely present the Tower of London ravens as his ancient legacy, though no ravens are recorded at the Tower before the late nineteenth century, and routinely state as fact that he was a Celtic raven god, an idea resting on early twentieth-century reconstructions now read as speculation. Both habits come from Victorian and Edwardian mythography layered over the medieval text.
handling.take: The whole tale is free: the giant king, the ruinous Irish war, the talking severed head, its burial at White Hill facing France, even Arthur digging it up, which the Welsh Triads supply. What to leave is the false framing, so do not pass off the Tower ravens as medieval or the god theory as settled, and do not dissolve the tale into a generic Celtic setting, because it is specifically Welsh and its place names and personal names carry that identity. Get the Welsh names right or use the anglicised Bran the Blessed consistently.
handling.cite: Sioned Davies's translation of the Mabinogion (Oxford World's Classics, 2007) for the tale, and Rachel Bromwich's Trioedd Ynys Prydein for the Triads material.

ysbaddaden.fullDescription: His eyelids were too heavy to lift on their own. Servants held them open with forks.
ysbaddaden.mysteryNote: Servants with forks decided when he could see. Everything he learned about the world arrived at someone else's convenience.
ysbaddaden.fate: Killed by his own nephew when his daughter married, exactly as he was fated to be.

sections.story:
Ysbaddaden Bencawr is the chief of giants in *Culhwch and Olwen*, one of the earliest Arthurian tales in Welsh. He is the father of Olwen, and the whole story turns on his refusal to let her go: he sets Culhwch a long list of impossible tasks, because he is fated to die when his daughter marries. He is killed at the end by his own nephew.

The detail that fixes him in place is the eyelids. They had to be propped up with forks before he could see anything at all.

Balor, across the Irish Sea, needed a rope and a pulley to raise the lid of his single destroying eye. Two neighbouring Celtic traditions, and the same strange specific image of a giant whose weapon is his sight and whose problem is opening it.
sections.origins:
Culhwch ac Olwen survives in two medieval Welsh manuscripts. The White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MSS 4 and 5), copied around the middle of the fourteenth century, lacks the final third of the tale. The complete text is in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111), written between about 1382 and 1410.

The narrative is older than either copy. Idris Foster, and later Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans in their edition Culhwch and Olwen: An Edition and Study of the Oldest Arthurian Tale (University of Wales Press, 1992), placed its composition around 1100, which would make it the earliest surviving Arthurian prose tale.

It reached a general readership through Lady Charlotte Guest, who translated it within The Mabinogion, issued in parts between 1838 and 1845 and collected in three volumes in 1846. It is not one of the Four Branches, but one of the other tales Guest gathered under that title.
sections.disputed:
The date is contested. Composition is conventionally placed around 1100, following Idris Foster and the Bromwich and Evans edition. Simon Rodway, in "The date and authorship of Culhwch ac Olwen: a reassessment" (Cambrian Medieval Celtic Studies 49, 2005, 21 to 44), argued on orthographic grounds for the middle of the twelfth century instead.

The tale's unity is argued over too. Bromwich and Evans treated the long list of Arthur's court as an accretion rather than part of the original narrative. On that reading the giant's story is the older core, with other material gathered around it.

Whether Ysbaddaden is an inherited figure at all is a further question. Kenneth Jackson, in The International Popular Tale and Early Welsh Tradition (University of Wales Press, 1961), read such material as local tellings of widely distributed folktale types. Ronald Hutton, in "Medieval Welsh Literature and Pre-Christian Deities" (Cambrian Medieval Celtic Studies 61, 2011, 57 to 85), warned against reading medieval Welsh characters as demoted pagan gods.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Ysbaddaden Bencawr belongs to no living faith and no community holds custodial claims on him; medieval Welsh mythological narrative has no continuous practising religious body, and scholars including Ronald Hutton caution specifically against reading such figures as demoted pagan gods with any surviving cult. He survives purely as medieval literature: a manuscript tradition (White Book of Rhydderch, Red Book of Hergest) studied by Celticists and popularized since Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion translations of the 1840s.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening folds Culhwch and Olwen into generic "Arthurian legend" as though it were of a piece with later French romance, obscuring that it is a much earlier, stranger, and distinctly Welsh text with its own narrative logic (the giant's fated death, the escalating list of impossible tasks). A second distortion treats Ysbaddaden's eyelid detail in isolation as quirky color rather than noting its close, likely meaningful parallel to Balor's raised eyelid in Irish tradition, missing a genuine cross-Celtic pattern worth preserving rather than smoothing away.
handling.take: This is freely usable public-domain medieval literature: the impossible-tasks structure, the eyelids propped with forks, the fated death tied to his daughter's marriage, and the killing by his own nephew are all open to direct adaptation. Be careful about dating claims, since composition is conventionally placed around 1100 following Bromwich and Evans but Simon Rodway has argued on orthographic grounds for the mid-twelfth century instead, so treat the earliest-Arthurian-tale claim as contested rather than settled. Avoid asserting he was originally a pagan deity later demoted into folktale; Hutton's scholarship specifically warns against that move for medieval Welsh material, and Kenneth Jackson's international-tale-type reading is an equally live alternative.
handling.cite: Credit Culhwch ac Olwen itself (Red Book of Hergest, Oxford, Jesus College MS 111) and the scholarly edition by Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans, Culhwch and Olwen: An Edition and Study of the Oldest Arthurian Tale (University of Wales Press, 1992); Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion translation (1838-1845) is the standard public-domain popular text.

tombe-dei-giganti.fullDescription: Around eight hundred of them across the island. They are called giants' tombs because nothing else seemed large enough to need one.
tombe-dei-giganti.mysteryNote: The door cut in the central stele is too small to walk through. The living sat outside it, and slept, and waited to be answered.
tombe-dei-giganti.fate: Not a being but a site tradition: the tombs still stand, and the seats outside them were slept on to reach the dead.

sections.story:
These are the monumental collective tombs of the Nuragic culture. The facade curves out in a semicircle shaped like a pair of bull's horns, built from great slabs driven upright into the ground, with a single tall stele at the centre pierced by a door too small for anyone to walk through standing.

Sardinian folk speech calls them, and the nuraghi, sa domu e s'orku: the house of the ogre. The giants' name comes from the size of the stones and from reports of enormous bones found inside the chambers, at a time when there was no archaeology to say otherwise.

The detail that belongs to no one else is what people did there. Along the outside of the curved facade there are stone seats, and relatives of the dead slept on them in order to reach the dead through dreams. The practice has a name: incubation, from the Latin for sleeping upon.

Sites worth naming: Coddu Vecchiu, Li Lolghi and Capichera at Arzachena, Pascaredda at Calangianus, Mont'e s'Abe at Olbia, Imbertighe, Is Concias, Sa Domu e S'Orku at Siddi, and Su Cuaddu de Nixias at Lunamatrona, the oldest.
sections.origins:
The monuments are Nuragic and Bronze Age. The name is not. Sardinian vernacular calls them tumbas de gigantis, and the Italian tomba dei giganti follows popular usage, a term archaeologists then took over as standard.

Nineteenth century Sardinian topography carried the local accounts into print. Vittorio Angius (1797 to 1862) supplied the Sardinian material for the geographical dictionary compiled by Goffredo Casalis and published in Turin from 1833, describing the monuments and the beliefs attached to them.

Antonio Taramelli (1868 to 1939), superintendent of antiquities for Sardinia, carried out the first systematic survey and excavation of the sites in the early twentieth century.

The incubation reading has its own lineage. Aristotle, Physics IV.11, refers to those in Sardinia said to sleep beside the heroes, and Simplicius glossed the passage in his commentary. Raffaele Pettazzoni tied that testimony to the monuments in La religione primitiva in Sardegna (Piacenza, 1912), and Karoly Kerenyi returned to it in Miti e misteri (Turin, 1950).
sections.disputed:
The regional authorities describe the giant-burial idea plainly as popular belief, and the tombs as an architectural evolution of earlier gallery graves. That is the archaeology and it is not in serious doubt. The structures are nuragic funerary monuments; the name is folk taxonomy, not an osteological finding.

Separately, a belief in some unidentified form of Sardinian gigantism has spread over the last few decades, reportedly reaching some academic and popular-science circles. That claim has not been substantiated in the sources checked for this entry and is repeated only as a claim, not as a result. A visitor who stands at a tomba di gigante is looking at real stone and a real naming habit. They are not looking at a verified giant burial, and the entry refuses to blur those two facts.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A name that came from the villages
scholarlyNotes.body: The Italian tomba dei giganti translates Sardinian vernacular usage rather than preserving anything the builders called these monuments, who have left no readable writing. What survives is what islanders said about the stones, and that speech reached print through the Dizionario geografico storico-statistico-commerciale degli Stati di S. M. il Re di Sardegna, compiled by Goffredo Casalis (1781 to 1856) and published in Turin between 1833 and 1856 in twenty-eight volumes. The Sardinian articles in it were written by Vittorio Angius (1797 to 1862), who worked from archives and from visits to the villages. Within a few decades the folk term had become a working category in foreign scholarship as well: Duncan Mackenzie reported the British School at Rome expedition of 1908 under the title "The Dolmens, Tombs of the Giants, and Nuraghi of Sardinia", in Papers of the British School at Rome 5 (1910), pages 88 to 137. So a Bronze Age tomb type carries, in technical literature, a peasant description of the masonry, and it names beings the archaeology does not require.

scholarlyNotes.heading: What Aristotle actually says
scholarlyNotes.body: The ancient testimony behind the incubation reading is very short. In Physics IV.11 Aristotle argues that time is not registered where change is not registered, and he reaches for an illustration. In one English translation the sleepers appear like this: we fail to notice that time has passed, "any more than those who are fabled to sleep among the heroes in Sardinia do when they are awakened". That is the whole of the reference. Aristotle names no building, no site and no rite, he offers the sleepers as fable rather than as observed practice, and his interest is in the psychology of time, not in Sardinia. Everything more specific comes from the late antique commentators, assembled by Pettazzoni in 1912. Simplicius identifies the heroes as the sons of Heracles by the Thespiades, who went with Iolaus to settle the island and whose bodies were said to have stayed intact after death, so that they resembled sleepers rather than corpses. Philoponus adds a purpose and a duration: the sleeping was therapeutic, and those who practised it lay by the tombs for five days.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Pettazzoni's step from the text to the stones
scholarlyNotes.body: Nothing in the ancient testimony mentions these monuments. The connection was made by Raffaele Pettazzoni (1883 to 1959) in La religione primitiva in Sardegna, published at Piacenza by the Societa editrice pontremolese in 1912. Pettazzoni glosses Aristotle by reasoning that sleeping beside the heroes means sleeping beside the dwellings of the heroes, and that those dwellings are the tombs. He then files incubation, ancestor veneration and hero cult at the tombe dei giganti under the animistic side of Sardinian religion, set against a naturalistic side represented by the water cult. The reasoning is legible, and it is also the joint that carries the load: the identification of the heroes' dwellings with this monument type, and of the exedra benches with the place of sleeping, is inference rather than a statement in any ancient source. The purpose the commentators report is worth holding beside it. Philoponus describes a cure sought over five days, which sits alongside, rather than confirms, the idea of seeking the dead in dreams.

scholarlySources: Aristotle, Physics IV.11 (218b), on time unnoticed where change is unnoticed
Raffaele Pettazzoni, La religione primitiva in Sardegna, Piacenza: Societa editrice pontremolese, 1912
Duncan Mackenzie, "The Dolmens, Tombs of the Giants, and Nuraghi of Sardinia", Papers of the British School at Rome 5, 1910, pages 88 to 137
Goffredo Casalis, Dizionario geografico storico-statistico-commerciale degli Stati di S. M. il Re di Sardegna, Turin, 1833 to 1856, Sardinian articles by Vittorio Angius

handling.living: As of the 2020s the Tombe dei Giganti are Bronze Age Nuragic monuments with no living faith or continuous cult attached to them; Nuragic religion did not survive as a practised tradition. The giant name and the folk belief in giant burials are themselves a later, vernacular naming habit layered onto the archaeology, not evidence of a living custodial belief system.
handling.distortions: Popular treatments routinely present the "giant burial" name as if it reflected an actual belief that giants were interred there, when the regional archaeological record treats it plainly as folk taxonomy driven by the size of the stones and misidentified large bones, with no ongoing giant-burial belief among Sardinians today. A second distortion, increasingly visible in popular-science and pseudo-archaeology circles, asserts an unidentified form of ancient Sardinian gigantism as if it were an established finding, when it has not been substantiated in the scholarly record and should be treated only as an unverified claim.
handling.take: The archaeology and the folklore are both freely usable and should be kept clearly distinguished: describe the monuments, the horn-shaped facade, the incubation practice of sleeping on the outer stone seats to dream-contact the dead, and the vernacular naming (sa domu e s'orku) as what they are, real structures and a real naming tradition. Do not present the giant-burial idea as a literal ancient belief in giant occupants, and do not repeat the modern "Sardinian gigantism" claim as fact; flag it explicitly as an unsubstantiated fringe claim if you mention it at all.
handling.cite: Cite Antonio Taramelli's early-twentieth-century site surveys and current Sardinian regional archaeological/superintendency documentation for the monuments; for the incubation reading, cite Aristotle, Physics IV.11, with Raffaele Pettazzoni, La religione primitiva in Sardegna (1912), and Karoly Kerenyi, Miti e misteri (1950).

nemri.fullDescription: They are called the old people. They could not die a natural death.
nemri.mysteryNote: Not dying is told as a condition, not a gift. The carved stones the tradition attaches them to were cut by other hands, centuries later.
nemri.fate: A lost people who could not die naturally, remembered where the stecci stand.

sections.story:
Across the Velebit range and through Lika, the giants are the Nemri, and ethnologists treat them as a genuine local particularity rather than something borrowed. The term is still recognised among people of the Dinaric country.

They are described as a lost people who lived here before the Greeks, and who could not die naturally. That is not stated as a power. It is stated as a condition, and it implies that something went wrong for them.

A large part of the Nemri tradition attaches to the places where stećci stand, the medieval tombstones of the Dinaric interior.

They belong with the Kāhui Tipua of New Zealand, the Fomorians of Ireland and the Quinametzin of Mexico. Four traditions with nothing in common, each explaining an inherited landscape by putting a larger, earlier people in it.
sections.origins:
There is no medieval text. The Nemri are an oral tradition of Lika, the Velebit Podgorje and the wider Dinaric interior, recorded by collectors rather than composed by authors.

Nineteenth-century collectors working in Lika and in Bosanska Krajina published accounts of a giant old population in regional periodicals. Maja Bošković-Stulli gathered folklore from the immediate area in the 1950s, in "Folklorna građa okolice Lovinca u Lici" (1955) and "Folklorna građa sa Zrmanje" (1957).

The comparative frame is Vlajko Palavestra's work on traditions of an earlier population across the Dinaric lands: "Narodna predanja o starom stanovništvu u dinarskim krajevima" (1966), and later "Historijska usmena predanja iz Bosne i Hercegovine" (2004).

The modern survey is Matija Dronjić, "Prilog istraživanju predaja o starom narodu na području Like i Podgorja", in Senjski zbornik 39 (2012), which gathers the Lika attestations and sets the Nemri against the Grci traditions of the same region.

Transmission is local and site-bound: hillforts, stećak necropolises, large bones turned up in fields.
sections.disputed:
The relation between Nemri and Grci is argued. Dronjić (2012) reads them as two layers: an older Nemri stratum carrying the fantastic attributes, giant stature, superhuman strength, unnatural longevity, and a younger Grci stratum in which those attributes are absent. Whether that is genuine chronological layering or parallel naming within one region is not settled.

Where the Grci label comes from is the sharper disagreement. Palavestra's explanation is confessional, deriving it from the Orthodox "Greek" church. Dronjić argues instead for westward diffusion with populations moving ahead of Ottoman expansion, noting that the term is attested in Senj before settlement in Lika is documented.

The name Nemri itself has no agreed etymology. Dronjić's survey offers none, and the transparent Slavic reading has not been established philologically.

The stećci are the standing misreading. They are medieval tombstones. The folk attribution of them to a giant race is a tradition about the stones, not evidence about them.

handling.living: As of the 2020s the Nemri belong to no living faith; this is regional Dinaric/Croatian folk tradition of Lika and the Velebit Podgorje, still recognised as a local term and studied by living ethnologists (Dronjić's 2012 survey, Perinić Lewis's 2019 work), but with no religious body or custodial community restricting it. It is heritage and folklore-studies material, comparable in status to other Balkan 'old people' traditions.
handling.distortions: The most common distortion is literalizing the stećci connection, treating the medieval Dinaric tombstones as physical evidence of an actual giant race rather than a folk explanation later attached to unexplained monuments; the entry itself is explicit that this runs backwards. A second distortion is collapsing the Nemri and Grci traditions into one undifferentiated 'old people' legend, when Croatian folklorists (Dronjić, Palavestra) treat their relationship and the origin of the Grci label as live, unresolved scholarly questions rather than settled synonyms.
handling.take: The recorded motifs are freely usable: a lost people from before the Greeks who could not die naturally, associated with hillforts and standing stones, paired comparatively with traditions like the Kāhui Tipua, Fomorians and Quinametzin as instances of a common 'earlier, larger people explain the landscape' pattern. Don't present the stećci as evidence for the giants, they are documented medieval tombstones, and the giant attribution is folklore about the stones, not information from them, and keep the Nemri/Grci distinction and the unresolved etymology visible rather than smoothing them into a single tidy legend.
handling.cite: Credit Matija Dronjić, 'Prilog istraživanju predaja o starom narodu na području Like i Podgorja,' Senjski zbornik 39 (2012), and Vlajko Palavestra's work on Dinaric 'old population' traditions, alongside Maja Bošković-Stulli's 1950s field collections from the immediate area.

klek.fullDescription: Seen from Ogulin, the mountain is a sleeping man. The peak is his head. The two crags below are his legs.
klek.mysteryNote: He was struck while running, and the wound has not stopped running either. From Ogulin you can still see where he came to rest.
klek.fate: Struck by Perun's arrow as he fled and turned to stone. The wound is the river Dobra.

sections.story:
Klek, Orjen and Snježnik are giants who were turned to stone. Klek is the one people can still read at a glance: from the Ogulin side the ridge lies down as a sleeping giant, the summit at 1181 metres is the head, and the Klečice crags coming up out of the treeline are the legs.

He was running when it happened. Perun struck him with an arrow in the right vein as he fled, and the people named that vein the river Dobra, also called Đula.

That is worth sitting with. The river is not named after the wound. The river is the wound. It is the same logic that turns Ymir's blood into the sea, worked at the scale of one valley.

Klek carries a second tradition on top of the first. Witches gather there, and the lightning around the mountain is their assembly. The two stories share the mountain without much interfering with each other.
sections.origins:
The tradition is local and topographic, fixed to one ridge in the Velika Kapela massif above Ogulin: Veliki Klek at 1181 metres, with Klečica at 1062.

The earliest written notice belongs to the witches rather than to the giant. Johann Weichard von Valvasor, author of Die Ehre dess Hertzogthums Crain (1689), is credited with recording the Klek assembly in the seventeenth century.

The petrifaction story reaches print through twentieth-century Croatian collecting. Stjepan Banović's Vjerovanja (Zaostrog u Dalmaciji) appeared in 1918. Nikola Sučić's Hrvatska narodna mitologija was published in Zagreb in 1943 and reprinted in 2013 with an afterword by Tomislav Pletenac that presents it as a monument to its own period rather than as method. Maja Bošković-Stulli (1922 to 2012), of the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research in Zagreb, supplies the critical baseline for Croatian oral legend.

Later transmission ran through mountaineering writing, Klek being called the cradle of Croatian mountaineering, and through Ogulin's modern fairy-tale tourism.
sections.disputed:
Perun is one of the few Slavic deities securely attested rather than reconstructed, which gives this tradition a firmer footing than most Croatian material that claims pre-Christian origin. Much of what circulates online as Croatian or Slavic mythology, including elaborate creation stories and full pantheon genealogies, is nineteenth or twentieth century reconstruction or modern invention. This entry is not that: the mountain, the petrification story and the association with a known thunder god sit on firmer ground than the inventiveness of modern retellings.

Even so, the surrounding material should be treated with care. Place-legend and god-name do not automatically yield a continuous pagan cult. The story that a giant or god was turned to stone on Klek is the traditional claim; how old each detail is, and how much later collectors shaped the wording, cannot be settled from the popular versions alone. What can be said is that this is a real-site tradition with a better mythological anchor than most of its online neighbours.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Klek belongs to no living faith; Slavic paganism, including the cult of Perun, has no continuous practising body, and the tradition survives as regional folklore, mountaineering culture and Ogulin's fairy-tale tourism rather than active belief. There is no custodial community with authority over the story comparable to a living Indigenous nation; the relevant institutional voice is scholarly (Zagreb's Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research) rather than religious.
handling.distortions: The most common mangling is treating this as generic "Slavic mythology" of the elaborate-pantheon, full-creation-myth variety that circulates widely online, when most of that broader material is nineteenth- or twentieth-century reconstruction or outright modern invention; Klek's tradition is unusual precisely because it anchors to a securely attested deity (Perun) and a specific, still-visible landform. A second distortion is treating the petrification story as if it were an unbroken pagan survival, when how old any given detail is, and how much twentieth-century collectors like Sučić shaped the wording, cannot be settled from the popular versions alone. A third is merging the giant-petrification story with the separate witches'-assembly tradition on the same mountain, when the two share only a location.
handling.take: The core material is usable and comparatively well-grounded: the mountain's giant-shaped silhouette, the Perun-arrow petrification, the river-as-wound imagery, and the separate witches' assembly recorded by Valvasor in the seventeenth century. Flag, rather than erase, the real uncertainty about how far back the petrification story itself goes versus how much is filtered through twentieth-century collecting (Banović 1918, Sučić 1943), and don't borrow the confident tone of invented "full Slavic pantheon" content that circulates online, this entry sits on firmer ground than that material but is still popular tradition, not liturgy.
handling.cite: Cite Johann Weichard von Valvasor's Die Ehre dess Hertzogthums Crain (1689) for the witches' assembly, Stjepan Banović's Vjerovanja (Zaostrog u Dalmaciji, 1918) and Nikola Sučić's Hrvatska narodna mitologija (1943, reprinted 2013 with Tomislav Pletenac's critical afterword) for the petrification story, and Maja Bošković-Stulli's work at the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research, Zagreb, as the critical scholarly baseline.

uriasi.fullDescription: The Danube came up to their ankles. They could reach the handles of the sky. Their age ended with the Flood.
uriasi.mysteryNote: The Flood took them. Their names stayed behind on the map, including one gorge that was eventually called something else.
uriasi.fate: Ended by the Flood, leaving their names across the map.

sections.story:
Romanian tradition calls its giants uriași, and regionally novaci, jidovi, căpcăuni, coloși and tătari. They were here before people, they were enormous beyond measuring, and the Flood ended them.

Two of them have names and have stayed in the language: Sfarmă-Piatră, Crush-Stone, and Strâmbă-Lemne, Bend-Wood. Iovan Iorgovan belongs to the same company.

Their names are on the map. The town of Novaci in Gorj county. Jidova, Jidovița, and Jidvei in Alba. A gorge in the Eastern Carpathians called Valea Jidovului for a long time before the name was changed.
sections.origins:
Romanian giant tradition is oral rather than literary. There is no founding text behind it: the material survives in folk narrative and in the ordinary vocabulary of the language, and it reached print only when collectors began gathering Romanian popular material in the nineteenth century.

The naming is regional, which is part of why the tradition was recorded piecemeal. Uriași is the general word, with novaci, jidovi, căpcăuni, coloși and tătari used in different areas. The named figures, Sfarmă-Piatră, Strâmbă-Lemne and Iovan Iorgovan, come down through the same folk collections.

The modern reference point is Ion Taloș, the Romanian ethnologist whose mythological dictionary gathers the scattered material into usable form.

Place-names carry the tradition independently of any text: Novaci in Gorj, Jidova, Jidovița and Jidvei in Alba, Valea Jidovului in the Eastern Carpathians.

A separate and much later stream begins with Nicolae Densușianu's Dacia preistorică, published posthumously, which absorbed the giants into a nationalist prehistory. That stream is not folk transmission.
sections.disputed:
This entry needs a warning that the others do not.

The folklore is real, and Ion Taloș is a real ethnologist whose mythological dictionary is the source to build on. But searches on Romanian giants return a large body of material presented as fact that is nothing of the sort: five-metre skeletons, eighty giants exhumed at one site, bones described as pink as though irradiated, a skeleton urgently removed to Moscow, the intelligence service sealing a mine shaft, and a deliberate historiographic cover-up. Around it sit Atlantis, hyperboreans, and the claim that the Greek gods and Titans were Dacians.

The founding text of that tradition is Nicolae Densușianu's *Dacia preistorică*, the origin point of Romanian protochronism, a nationalist pseudo-history that has been thoroughly discredited. It is cited constantly and should not be used here.

Note also that jidov and its relatives carry real sensitivities in Romanian, and the same naming habit appears in Bulgarian tradition, where Iliev's 1890 collection describes the ispolini as called Greeks, Jews and Latins.

handling.living: As of the 2020s the uriași belong to no living faith and no community holds custodial claims on them; this is Romanian folk narrative and everyday vocabulary, not the property of an active religion or Indigenous institution. Regional oral tellings and place-names (Novaci, Jidova, Valea Jidovului) continue to circulate as heritage culture, and Ion Taloș's mythological dictionary is the standard modern scholarly touchstone, but there is no governing body analogous to a tribal council or UNESCO listing attached to the figures themselves.
handling.distortions: The overwhelming modern distortion is not media flattening but pseudo-archaeology: search results and popular retellings are saturated with fabricated claims of giant skeletons excavated in the Carpathians, secret Soviet removals, and intelligence-service cover-ups, all descending from Nicolae Densușianu's discredited nationalist protochronist tract Dacia preistorică. A secondary distortion collapses the regionally distinct naming (novaci, jidovi, căpcăuni, coloși, tătari) into one generic "giant race," erasing the local specificity that place-names like Novaci or Jidvei actually preserve.
handling.take: The genuine folk material is freely usable: the flood-ended giant race, the named figures Sfarmă-Piatră and Strâmbă-Lemne, Iovan Iorgovan, and the place-name evidence scattered across Gorj, Alba, and the Eastern Carpathians, all sourced through Ion Taloș's dictionary and legitimate nineteenth/twentieth-century folk collections. Firmly avoid Nicolae Densușianu's Dacia preistorică and the entire protochronist giant-skeleton mythology it spawned (Moscow removals, sealed mine shafts, pink irradiated bones); none of it is folklore in any real sense, it is fabricated nationalist pseudo-history, and repeating it even as "legend" lends it false credibility. Also handle the word jidov with care, since it and its cognates carry real ethnic sensitivity in Romanian and the same naming pattern appears in neighboring Bulgarian tradition.
handling.cite: Credit Ion Taloș's Romanian mythological dictionary and legitimate nineteenth-century Romanian folk collections as the source base; explicitly exclude Nicolae Densușianu's Dacia preistorică (posthumous, protochronist) from anything presented as factual or folkloric record.

croatian-giants-lesser.fullDescription: Four smaller Croatian traditions, each too thin to stand alone and too specific to lose.
croatian-giants-lesser.mysteryNote: The mounds are still there, and still closed. Whatever the valley decided was lying under them, it decided without ever looking.
croatian-giants-lesser.fate: Different endings: the Vedi withdrew into the forests, and Sambo lies petrified beneath Samobor.

sections.story:
**The one-eyed giants of Brač and Paklenica.** On the island of Brač there are traditions of powerful men with a single eye in the middle of the forehead. In Paklenica there was a one-eyed giant who lived in a cave. This is a Croatian cyclops tradition on the Adriatic, in the same sea as Polyphemus but in a separate stream of storytelling. Whether that is independence, shared inheritance, or later borrowing from classical material is the same open question raised under the Katallani entry in Albania, and it is not settled here either.

**The Vedi.** In the Bilogora country, giants who left their original settlements and withdrew into the forests. Not driven out, not killed. They simply went.

**The Hajdi and Sambo.** Samobor and the Samoborsko gorje were theirs. The church of Sv. Križ at Otruševec is credited to them. The giant Sambo is said to lie petrified beneath Samobor, which puts him with Klek, Orjen and Snježnik among the giants who became landscape.

**The giants of the Neretva valley.** Here the tradition is attached to Illyrian burial mounds, and the giants are remembered in a specific phrase: those who were here before us. Local estimate put the bones in the mounds at up to two and a half metres.

The mounds were never dug up. They were treated with respect and left alone, and that is the part of this tradition worth keeping. The interesting thing is not what was in the ground. It is that a community found something it could not explain, decided it belonged to an earlier and larger people, and then chose reverence over excavation.
sections.origins:
Four separate local traditions, recorded in four different parts of Croatia: Brač, Paklenica, the Bilogora, Samobor and the Samoborsko gorje, and the Neretva valley.

The oldest named source is Stjepan Banović's Vjerovanja (Zaostrog u Dalmaciji), 1918, a monograph of folk belief from a single Dalmatian place. Work of that kind was produced inside a collecting apparatus built a generation earlier: the Academy's Zbornik za narodni život i običaje Južnih Slavena, founded 1896, and Antun Radić's Osnova za sabiranje i proučavanje građe o narodnom životu, 1897, a detailed fieldwork guide that had local intellectuals record peasant life in its own dialect.

Maja Bošković-Stulli (1922 to 2012), of the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research in Zagreb, left 34 manuscript collections and 59 tape recordings from almost all of Croatia. Ana Perinić Lewis, "Junaci, divovi i patuljci Gorskoga kotara", 2019, is the recent scholarship.
sections.disputed:
The word itself is contested. The Hrvatska enciklopedija of the Leksikografski zavod Miroslav Krleža derives div from Turkish dev and Persian dīv, and places the shift in sense from demon to giant inside Turkish. Against that stands the reconstruction of an inherited Proto-Slavic *divъ, connected either to Proto-Indo-European *deywós, god, or to *dyew-, to be bright, with the demon sense arising later, possibly by demonisation under Iranian contact, on the pattern by which Sanskrit deva became Avestan daēuua. Loanword or inheritance is not settled.

The one-eyed giants of Brač and Paklenica raise a second question that is also open: independent local invention, shared inheritance, or borrowing from classical material carried along the Adriatic.

The sourcing carries its own caveat. Nikola Sučić's Hrvatska narodna mitologija is cited for this material with its scholarly standing recorded as unverified, and nothing in the present checking settled it.

handling.living: These are heritage folk traditions, not a living faith: Croatian Catholic and civic culture today has no ritual practice or custodial body attached to the Brač cyclops, the Vedi, Hajdi and Sambo, or the Neretva mound-giants. They survive as recorded local legend, kept alive mainly by regional ethnographic scholarship (the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research in Zagreb) and local tourism rather than by any continuing belief community. The one live thread is the Neretva valley's inherited reverence for the Illyrian burial mounds themselves, which some locals still treat as places not to be disturbed.
handling.distortions: The most common flattening is treating "div" traditions as a single uniform Croatian mythology, when the input material is explicit that these are four separate, geographically distinct local traditions with no shared narrative. A second distortion is importing classical cyclops iconography (Polyphemus, Odyssey beats) onto the Brač/Paklenica one-eyed giants as if the connection were settled, when the relationship between them is an open scholarly question, not a borrowing that can be assumed.
handling.take: The place-legends themselves (Vedi withdrawing into the forest, Hajdi and Sambo credited with the Otruševec church, Sambo petrified beneath Samobor, the Neretva bone-mounds) are folk material safely retellable. Keep the etymology of "div" (Turkish/Persian loan versus inherited Proto-Slavic) and the cyclops-independence question presented as unresolved rather than picking a side, since scholarship hasn't settled either. Flag Nikola Sučić's Hrvatska narodna mitologija as a source of unverified scholarly standing if you lean on it, and preserve the Neretva valley detail that the mounds were deliberately left unexcavated, that restraint is the most interesting and citable fact in the set.
handling.cite: Credit Maja Bošković-Stulli's Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research archive, Stjepan Banović's 1918 Vjerovanja monograph, and Ana Perinić Lewis's 2019 "Junaci, divovi i patuljci Gorskoga kotara"; treat Nikola Sučić as a secondary source needing independent verification.

british-giants-lesser.fullDescription: Britain kept more giants than it had room to remember properly. These are the ones who left a name and not much else.
british-giants-lesser.mysteryNote: Four names, and between them barely one whole story. A mountain still called a chair is most of what is left of the man said to have sat in it.
british-giants-lesser.fate: Different endings: Blunderbore killed with rope in his sleep, Idris remembered only through his chair.

sections.story:
**Idris Gawr.** Cader Idris in Wales is his chair, and the mountain carries his name to this day. A giant remembered entirely through furniture, like Gargantua across the channel.

**Bolster.** The Cornish giant of St Agnes Beacon.

**Blunderbore.** Another Cornish giant of the Jack the Giant Killer cycle. In the story Jack, having already killed Cormoran, is captured by Blunderbore and thrown into the dungeon of his castle to be eaten later. He escapes and kills both Blunderbore and his brother while they sleep, with rope.

**Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll.** A giant husband and wife in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, who bring the Cauldron of Rebirth out of Ireland to Wales. A cauldron that returns the dead to life, but returns them mute. They are the couriers of the single most dangerous object in the tale, and they are giants because nothing smaller could carry it.
sections.origins:
The four figures reach the catalogue by three separate routes.

Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll belong to Branwen ferch Llyr, the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. The tales survive in two Middle Welsh manuscripts: the White Book of Rhydderch, in the Peniarth collection at the National Library of Wales, written about 1350, and the Red Book of Hergest at Jesus College, Oxford. Lady Charlotte Guest's English translation, issued in parts between 1838 and 1849, gave the collection the name by which it is now known.

Blunderbore comes from print rather than from field collection. He belongs to the Jack the Giant Killer chapbooks, the earliest recorded being The History of Jack and the Giants, published in two parts by J. White of Newcastle in 1711.

Bolster reaches us through Robert Hunt, who walked Cornwall for ten months from 1829 collecting drolls from the last of the droll tellers, and printed them a generation later in Popular Romances of the West of England.

Idris is attached to Cadair Idris, the Chair of Idris, by topographic tradition. No medieval Welsh narrative about him survives.
sections.disputed: British searches turn up a large nineteenth-century antiquarian literature reporting giant skeletons: a thigh bone from a man eight feet nine inches tall, a skeleton of fourteen feet ten inches, remains above the common size of men. These are reports about reports, made before modern archaeology and often at second hand, and they circulate today mainly in contexts that have already decided what they want them to prove. They belong in Bones & Shadows, if anywhere, and not in this entry.

handling.living: As of the 2020s these figures sit at three different temperatures: the Mabinogi is living Welsh national literature, still translated, taught and retold; Bolster has an active community life in St Agnes, where villagers process a giant effigy over the cliffs each May; Blunderbore survives only as pantomime and chapbook memory, and Idris only as the name of a mountain.
handling.distortions: The commonest mangling is merging the Jack the Giant Killer giants with the Jack and the Beanstalk giant into one generic ogre, a confusion the Victorian nursery-book trade produced by printing the tales side by side. The nineteenth-century giant-skeleton reports noted in the disputed section are also still recycled online as physical evidence, which they are not.
handling.take: All four figures are free to use: medieval literature, an authored chapbook cycle and drolls collected in print carry no community protocols, and none are known for any of them. The Cauldron of Rebirth is free too, but it comes with its own logic, revenants who return mute, and stripping that cost turns a Welsh tragedy into a stock magic item; the Welsh names likewise carry real pronunciation and real places, so keep them or change them, but do not garble them. The one thing that is not simply raw material is the modern Bolster pageant itself, which is a specific ongoing St Agnes event and should be depicted as theirs, not invented over.
handling.cite: Sioned Davies's translation of the Mabinogion (Oxford World's Classics, 2007) for the Welsh material, and Robert Hunt's Popular Romances of the West of England for the Cornish.

koljo.fullDescription: A giant who survives mostly as place-names, and a scholarly argument about whether he was ever a giant at all.
koljo.mysteryNote: Follow a Koljo name to an island in the lake country and the dead are often already there, in ground no parish ever consecrated. The giant may be the last shape a word for death took.
koljo.fate: No death: he survives as a name on the ground, first recorded in the Savo land register of the 1560s.

sections.story:
Koljo is a Finnish name for a giant, and the tradition around him has been studied more carefully than most, in a paper whose title asks the right question: giant, devil, or death?

The name is attached to the ground. The earliest recorded example, Kolionmäki, Koljo's Hill, appears in the first land register of Savo in the 1560s, which makes it older than most written folklore anywhere in this catalogue.

The Koljo names cluster in a defined area, while others, like Kalevanpoika in southwest Finland and Estonia, cluster elsewhere. Mapped together they show something the stories alone do not: giants are not evenly distributed. Each name belongs to a region, and where the names blur into one another over time, the tradition behind them has usually already begun to fade.
sections.origins:
Koljo is documented first in administrative records rather than in literature. A Nicki Koljolainen appears in the Kangasala district court records in January 1486. The place-name Kolionmäki is entered in the first land register of Savo in the 1560s, together with kolian nemi and kolion nemi at Särkilahti in Sääminki.

The word reaches lexicography in Renvall's Finnish dictionary of the 1820s, glossed as a large or gigantic person and as a mythical giant. More than 150 place-names containing koljo and its variants can still be read off modern maps, concentrated in the old Häme region and in eastern Finland.

The modern study is Juha Ruohonen's, published in Finnish as "Jättiläinen, paholainen, kuolema? Koljo kansanperinteessä, nimistössä ja maastossa" in Sananjalka 52 (2010), pages 148 to 162, and in English as "Giant, Devil or Death?" in Culture Crossroads volume 5 (2011), pages 101 to 115, the Latvian Academy of Culture's proceedings of a 2009 conference on natural holy places held at the Turaida Museum Reserve.
sections.disputed:
Ruohonen's title is a real question rather than a rhetorical one. He argues that koljo originally carried senses of death and of notable terrain, and that the giant is a later development, following the account of Christianisation reshaping older belief vocabulary set out by Koski in 1967. That is an argument in progress, not a settled result.

The etymology is unresolved. Setälä in 1912 connected koljo with Estonian koll, a word for the dead. Comparisons have also been proposed with Germanic halja and hel, and with Permic and Ob-Ugric words meaning serious disease, plague, devil and god of the underworld. Ruohonen calls the word ambiguous and in part blurred.

How far the biblical Goliath, Finnish koljatti, shaped the giant sense rather than merely darkening it is not established.

Ruohonen also rejects deriving related kuolio names from Saami guolli, fish, on archaeological grounds. That alternative etymology stands in the literature.

handling.living: As of the 2020s Koljo belongs to no living faith or practising community; this is heritage folklore and toponymy studied by Finnish philologists and folklorists, not an active tradition with claimants. The material survives almost entirely in administrative records, place-names and academic papers rather than in any continuing oral practice.
handling.distortions: The main distortion is treating "Koljo" as a settled giant-figure with a fixed identity, when the leading modern scholarship (Ruohonen 2010/2011) argues the word may originally have meant death or notable terrain, with the giant sense a later Christianisation-era development, and the etymology remains genuinely unresolved between Estonian koll, Germanic halja/hel, Permic/Ob-Ugric disease-and-underworld words, and possible influence from biblical Goliath (koljatti). A second distortion is conflating Koljo place-names with the unrelated Kalevanpoika giant-toponym cluster, when the paper's whole point is that these are geographically distinct naming traditions that shouldn't be merged. A third is presenting the rejected kuolio-from-Saami-guolli (fish) etymology as viable when Ruohonen rejects it on archaeological grounds.
handling.take: This is safe, freely usable material precisely because it's thin and well-sourced: the giant sense of Koljo, the place-name clustering in Häme and eastern Finland, and the open etymological debate are all fair to present, but present the etymology as unresolved rather than picking a winner, since that unresolved status is the actual scholarly finding. Don't manufacture a story or personality for Koljo beyond what the toponyms and Ruohonen's analysis support; the honest entry here is closer to historical linguistics than to narrative myth.
handling.cite: Cite Juha Ruohonen, "Jättiläinen, paholainen, kuolema? Koljo kansanperinteessä, nimistössä ja maastossa," Sananjalka 52 (2010), and its English version "Giant, Devil or Death?" in Culture Crossroads vol. 5 (2011); the Finnish land register of Savo (1560s) is the primary documentary source for the place-name.

santa-elena-giants.fullDescription: In 1553 a Spanish chronicler wrote down what the Manta people told him about the giants who landed on their coast. Four centuries later, someone worked out what the bones were.
santa-elena-giants.mysteryNote: They dug their wells down into living rock, and the wells are still there. Bones came up out of that same peninsula for four hundred years before anyone could name the animal.
santa-elena-giants.fate: Destroyed, in the ending Cieza de Leon added, by an angel with a sword of fire.

sections.story:
Pedro Cieza de León did not claim to have seen anything. He recorded what he was told, and he said so, which is more than most of his contemporaries managed.

The giants came by sea, on rafts made of bundled reeds, and landed at the Punta de Santa Elena near Puerto Viejo. They were built so that from the knee to the ground they matched a full-grown man, and the tallest Castilian would not have reached their waists. Their hair hung loose down their backs. They had no beards. Their eyes were described as the size of small plates. Some wore skins. Some wore nothing.

They brought no women with them.

They dug wells down into the living rock to reach water, and those wells are the part of the story you can still visit. They fished, and they hunted the local forest, and they raided the village, and by Cieza's account they ate what they took, the people included. One of them was said to eat as much as fifty of the local men.

Later chroniclers repeated and extended the account. Herrera has them arriving from the coasts of the Río de la Plata. Some versions have the Inca Túpac Yupanqui attempting to bring them under control. Bones and skulls of extraordinary size were reported across the peninsula for centuries, and in the eighteenth century a colonial official compiled a formal report on the petrified bones and an enormous molar found there.

The bones were real. Research into how Ecuadorians historically made sense of mastodon remains connects the Andean and coastal giant traditions directly to fossil finds. Santa Elena sits on ground that produces the bones of animals nobody in the sixteenth century had a category for.
sections.origins:
Pedro Cieza de León is the source. He travelled in Peru between 1548 and 1550, and published the first part of his Crónica del Perú at Seville in 1553, with an Antwerp printing in 1554. The giants occupy chapter LII, which pairs them with the wells at the point of Santa Elena. Cieza gives the account as something he was told.

Later chroniclers carried it forward: Agustín de Zárate (Antwerp, 1555), Garcilaso de la Vega in the Comentarios Reales de los Incas (Lisbon, 1609), and Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas, whose Décadas appeared between 1601 and 1615. Pedro Gutiérrez de Santa Clara wrote in the 1550s but stayed unpublished until Manuel Serrano y Sanz issued his chronicle in Madrid between 1904 and 1929.

The bones held the story to the ground. An eighteenth-century colonial report by García de León y Pizarro described petrified remains and a great molar from the peninsula, and modern work on how mastodon finds in Ecuador were read has since linked the tradition to them.
sections.disputed:
The ending is not Manta tradition.

Cieza's account closes with the giants, having no women of their own, turning to each other, and a Christian archangel descending to destroy them with a sword of fire as punishment. Scholarship on this material (including Uribe and Hechler) treats the ending as Cieza's Christian framing and interpretation rather than as a line that can be shown to belong to Manta tradition. That is slightly softer than saying the chronicler invented every beat, and still firm enough: the sword of fire arrives in a datable Spanish text.

That is worth pausing on, because it is rare. Usually the Christian layer over an indigenous story has to be inferred. Here it can be watched being applied, in a datable document, by a named man, in 1553.

chain.claim: The giants who landed by sea at the Punta de Santa Elena were destroyed by fire that came down from heaven, a punishment the local people remembered and the Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon wrote down in 1553.
chain.verdict: The wording that carries this claim is documented in a printed chronicle of 1553, where the destruction sentence is introduced as something people say and the fire is attached to a charge of sodomy; the scholarship consulted here reads the fire and the angel as the chronicler's own framing, and the bones on the peninsula were being called animal rather than human by the end of the eighteenth century.

rungs.witness: Ryan Scott Hechler and Daniel Zurita-Altamirano, Podrian ser gigantes: una etnografia arqueologica sobre los procesos historicos de racionalizacion de las megafaunas, los mastodontes y las primeras interacciones humanas en Ecuador, ANTROPOLOGIA. Cuadernos de Investigacion 27 (2023), pages 44 to 63, DOI 10.26807/ant.vi27.298
rungs.reads: It treats the destruction as Cieza's reading rather than as testimony: the article describes his account as ending with a Christian archangel killing the giants with a fiery sword to punish them for the supposed sin of homosexuality. It then does the thing that matters for the claim, which is to put the story back on the ground. It notes that Santa Elena and the Portoviejo area were named by chroniclers because of quantities of dead giants, and that in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the same area became known for Late Pleistocene megafauna, particularly mastodons. It also reports that Zarate's 1555 version is much abbreviated and turns on Spaniards finding enormous ribs and whole skulls while digging.
rungs.evidence: Full text at https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/9052563.pdf, fetched three times with different questions; it returned the archangel and fiery sword description, the mastodon link, the Zarate summary, and the bibliography entries for Cieza, Zarate and Garcilaso. Journal record, issue 27, 2023, pages 44 to 63, DOI 10.26807/ant.vi27.298, at https://www.cuadernosdeantropologia-puce.edu.ec/index.php/antropologia/article/view/298. Also indexed at https://dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=9052563, whose record dates the issue August 2022 to January 2023.
rungs.note: The Dialnet record and the journal's own record give slightly different years for the same issue, 2022 and 2023. I have followed the journal.

rungs.witness: Ignacio Uribe M., Pedro Cieza de Leon, los gigantes y Mercurio, Agora. Estudos Classicos em Debate 24 (2022), DOI 10.34624/agora.v24i0.27979
rungs.reads: It prints the 1553 destruction passage and then argues about where the shape of it came from. Uribe's position, in his own words, is that Cieza creo una correspondencia entre la historia de los edificios de Tiahuanaco y los gigantes de Santa Elena, introduciendo elementos tomados del pasado griego. He connects the scene to the account Juan de Betanzos had from indigenous informants, and he reads the shining figure with the sword against classical material, Mercury and Argos. He does not say in so many words that the ending is an invention; what he documents is a chronicler assembling it.
rungs.evidence: Article record and DOI at https://proa.ua.pt/index.php/agora/en/article/view/27979, which gives the author as Ignacio Uribe M., the journal as Agora, volume 24, 2022, and the abstract proposing a relationship between the narration and engraving of the Saint Helen's giants in the Primera parte de la chronica del Peru (1553) and the myth of Argos. Full text fetched at https://www.redalyc.org/pdf/3210/321081234012.pdf and https://proa.ua.pt/index.php/agora/article/download/27979/20086; both returned the correspondencia sentence and the Betanzos and Greek material. Also indexed at https://dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=8368575.

rungs.witness: Federico Gonzalez Suarez, Historia general de la Republica del Ecuador, tomo quinto, chapter titled Capitulo sexto: El presidente don Jose Garcia de Leon y Pizarro
rungs.date: One of the seven volumes published at Quito between 1890 and 1903. I could not confirm the separate year of this volume. The events it reports belong to the 1780s.
rungs.reads: It is silent on fire from heaven and it takes the ground out from under the giants. Gonzalez Suarez reports that the president of Quito, Jose Garcia de Leon y Pizarro, went to Santa Elena himself, had the tar seam examined, and concluded, in the text's words, que los huesos fosiles que se encuentran en aquella comarca, no eran humanos, sino de animales, cuyas especies habian desaparecido ya de la superficie del globo. An eighteenth century colonial official, looking at the bones the story was hung on, called them animal.
rungs.evidence: https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra-visor/historia-general-de-la-republica-del-ecuador-tomo-quinto--0/html/0016c7de-82b2-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_23.html, fetched twice. Both fetches returned the same Spanish sentence about the huesos fosiles and the same chapter heading naming the president as Jose Garcia de Leon y Pizarro; the first also returned the preceding sentence, Visito personalmente todo el territorio de Santa Elena, reconocio y mando examinar la mina de brea. Authorship confirmed at https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra/historia-general-de-la-republica-del-ecuador-tomo-cuarto--0/ and the sibling volume records, which give the work as escrita por Federico Gonzalez Suarez; the span of seven volumes between 1890 and 1903 from https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Gonz%C3%A1lez_Su%C3%A1rez.
rungs.note: The two fetches of this page reported different page numbers, 271 and 308, so I have not cited a page. The catalogue entry's spelling of the official's first name as Jose is borne out by this chapter heading.

rungs.witness: Clements R. Markham, translator and editor, The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de Leon, A.D. 1532 to 50, Contained in the First Part of his Chronicle of Peru, London, Hakluyt Society, 1864, chapter LII
rungs.reads: This is the route by which Cieza's chapter reached English readers. Its chapter heading calls the subject the wells at the point of Santa Elena, the story they tell respecting the arrival of giants in those parts, and the tar which is found there. That heading is itself evidence about the claim's standing: the translator's title marks the giants as a story told, not as a report. On the fire this rung is silent, because the chapter body was not readable through any route open to me.
rungs.evidence: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/48770/48770-h/48770-h.htm and https://www.gutenberg.org/files/48770/48770-0.txt and https://archive.org/stream/travelsofpedrode33ciez/travelsofpedrode33ciez_djvu.txt. All three returned the title page details (Markham, Hakluyt Society, M.DCCC.LXIV) and the contents entry for chapter LII in the wording given above. Asked directly to transcribe the chapter body, the fetch of both Gutenberg files answered BODY NOT VISIBLE and named chapter LI as the last chapter whose text it could see; the Internet Archive text truncated earlier still, inside Markham's introduction. The Cambridge University Press reissue lists the same chapter under the same title at https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/travels-of-pedro-de-cieza-de-leon-ad-153250/of-the-wells-which-there-are-at-the-point-of-santa-elena-of-the-story-they-tell-respecting-the-arrival-of-giants-in-those-parts-and-of-the-tar-which-is-found-there/9F4F2D2FE1D39DFFAAE358C669AEF4AB, though that page itself returned a 403 when fetched.
rungs.note: Included for what it fixes, the existence and framing of the chapter in an 1864 printing, and not for more. It is a translation of rung one, not an independent witness to the event.

rungs.witness: Pedro Cieza de Leon, Parte primera dela chronica del Peru, Seville, Martin de Montesdoca, 1553, chapter LII, folios 65v to 66v
rungs.date: Printed at Seville in 1553. This is a printed book of that year and copies of the printing survive, but the wording used here was read in a modern scholar's transcription of it rather than in a facsimile of the folios.
rungs.reads: It carries the claim, and it carries more than the claim. The destruction sentence is introduced with the word dizen, they say, and the fire is not free standing: it falls on the giants while they are, in Cieza's words, wrapped up in their cursed sodomy. The transcription reads: dizen, que estando todos juntos embueltos en su maldita sodomia, vino fuego del cielo temeroso y muy espantable, haziendo gran ruydo: del medio del qual salio vn angel resplandesciente con una espada tajante y muy refulgente, con la qual de un solo golpe los mato a todos, y el fuego los consumio. So the fire from heaven is there in 1553, but it arrives already fitted with a shining angel, a cutting sword, a single blow, and a sin out of Genesis.
rungs.evidence: Read twice, through two different hosts of the same article, to check the transcription against itself. https://www.redalyc.org/pdf/3210/321081234012.pdf and https://proa.ua.pt/index.php/agora/article/download/27979/20086 (Ignacio Uribe M., Pedro Cieza de Leon, los gigantes y Mercurio). Both returned the same Spanish string letter for letter and both attached the same reference, CIEZA (1553) 65v to 66v, chapter LII. Uribe's bibliography entry is CIEZA DE LEON, P. (1553), Parte primera dela chronica del Peru. Sevilla, Martin de Montesdoca. The same imprint appears independently in the bibliography of Hechler and Zurita-Altamirano at https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/9052563.pdf, which prints Cieza de Leon, P. de. 1553, Parte primera dela chronica del Peru. Martin de Montesdoca, Sevilla.
rungs.note: I could not open a facsimile of folios 65v to 66v this session, so the folio numbers and the spelling rest on Uribe's citation, not on my own sight of the leaf.

chain.floor: The 1553 chronicle is where the fire from heaven is documented, and it does not present it as something seen. The destruction sentence opens with dizen, they say, and the fire falls specifically on the giants' sodomy, arriving in the same breath as a shining angel and a sword that kills them all at one blow. Nothing in what survives puts a witness near the event, and the bones that kept the story alive on the peninsula were being described as animal, not human, by the 1780s.

handling.living: The Huancavilca/Manta cultural sphere that reportedly told this story to Cieza de León no longer exists as a distinct living ethnic or linguistic community; the Huancavilca language is extinct and the coastal Santa Elena peninsula is now largely mestizo Ecuadorian, with no continuing indigenous nation asserting custodial ownership of this specific narrative the way, for example, Paiute or Sámi communities do for theirs. The wells attributed to the giants are a real, visitable archaeological feature, and the story persists mainly as regional heritage and chronicle material rather than active belief.
handling.distortions: The most common distortion is treating Cieza de León's full account, including its climactic angel-with-a-sword-of-fire ending, as untouched indigenous tradition, when scholarship (Uribe, Hechler) identifies that ending as Cieza's own Christian interpretive framing layered onto what he was told. A second distortion, shared with the Quinametzin entry, is pseudo-archaeological treatment of the giant bones as literal proof of a giant race, when the region's fossil record of Pleistocene megafauna gives a well-understood physical source for outsized bones and molars found on the peninsula.
handling.take: The narrative core, the reed-raft arrival, the wells dug into rock, the raiding and cannibalism accusation, and the tie to real fossil and well remains, is usable chronicle material and not the property of an identifiable living community, but a writer should flag the sword-of-fire ending explicitly as Cieza's own Christian gloss rather than presenting the whole account as a transparent record of what coastal Ecuadorian informants said in the 1540s. Avoid stating flatly that this is 'Manta belief' without that caveat, and avoid folding it into modern lost-race pseudoarchaeology.
handling.cite: Cite Pedro Cieza de León, Crónica del Perú (1553), chapter LII, as the primary source, with Garcilaso de la Vega's Comentarios Reales de los Incas (1609) and Antonio de Herrera's Décadas (1601-15) for the elaborated later versions, and modern scholarship on Ecuadorian mastodon-remains interpretation for the physical context.

mapinguari.fullDescription: One eye. And a mouth that opens vertically, from the nose down to the stomach.
mapinguari.mysteryNote: Around sixty people told the ornithologist they had seen it. Twenty years of looking produced no animal, and no end to the accounts.
mapinguari.fate: Not killed: said to be stopped only by a blow to the head, and better avoided from up a tree.

sections.story:
A great simian humanoid with long arms and heavy claws. Its hide is described as thick as a turtle's shell or an alligator's back, which is the usual explanation for why arrows and bullets are said not to enter it. Black fur in some accounts, red in most. In some regions its feet point backwards, a trait borrowed from the Curupira.

The mouth runs vertically from the nose to the stomach and is set with thousands of teeth. The single eye sits in the centre of the face.

It is also, unusually for a creature of folklore, awake in the daytime. It moves through the forest by day and rests at night in caves and hollow trunks. It is said to be able to make a person dizzy enough that the day appears to turn to night.

Domingos Parintintin, a chief of an Amazonian people, gave the practical advice: the only way to kill one is a blow to the head, and the better plan is to climb a tree and stay quiet.

Some accounts hold that a Mapinguari is what an indigenous elder eventually becomes, which it shares with the Capelobo tradition. It has also absorbed traits from other Brazilian figures it displaced in various regions, among them the Gorjala and the Pé de Garrafa.
sections.origins:
The Mapinguari is Amazonian oral tradition rather than a text. It is attested in the forests of Pará, Amazonas and Acre into the twentieth century, and is known to the Karitiana people of Brazil under other names, among them Kida harara.

Luís da Câmara Cascudo (1898 to 1986) is the collector who fixed it in print. It has an entry in his Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro, first published in 1954, and in Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros, first published in 1947 and reissued in 1976. Cascudo derived the name from Tupi-Guarani, roughly the thing with a crooked or backward-turned foot, and treated the figure as a composite of older Brazilian creatures.

The twentieth-century record is largely interview material. David Oren of the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi collected accounts in the Tapajós basin between the 1970s and the 1990s and published his case in 1993 and again in 2001. Transmission remains oral: hunters, rubber tappers and river communities.
sections.disputed:
This is one of the few entries in the catalogue where somebody went looking.

David Oren, an American ornithologist and former research director at the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi in Belém, spent over twenty years on it. Around a hundred people told him they had encountered the animal or heard its cry. Around sixty said they had seen it. No expedition produced one.

Oren's hypothesis, anticipated in the nineteenth century by the Argentine palaeontologist Florentino Ameghino, is that the Mapinguari preserves a memory of the ground sloths. Megatherium and Eremotherium reached six metres and were still in South America ten to twelve thousand years ago, which overlaps with the first human population of the continent.

Ameghino built the idea partly on a report from the explorer Ramón Lista, who said that while hunting in Patagonia in the 1890s he met a large unknown animal and that his bullets had no effect on it. Ameghino tied that to indigenous Patagonian descriptions of an animal whose hide arrows could barely pierce.

Whether any of this is the origin of the Mapinguari or a later scientific story laid over an older one is unresolved, and the entry does not resolve it.

handling.living: The Mapinguari is a living oral tradition among multiple Amazonian peoples and rural forest communities across Pará, Amazonas and Acre, including the Karitiana (who have their own names for a related being, such as Kida harara) and communities visited by Domingos Parintintin's people; it is also actively told among non-Indigenous rubber tappers and river dwellers (caboclos, seringueiros) as regional folklore. It is not tied to a single named religious institution or governing body the way some Indigenous sacred traditions are, but it remains a currently-told belief with recent testimony (Oren's fieldwork ran into the 1990s), not a dead literary relic, so a writer should treat the living communities who tell it with the same care given to any active oral tradition rather than assuming it is fully public folklore.
handling.distortions: Cryptid media tends to strip the Mapinguari of its cultural context entirely and reprocess it as a generic 'Bigfoot of the Amazon' or a straightforward lost-megafauna reveal, presenting Oren's ground-sloth hypothesis as a confirmed answer rather than one unresolved scientific speculation laid over a folk tradition. Retellings also commonly merge it wholesale with unrelated Brazilian figures like the Curupira (backward feet) or Capelobo without noting that the figure is itself already a regional composite that displaced older local beings like the Gorjala and Pé de Garrafa, obscuring which traits are old and which are borrowed.
handling.take: The physical description (the hide, the vertical mouth, the single eye, day-active habits, the cave-dwelling) and the general folkloric shape are documented in print via Cascudo and Oren and are reasonably safe to use as a folklore figure, not a real cryptid claim. Be careful not to present it as a settled scientific fact that this is 'really' a surviving ground sloth, since that is Oren's and Ameghino's hypothesis, not established science, and avoid attributing the tradition to 'Amazonian Indians' generically; name the actual peoples where you can (Karitiana, Parintintin, and mixed forest communities) rather than treating it as one undifferentiated 'Amazon legend.' Do not invent named specific rituals or community-restricted details beyond what Cascudo and Oren recorded.
handling.cite: Credit Luís da Câmara Cascudo's Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro and Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros for the print synthesis, and David Oren (Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi, 1993/2001) for the fieldwork and the ground-sloth hypothesis, noting Florentino Ameghino and Ramón Lista as the 19th-century precedent for that idea.

humbaba.fullDescription: Huwawa in Sumerian, Humbaba in Akkadian, with the oldest recorded form attested at Mari and Tell Harmal. The origin and meaning of the name are unknown, which is itself a measure of how far back this goes.
humbaba.mysteryNote: Mercy was offered once. The sack was heavier than the trees.
humbaba.fate: Beheaded after asking for mercy. Enlil was not pleased.

sections.story:
Enlil set him over the Cedar Forest, the dwelling of the gods, and made him a terror to human beings so that no one would enter it. He did the job. His hearing covered the whole forest, so that nothing moved in it without his knowing. His look was described as death, his roar as a flood, his breath as fire.

His face was drawn as a single continuous coiling line, like the coiled entrails of an animal, and Mesopotamian diviners read omens from exactly such coils. Clay heads of him have been found, made to be hung up for protection. The face that frightened people was also used to keep worse things away.
